The winner of the, Queen't?.. Prize, Mr. M.S.Rennie, would afford a study in heredity. None of his rela- tions have shown tastes in any sporting depart- ment. He comes of ancestors that have furnished the Church with ,preachers.. His grandfather on the mother's side was the.Rev:James Stark,of Wellpark Free Church., Greenock, one of the youngest minis- ters that came outof the Disruption. Mr. Rennie's father was a studious,,quiet,retiring man, who was for many years a preacher in Maryhill, where the winner of th-e sQueen's.Prize was born, and not at Glasgow, as has been stated. He has a brother practising as a doctor at Coatbridge, and another a lawyer in Glasgow. Mr.. Rennie is the youngest of the three. He had an uncle, a brother of his mo- ther,who won great distinction at Glasgow Univer- sity. In addition to carrying off numerous prizes in his classes he gained the silver medal for the best essay in the department of .mental philosophy, the subject being "Nominalism and Realism." The Starks originally came from Germany to the Grangemouth district, and migrated westward to Dumbartonshire.

Lord Rothschild has-beea trying the experimemt of breaking zebras to harness, lie owns three, now in the hands of a trainer in South Kensington. Much difficulty was experienced with the animals at first, but they were " educated " by being har- nessed with a quiet pony one at a time. On Wednesday morning one zebra alone was driven in a light dogcart through the streets, and he trotted past a steam roller without wincing.

Liberals have been quick to seize upon the re- markable tributes paid by Mr. Chamberlain to the Government and Parliament in respect of theirH great legislative achievements. The I,4'ational Liberal Federation is at once preparing a lac-simile of a recent and mach-hawked Tory kquib. -The jest conisted in entitling a number of blank papers "What Liberals have done." The Liberal edition of this publication.gives, under the same heading, Mr. Chamberlain's glowing vindication of the un- paralleled results accomplished by the present Parliament.

It is not generally.known: that Sir E. Grey, the Under-secretary for Foreign Affairs, does not speak French. Until recently it has been thought that an indispensable quahficatiou for the iForeign Office was a knowledge of French, but Sir E. Grey has proved that a man may be a very successful under- :Secretary and 3 et not know the language of diplom- acy. Almost all his predecessors spoke French well. lir. J. W. Lowther was a.first-rate linguist, and Sir J. Fergussou could talk French well enough to converse with visitors at the Foreign Office who did not know English.. 'the . previous Liberal Under-Secretaries at the Foreign Office—Alr. Bryce, Lord E. Fitztnaurice and Sir Charles Dilke—were all first-rate French scholars, and the last two, indeed, can :speak the language-as well as.they do English.

There are many distinctions open to a man—the Premiership, the proprietorship of a splendid race- horse, an earldom, and so on. But there is yet another awaiting Lord Rosebery. He has been more than twenty years Honorary Colonel of the Eighth (Linlithgow) Volunteer .Battalion of the Royal Scots, and has, I believe, been recommended for the Volunteer 01ficers' decoration.

An American journalist, Mr. .Stanley Waterloo, broke the record lately in writing a book. A Chi- cago publisher sent for Mr. Waterloo, and asked him whether he could have a book on the Coxey movement ready for the press in four days. Mr. Waterloo, being a well-equipped writer, full of resource and knowing not the word " said he could. This was on a Monday morning. The pub- lisher said " Go ahead,".and gave him.carte blanche as to expenses staff or writers was organised, specialists were engaged for the historical part of the work, photographers took thefield, typewriters clicked day and night., and Mr. Waterlqo hardly ate or slept. Tie result, was that on-Thursday night the copy }or a book of over one hundred thousand words, with forty illustrations, wain the hands of the printers. -

Most of the English journalists.who.attended the International Press Congress have now returned to • England.As a gen,tral rule.their fundawere•exhausted They have been received on the. Continent with a profuse hospitality that will seem incredible .when the story is told in our own.rightlittle tight little island. The truth is, however, that no 'hospitality can make up for the inborn rapacity of .the'Con- , tinent al hotel-keeper. The Englishman in particu- lar is regarded a heaven-sent "victim .At an hotel in Ostend on Saturday an attempt was made to obtain thirteen francs for two-thirds of a bottle of • whisky. This demand was preceded by a bill for one fri:ne fcr a little water from a syphon and two francs for a bottle of pale ale. soap costs a franc a day. At Antwerp they placed a Union Jack .out- side the bedroom window of one of our pressmen, but they charged ten francs a night for the TOG.M,. which is just double what they are able to get in the tn•nal run of things. Antwerp is trying to boom itself in a very decided manner just .now., but the hotel-keepers are making a successful boom altogether impossible.

"The Press, from various points of Tie,w, have criticised Lord Rosebery's refusal on the part .of Her Majesty's Ministers to -dine with the Lord Mayor; but it is a pity that the correspondence 'be- t ween the Prime Minister and the Chief Magistrate was not printed, as it would at once have silenced those critics who saw in the reply only an inten- tion to insult the City. So tar from that being the a.e Lord fiosebery looked forward to the civic festival of November next to meet the citizens., and attributed entirely to the pressure of public business and to the constant sitting,: of Parliament, the reluctance of Ministers to:attend an earlier itian- quet." And this is from the -staunch Tory journal, the "

111 r. Justice Dames, who is, thinks " Casseli's Sat- urday Journal:' probably the best Admiralty judge we have ever had, feels very eaueli out of hiscle- inent when, by rotation, he has to hear cases in the Divorce Court. Indeed, he has .more than (Aloe dropped the unofficial remark that he regards that court as a social liogetve. whereas the Admiralty Bench is as plea.,ant to him as a trip to the seaside. His lordship has always been as•sociated with mari- time matters, in early life being km,ployed in the (axe of a Liverpool firm of solicitors. His great love of nautical concerns suggested that he should read for the Bar and make a speciality of Admiralty practice.

Though NI t .Labouchere has put down for an"early day " his resolution for the mending of the House of Lords, he does not propose to move it till next session, lie will then persistently prose it forward having, upon counting heads, assured himself of a majority in its support.

Mr. Stanley Leighton has blocked Mr. George Russell's motion for returns showing the income and grants of the Ecclesiastical Commissioners, and the revenues of the Church of England hi Wales and Monmouthshire. The effect of this will probably be that these important particulars will ri,lt be forthcoming for the information of the House when, early next cession, it is called upon to dezide ni.on the question of the dUestablishment of the Chruch in Wales.

It is ialt often that the House of Commons enjoys .the sensation ot one of its members fainting, or nearly fainting, whilc addressing it, but it had that sensation en Tuesday night. Mr. Cohen, who is the Conservative member for East Islington, ccm- pkttely collapsed while be was supporting the .eq.ualisation ot Rates Bill for London. l'erlipps the excitement of breaking away from his party had affe.oted his heart or his nerves. It would have been a bokl thing to do under ordinary circum- stances.; but in the present state of affairs he had not. the terror of his constituents before his eyes, as they are also in favour of the measure, They would get £21,000 under it, so eflll afford to view, it with unqualified delight. 111 r. Bartley another Islington member, took quite the opposite tack, and broke away from his constituents to support his party. Mr. Bartley acknowledged that he expet teel to be taken to task for this whenever he presented him- self on an Islington plat form, but still his con- science c4mp.Bed him to be fair. He was not, how- ever, trouble with any collapse of his nerves. Mr. Cohen was. not able to complete his speeeb, and was attended to in the House by Sir W. Poster.

MY DRAREST NELLIE,

It is no longer fashionable, and it was never desirable, for growing girls to wear their skirts very short. Toe orthodox length, when the wearer is between 8 and 12, reaches about five Inches below the knees, and when a girl has entered upon her trens, the length is increased by gradual degrees. There are mothers who put their grow- ing daughters into tight, boned curets with the idea of training their figures to the orthodox fashionable dimensions ; hut. es a rule, a broader view is taken of the rights of every human being to opportanities for its own development. Even from the ordinary fathionabie mottier's own point of view, any prfssure exerthsed upon the frame is a mistake, teutilog to faults of carriage that are inimical to grace of baring and in walking. Another reprehensible practi,rs is that of forcing girls to wear tight, short boots in the endeavour to keep their feet from growing large. The suffering that this involves is almost greater than that induced by tight-lacing. An idealised serge coat and skirt for a girl aged from 10 to 15 looks extremely well made in one of the new blue serges with the monster collar of cream-coloured batiste, the inner skirt of blue silk, the belt round tho waist also of blue, and the collar round the throat turned down.

A becoming costume which has come under my notice combines the charms of the slightly-draped skirt with the superior appearance of the partially - banned bodice. The material of which this gown is composed is the most delicate shade of French grey faced °loch. A charm- ing promenade costume shows the gown in orepon cloth with antique blue and pinkish silk.

Miss Eugenia Viale' who obtained the degree of Ph. D. at Genoa last year, has now obtained a doctor's degree in Belleslettres. The loveliest girl of Irish birth is Miss Daisy Tanner, niece of Dr. Tanner, M.P., says " Pearson's Weekly." Iler portrait was chosen for exhibition at Chicago last year. At the close of Buffalo Bill's season in Brooklyn, Miss Annie Oakley, the little rifle shot, will come to England with an American company of her own to appear in two frontier plays as a " star.' Most of her time will be spent in the provinces. This is what the Reverend Stopford Brooke says : " Many women in the present day seem to look with a certain contempt on sentiment, on imagination, on beauty and art,on the affectionseon the high passions of the ideal or of the religious life. It is a fatal pride, and a folly for which they will sorely suffer." An English woman physician, Dr. Anderson Brown, has established an industrial farm for inebriate women, an experiment that will be watched with interest by all students of social econotnics,as well as the world of law and order. The test is to be made under the auspices of the Women's Temperance Association, and one of its chief features is to be the number of outdoor occupa- tions to be provided. The recent distinguished foreign visitors to Windsor were greatly struck by the magnificence of the royal plate at the Castle. Even the Czarevitch, accustomed to the almost barbaric splendour of the Court functions in his native land,was fain to admit that for solid worth he had never seen the equal of the English plate. When the Crown Prince of Denmark attended an examination in a Copenhagen school the other day, he noticed that one of the little girls was so confused that she could not recite her lesson. He therefore took her on his lap, after which she answered every question cor- rectly, and naively explained later: Why, the Crown Prince whispered all the answers to me." The Queen has made, says "Woman "quite a number of articles for the forthcoming bazaar at Balmoral, con- sisting of three-cornered woollen shawls of the correct " Grandma " pattern, made of the real Scotch " finger- ing " wool, of which Her Majesty buys large quantities at the Crathie shop. The Empress Frederick and Prin- cess Louise contribute a collection of their own sketches I which are tolerably certain to realise handsome sums. Lady Mildred Jessup, a younger daughter of Lord and Lady Strathmore, is described by the " Allahabati Morning Post," as the latest wonder of the world. She is the first woman on record who has written a successful opera. The measure of the success which Lady Mildred has secured may be gauged when it is borne in mind that the work was presented anonymously to the fasti- dious musical public of Florence, and that on the very first night it excited enthusiastic approval. The name of the compeser was not disclosed until the second night, when Lady Mildred", who is oniy little more than twenty-five years of age, and has been married four years, came before the curtain to bow her acknowledg- ments. "One hardly expects to find an Arctic explorer— particularly of the weaker sex—in the precincts of Mayfair, and it was with more than the usual trepida- tion of the conventional interviewer that I timidly pre- sented my card at the old-fashioned house of Sir Robert Peel in Stratton-street," says Mr. J. M. Price in the " Sketch." "It was difficult to believe that the charming girl before me was one of the first ladies to travel away to Siberia by way of the Kara Sea, and to return with material for a book so cleverly written as Polar Gleams.' I always had a great taste for travel and adventure,' she told me, though the idea of this particular voyage was ereatly created by the perusal sf your book, "From 1 the Arctic Ocean to the Yellow Sea,"' she added with a smile. 'I always wanted to go to Siberia,' she con- tinued, and, as luck would have it, I found myself invited to go to Siberia by Mr. Leybourne Popham, on his yacht, the Blencathra. I had never been on a sea vo-, age before, except across the Channel, in which short trips I always succeeded in getting very ill. I must confess that the journey to the North Sea tried my determination very much, as I was very ill, and often wished myself back again shopping in Piccadilly." A Pretty Dress For a Child. Nowadays children's dress is so prettily fashioned that even the plainest child can be made to look picturesque. The loose smock with its artistic folds is never likely to lose favour, but now and again mothers are glad to welcome a slight change from this mode. A pretty dress is of cream crepon, and is made with a yoke or lace over cteam silk and with lace frills falling over the shoulders. The dress is smocked from beneath the yoke to the waist line,and ribbons of cream satin coming from rosettes are crossed over in front and fasten behind in another rosette. Another charm- ing frock for a child is of white book muslin made Empire fashion over a coloured sateen or silk slip. The round silk ye;ll,-, is covered with four gathered puffs of muelin ending in a muslin frill edged with lace, and an important look- ing hies of white silk placed near the left shoulder falls in long ends to the hem of the skirt.

The charwoman good by the vicarage back door. The early morning sun lighted up her round, red face, her ample smile, and her big soap suddy arms. Just out- side, on the uneven stone slabs, stood the village sweep. He was a small bent man, with the blackest of faces. Weak blue eyes, with pink rims, blinking up at the massive scrubber, gave him an almost impish look. " Well, Mr. Larkins, what I says is this, you wants a wife to look arter yer." The little man fumbled nervously with the soot-bag string. "Er ?" • " A wife, Mr. Larkins," in louder tones, hut with a backward glance at the kitchen, where the servants were spring cleaning. "Yes, that's it, without no doubts. A good strop, woman, who ain't afraid of turning a penny herself', at . . . we'll saw charing three days, and who'ud turn yer out a nice dinner, and rub yer legs when then varieg,ated veins is had, and who'ud . . ." The little sweep wriggled a few steps from the door. " I'm a soli- tary man, ye knows,but I likes me quiet life—" " Ah ! but it ain't good for yer, d'ye see ? And if 1 says it's a wholesome, pleasing life, I'd be a story-telling woman ! Now, Mr. Larkins, you wants more than your own sect to deal with! A woman, I say, 'ud be the making of you !" She stuck her elbows offit, and nodded triumph- antly. "Er ?'' this very meekly. The charwoman stepped on to the crisp gravel. " Mr. Larkins," she said solemnly, " they says down street as I've got a temper, I've heerd 'em. But they's tellin' falsehoods, every one ! If, times, Ido sneak sharp,l'm crosser more than me temper is ! I tells yer truthful. Mr. Larkins, though I sez it as shouldn't, that I'm a hard-working,. agreeable woman. I make no 'owil'ye-do over tellin' you ! Como now, Mr. Larkins--." This genial invi- tation was responded to by a mournful—" E ---r ?" But the rubicund charwoman was unabashed. "No girls , would look at yer (not but what you've- exlent pints. Mr. Larkins), but young women can't (Ispeose with features ! I says, 'and-some is as 'andsome does ! Eli ?" "Er ?" very gloomily. " Well, come now, then," she went on, with some impatience, laying her damp, wrinkled fingers; and the scrubbing brush,with affection- ate force on his shoulder, " don't yer think as I'm the very person yer want ? Lor' there, I knows yer do, but you've bin a bit too shy to say it! be your wife,Mr. Larkins—not but what I couldn't better myself any day —but I've took a fancy to ver, there's truth I We'll. keep company, eh ?" "Er." ." Then that's all settled. We'll be married four Sundays from next. We iiriust have the banns called, proper, and all. But come now,l mustn't stand a-wasting my thne like this. Just give us a hand with the soft-soap tin before yer goes, will yer, Bill !•'—" Atalanta."

div.head: THEY TOLD JAMES SPIIFFARD SO.
div.p: THEY TOLD JAMES SPIIFFARD SO.

Certain people told James Spuffard that from nineteen to twenty-one was a trying time. He says they told him so, just as he was about that age himself. What did they mean by it? Probably they had noticed some things that others don't notice. There are folks who see with their eyes, and folks who, having eyes, see nothing ; which proves that there is no real sight without intelligence. Spread this thought out and apply it, and you will pet ceive how big a thought it is. Not new? Oh, dear, no. Old as the hills.

First, though, let us have a sentence out of a letter written by Mr. Spuffard, dated September 3rd 1892. He says," When I sat down it seemed as if I should go through the bottom of the chair." What ailed him ? Surely not great weight ? Not a bit. It was great weakness. He felt collapsed ;as if there were no bones or muscles left in his body. He could'nt bear himself, he sank in a heap. This was after a days' work to be sure, yet nobody has any business to work so hard, as to knock the life out of him that iaah- ion. Nor did he. I happened differently. "It was early in May, 1887," he says, "that some- thing came over me; I couldn't make out what." Before that he had always been all right; strong and healthy. All of a sudden he lost his appetite, as he might have lost his watch or his purse. He wanted nothing to eat ; he had no relish to meet it with. When, for nature's sake, he forced down some simple food, it revenged itself on him immediately. It pinched his chest and sides and gave him a feeling of gnawing in the stomach, as if bread and meat had turned into rats to devour the flesh they are meant to sustain. Even milk and such things acted the same. Something serious was the matter with the machinery down there in the dark.

"My hands and feet," he goes on to say, "were cold and clammy, and at times I had sweats that made me feel so bad I could scarcely stanl It was as much as I could do to keep at my work, and when I got home I was so exhausted that, on sitting down, it seemed as if I should go through the bottom of the chair. Later on I got so bad I couldn't stand at my work. I was nine- teen years old, and people said that from nineteen to twenty-one was a trying time. My friends thought it would go hard with me; and I grew weaker, and became very anxious as to my fate. "In April, 18138, I first heard of Mother Seigel's Cura- tive Syrup, and, as all the remedies I had used had failed to ease me, I concluded to try it. I procured a bottle from Mr. Griffiths, chemist, at Slough, and after a few doses I felt a little relief. "The following Sunday, after morning service at

Farnham Chapel, our minister, Rev. H. Stone, said to me, ' What is the matter with you, James? How ill you look.' I told him I had been much worse, but had just begun with Seigel's Syrup. He replied, Seigel's Syrup is a good thing. I know many who have been

benefited by it.' "When I had taken one bottle all pain left me, my appetite improved, and my food gave me strength. By the time I had taken three bottles I was completely cured. I have since enjoyed the best of health, can eat anything and do any kind of work. If young people from seventeen to twenty.one would only take Seigel's Syrup, it is my opinion that thousands would be saved. (Signed) JAMES SPUFFARD, Florence Cottage, Farnham Common, Slough, near Windsor, September 3rd, 1892." Mr. Spuffard is a builder, carpenter, and plumber,and is well known and respected in the district where he lives. The people who tcld him that youth is a trying time were quite right. It is from young men and women that diseases reap their awful harvests ; the most common and dangerous of all being that from which he suffered, indigestion and dyspepsia, and its symptoms in the liver, kidneys, blood, lungs, and heart. We hope the young people who read his letter will remember the last line.

div.head: FIGHTING A RHINOCEROS.
div.p: FIGHTING A RHINOCEROS.
BY PERCY SELOUS.

" When we reached the spot where the rhineceros had drunk during the night, I had to sit down and rest myself so unfit was I," says Mr. Percy Selous in the " Newbery House Magazine." " The bush became now less dense, and emerging from a patch of thorns I saw him standing by some sugar thorns. His head was almost directly facing rue and I was down along flat in an instant. Not thgt I was afraid he would see me. He was distant about one hundred and fifty yards, aud evidently had not the slightest idea of my propinquity. As he stood, irrespective of distance, a shot would have been worse than useless; so, as with what little wind there was, was from him, I set about working round into a more favourable positioa. To do this I should have a good deal of crawling to do, the ground being patchy, but the herbage was rank and afforded some cover. "Squirming along, I gradually worked my way from bush to bush till I was about forty yards from him. He offered me now a fair broadside, and fearing I might alarm him if I ventured to try and get nearer, and p )3- sibly lose a chance of meat alter all, for there is practic- ally no limit to the distance a slightly wounded rhinoceros will go without stopping, I took careful aim at the back of his shoulder high up and fired. I fear the language I used would not have passed muster in select society, for, shaky and weak as I was, the recoil of the heavy piece, as it sent me sprawling, gave me the most excruciating pain. The rhinoceros gave a snort and a luse;11, bat, quickly recovering himst-.4, made off at what would have been a tremendous pace if he had only gone straight forward. Instead of this he dashed first to the right then to the left and then to the right again, sins:Thing everything before him like matchwaod, and in a way which at any other time would have been laughable. " These eccentric vagaries as suddenly ceased as they had commenced, and he came to a standstill, snorting violently and squirting out blood like a harpooned wha!re I had mechanically reloaded, without taking my eyes off the rhinoceros, as I lay where my rifle had so uncere- moniously deposited me, and as he now stood he was not a great deal further off than when I first fired ; he , had, however, worked round a little and had thus a slight advantage as to the wind, which be was not slow of utilising. Anyway, he thought he heard or smelt, as well as felt, something unusual, and certainly located me to a tftety. I was quite as touch on the quivive as he, though, and rolling over a time or two just avoided being pounded to mincemeat as thundered over the spot I had occupied the moment before. Thwarted in his revenge after smashing right into a thorn tree, he came again to a staud, but evidently nearly spent and labour- ing heavily. I think he would not have rsquired an- other ball and that he was really dying, but I gave him another shot,and over he went like a log. "1 felt relieved when 1 saw he was done, for I was al- most used up myself, even with such teifling exer don as I had had. On examination, I found that there was a old bullet-wound completely traversing the fleshy part of the neck between the poll and the withers, showine that it was net the first time he had encountered man, Arid no doubt in some psrt accounting for his My own first bullet had hit him exactly where I had wanted it to de, and had gone through both lungs. My second one had caught him so nearly in the same place as to give the wound the appearance of the figure eight, but as I was more in rear of him it had gone forward into the cervical vertebra."

div.head: HUMOUR. OF DICKENS.
div.p: HUMOUR. OF DICKENS.

Wonderful as are the riches of the various specific worlds which Dickens ransacked for his creations, there ' is nothing in him, says Richard Holt Hutton, in " Criti- cisms on Contemporary Thought," as the most realistic and picturesque of describers, to equal his humour. The wealth and subtlety of his contrasts, the fine aim ot his exatzgerations, the prese flee of mind (which is the soul of wit) displayed in his satire, the exquisitely pro- fessional character of the sentiments and metaphors which fall from his characters, the combined audacity and microscopic (It heavy of his shading in caricature, the quaint flights of his fancy in illustrating a monstr- ous ab,urdity, the suddenness of his strokes at one moment, the cumulative perseverance of his toriche3 at ant‘ther, all Make him such a Immourist as milady cen- turh-S.are mit likely t.) reproduce. But then humour of this kind k not necessarily connected with any deep know ledge f the heart and mind of matt, and of such a knowledge I can see lit le trace in Dickens. De had a memory whit.h could retain, and an imagination which could sublimate, and a fancy which could indefinitely vary almost any trait which had once fixed itself in his mind ; hat the traits which did so lix themselves saer,! almost always peculiarities, and his human figures are only real tyi far as they reproduce the real oddities of I life, or what to a man in Di( k-ns's rank and class seemed !ral oddities ; and of course, while there are many teal oddities in the world, th,se are not the staple of our I average lie—with which, indeed,Diciccus's genius never I dealt either willingly or successfully.

div.head: Ois, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.
div.p: Ois, THE HAMPTON MYSTERY.
By the Author of " Daliwoop."
CHAPTER XXIII. LORD ADLONVE RECEIVES A SHOCK I feel my sinews slackened with the fright, And a cold sweat thrills down o'er all my limbs, As if I were dissolving into water.

DRYDEN. A day or two subsequent to her return from Lon- don Giralda sat in the great bay-window of her pleasant chamber at Trevelyan Park, busy with a letter to her mother. It was to be sent to the as- sumed address given her by the Lady Beatrice, and the young girl was puzzling herself to chronicle her very meagre news in such a manner that no one save her mother would understand it should the

letter fall into hostile hands. "Dear, dear I" she sighed at last. "I have BO little to tell I I'm afraid that these small details of my daily life will look so small to mamma. I have nothing to report about the great task I have undertaken—nothing whatever." The loud rumbling of wheels on the gravelled avenue below caught her attention, and she looked out, beholding a waggon, laden with trunks and boxes, approaching the mansion. Putting down her writing-case, Giralda crossed the floor several times, absorbed in anxious musings. In the Midst of them she was aroused by a knock on the door, and the entrance of her little maid, followed by a couple of stout servitors, each bear- ing a heavy trunk which he deposited in the cen- tre of the room, then beating a hasty retreat. "If you please Miss," said the little maid, "here is a note from his lordship." The surprised young mistress took the missive, and hastily perused it. It simply informed her that the accompanying trunks, with their con- tents, were a present from his lordship to his

adopt scl niece. "They are unstrapped, Miss and here are the keys," said the maid. "Shall I help you unpack them, Miss?" Giralda assented, and the process of unpacking was hastily commenced. The trunks were found to contain a young lady's complete wardrobe including a riding habit and hat. There were also in abundance, and unmade, fine linen and cambrics, silks of various hues, and of the best quality, besides a box of gloves, and an elegant dressing-case, completely furnished, its fittings of silver-gilt. Giralda spread out her new possessions with a pleasant sense of proprietorship, delighted with the fine fabrics and soft hues. At this juncture the servitor again appeared, this time bringing a small Russia leather trunk. Giralda recognised it at once as her own property. The man set it down heavily, and proceeded to un- strap it, saying, apologetically "This trunk was not ordered by my lord, and was not discovered until the boxes of house furni- ture were looked over. There is no key, Miss. Shall we open it with a chisel?" "No ; I have a key to it," said Giralda. "You may go. And you too, Dolly," she added. • " will open this trunk myself." The man withdrew, followed by the little maid. Giralda hastened to lock the door, and then pre- pared to unpack the trunk with an interest the others had failed to elicit. "From home 1" she murmured, fitting one of the keys on the steel ring she had inadvertently brought from The Evergreens in her pocket. "Mamma has been home, then, since she saw me 1 Have they sent me any messages—any letters ?" She lifted the lid eagerly. In the deep trays were boxes containing collars, cuffs, and similar eleganeies, besides her own small writing-case, filled with writing materials, and her pretty mother-of-pearl work-box, with its dainty belong- ings. The upper part of the trunk was filled with under-clothing, the lower part with dresses, and at the bottom of all was a little packet of letters, 'which Giralda pounced upon with a cry ef joy. There was a letter from the Lady Beatrice, and one from Giralda's father. These were read first. Both were tender, confidential missives, contain- ing not a word of reproach, but breathing a world of faith and hope in the maiden's success in the task she had undertaken. The count's letter gave a full and truthful account of the event that had disgraced Geoffrey Treveiyen, and expressed. in conclusion the belief that it was through Giraida that the maligned heir of the marquis would finally be restored to his rights and the respect and esteem of his kinsman. The maiden's tears fell thickly on these letters, and she turned from them to those of Rupeat, of Fay, and of good Meggy Fleck, all of whom had written at length. Her brothers ignorant of her whereabouts and the reason for her abecres, implored her to return, declaring that else had taken with her all the light and warmth of their home. When Giralda had studied the letters until shs knew their contents literally by heart, she restored them to their hiding-place, locked her trunk, re- moved the traces of tears from her cheeks, and de- scended in search of the marquis, desiring to thank him for his presents. She found his lordship on the terrace, leaning on his gold-headed staff, absorbed in the contem- plation of a beautiful gray mare, which a man was leading back and forth betore him. The marquis's keen eyes caught sight of Giralda, as she stood, hesitating to approach him, and he beckoned to her, his grand old face glowing with a genial and kindly expression. "This way, my child,"- be said, pleasantly. " You are just in time. What do you think of my new purchase? Isn't she a beauty ?" "A beauty indeed 1" said Giralda with enthusi- asm, noting the large atal soft brown eyes and su- perb contour of the animal. "She's as gentle as swift. I've had my eye on her this year or two, but I had no one to buy her for," declared his lordship. " Her name is Zu- lime. She's part Arab. She is a present to you from me, .Giralda, and I should like to see you on her back. When will you try her ?" " Immediately 1" exclaimed the young girl, with sparkling eyes. "how kind you are to me uncle 1 1 know how to ride. I used to ride a pony at home. I love a boric, and I shall enjoy t.lie possession of. this one more than I can express!" " A horse is a necessity in this part of the coun- try," said the marquis, cutting short her grateful thanks. "Run and put on your habit my dear. I will send a man to attend you, while you take a fine canter over the hills 1" Giralda hastened to .do his lordship's bidding. In a brief space she attired herself for her ride, and came down again, flushed and pleased, her gray eyes glowing with a joyous light. Zuliise, saddled and bridled, awaited her at the porch ; the marquis assisted her with a displaY of old-time gallantry, to mount, lamenting his in- ability to accompany her; and the neat moment Giralda rode away down the avenue with swiftness and grace, closely attended by a groom. His lordship looked after her with a fond, proud smile. " How beautiful and graceful elle is 1" he thought. "how well she sits her saddle ! How strongly she resembles the Trevelyans It is almost im- possible that she ehould not be allied, even if remotely, to the Trevelyans. It seems incredible that such a marvellous resemblance can result from chance 1" He gazed after the young horsewoman until she had passed deteide the lodge gates, and then was about to re-enter the dwelling, when the gates opened again to give admittauce to a lumbering old fly. " Visitors, eh?" soliloquized the marquis. "It rnest be Adlowe. And that is his man, Haskins, on the box." This conclusion was soon verified. The fiy drove up to the porch, and Lord Adlowe alighted, an uneasy and discontented expression on his countenance as he marked the great improvement In the appearance of the place, and of his uncle, einee his recent visit. The cause of hi a lordship's unexpected return to the Park was simple, lie had called upon the Lady Beatrice at Hampton House, intendlng to force from her ladyship a confession of her identity with the so called Countess of Arevalo, but had found that Slie WaS ill the midst of one ef her mysterious seclusions or ateences. lie had calket a second time with no better efieet, and iieel;y becoming impatieut and wt.:Al:fel, had detereaieed on a Visit .! 0 Ti ely all Park, llenng to ea internedli ie some v free, Ch I,e Lord Trevelyan received him coldly, and with a cynical smile. "Back again so soon, Ormond ?" he exclaimed, bestowing a keen glance on his nephew. "To what do I owe this—ahem I—this pleasure?" "I 'ye only come for a day or two,. uncle," replied Adlowe, with assumed carelesse-:.-SS, as the two entered the largo, warm hall, " The truth is, I do not like to leave you so entirely to strangers. Besides, as your heir. !t: riot for :Ile to eeeee La bit lILVDIO in your old sae.'l
The marquis knitted his brows together In 6 black frown, and an ominous look gleamed in bis black eyes. With an effort, however, he con- trolled.his rising passions, and maintained a signift-
cant silence. "How you have changed the old place ! " ob- served Ad owe, as they sauntered into the drawing room. "The house is all open—the furniture uncovered and, as 1 live, there are new ser-

vents." a.vd "Yee," said Lord Trevelyan composedly, that is not all. The house is to be newly-furnished throughout. The boxes containing some of the new furniture arrived this morning. I have nought ttew horses for riding and for carriage use. Vie. conservatories, green-houses, and graperies arc to be put into immediate repair. I have lost several years, during which I lived like a hermit. I sin, only seventy-five now, with a constitution whico' even you might envy. Ours is a long-lived race,. • Ormond, and I am good for twenty years yet. Don't you think so ?" He certainly looked so as he drew up his colos- sal figure to its utmost height, his eyes sparkling. maliciously, his rugged face ruddy and fresh, bis whole being instinct with power and strength. A bitter curse arose to the lips of the scheming. nephew, and a sullen rage was visible in his every

feiture. . "Where is yGur young adventuress ? " he asked: with an uncontrollable sneer. "You haven't tired' . . of her already and sent her away ?" The old lord's eyes blazed. 1 "Another such allusion to Miss Arevalo," he . said, his tones hoarse with anger, "and my (Icls shall be closed against you while I live! Ta"ti care, Adlowe. lam not a patient man. He wh° insults my ward insults me I " Adlowe shrank before the storm he had raised and stammered an apology. It was not his pa' pose to break with his uncle. "To put the question properly," he said, &pre' testingly, "is Miss Arevalo at the Park ? " - "She is at present out riding," responded thei a .---- marquis, with haughty coldness. "If her innocen . beauty has attracted you to the Park, Adlowe, yol! _ seed not stay here. Her acquaintance le for you. Even had not the countess, her mothers "earned me to keep Giralda from your eight' . i should not have allowed you to make her acquaintance 1.. A strange light leaped to Adlowe's eyes. •"Her mother warned you to keep the girl out ' of my sight, eh ?" he exclaimed. " Strange ! Ne• - 4is not strange. I think, uncle," he added, "IY go up to my room and brush off this dust, and ma° myself presentable. 1 suppose I shall see MO • Arevalo in your presence ? ' - Scarcely waiting for a reply, he withdrew.; sauntering up stairs toward the apartment he ha' occupied on the occasion of his previous visit. Passing along the wide hall, he observed .the door of Giralda's room ajar. He moved towards it cautiously, and peered ini• It had been Geoffrey Trevelyan's room, and ha' been shut up closely for years. Strange memories ' swept over Adlewe's dark soul as he threw an , eager glande around the long-disused room, noticing the pieture of his banished cousin on the wall, crackling fire on the hearth, and the wealth of '. costly clothing scattered over the furniture 1104 bed. , -' "There is no fool like an old fool," he mutterea, 4 his brow darkening. "He is spending Wile/ lavishly on this stranger, while I am almost do; - perate for want of it. Silks, satins, laces, shawls ! One would think this the wardrobe 01st princess. The old dotard! He ought to be put irlw •.. an insane asylum. Ah ! there's a little writing- - .• desk on the table in the bay window. My ladY, ' has been writing—to. her mother, of course! 1 ; wonder if the letter has been posted." . He assured himself that no one was in the reenb ~. and then stole in softly, approaching the little '. desk. To his great joy it was not locked. he Ile lifted the lid eagerly, and looked into teA ' desk. There before him lay Giralda's untioishe' ' letter—the arrival of the trunks, the home letterot • and the marquis's latest gift, having caused the s maiden to forget it. a ' With many furtive glances at the window ell . A . door, Geoffrey Trevelyan'e enemy perused letter, his face growing blacker with every line. I. . It was a simple letter, with an account of Gira: be , da'a daily life, and of the tender kindness wh'cit : the marquis continually displayed toward her. contained several guarded allueious to the bidael 1.! home, and there was more than one expression 'ci• a regret that the writer had done so little toss.° ..T. the accomplishment of her great work. • "Her great work !" mused the scheming ene,l3 ' of the Lady Beatrice and Geffory Trevelyan. p, work which she comes to Trevelyan Park to °- cute I What call it be? " of ' Ile lifted his gaze thoughtfully to the rictus° - his wronged and banished ccusin. The glance enough. The truth came to his soul like an electric :' shock. . "Her great work is to clear the name of Geoff,rel Trevelyan !" he exclaimed, aloud. "I see it all i'n last. Geoffrey is alive ! See, here she spealo, :4 her letter of 'clearing poor papa's name. I overlooked that sentence. Geoffrey Trevelyans,7 .- old rival and unconscious enemy, is alive, in f a land, the husband of the Lady Beatrice 13.a.mPt° ' e the father of her child, or children !" He continued to look at the portrait with sterol: ...' ing oyes and livid complexion. His brain reeie the ond for a minute his plotting brain became _, theatre of a wild chaos. He sank down iu Gi17,1-,.. _. da's white-covered easy-chair, pallid and tress bling. . se is " This, then," he said,, in a hollow wieAssi:ele S explains the mysterious absences of the LadY bits e trice from her home. Geoffrey Trevelyan, yes , been all these years in England, while we belwilt° ere s him dead. He has been here, secluded 5011e,,0., under a false name, happy in Beatrice IlainPt°,.."o,os love, and serenely waiting for Lord TrevelPtist , death. Ten thousand curses! How she IT oV have laughed in her sleeve at my p5013°33: her '- marriage I How she must have despised ine in e heart for a weak, blind idiot I" He gnashed his teeth in his rage. ~.!„d "No doubt she has reported my love-maa'""s,se, e Geoffrey Trevelyan," he continued, still w,e/a, hollowly. ~ No doubt they have laughed tog for ~ over my folly in addressing a married womalijoes , ouch my Lady Beatrice is I My heart told the first that this young girl had a rigliweese Geoffrey's eyes—that she was his child I The,. shoe' I at the theatre ought to have told me all le,...eyee j learned from this letter. This Giralda is Geo u.`,.00. daughter, and consequently my uncle's heiLfell: The title— Oh, where are my wits? "and a P 5,1370,0, cry escaped his white lips. "Geoffrey Trell,olll' himself will inherit title and estates at elie! Trevelyan'e death; He has taken from in 01-- woman I love! He won from me in 00Y110Ga Os: uncle's heart ! He will come between ine an title and estates for which I have perilled raY s And I—" ibiing He gave utterance to a cry strangely resell that of a wild beast in deadly suffering. eel. All the facts of this position crowded on hi...°3001) with awful force. Great beads of PersPilA loo.°' stood out on his corrugated brows, and a so'..,ies e° came to his small, serpent-like eyes. It sceS Ora' though a temporary madness had ize bd 0 Flinging down the letter whose contents he roeene treacherously learned, he dashed out of the hurrying madly to his own chamber. ---- to`,; It Often falls to the lot of a progressive newspaper a bit of detective work, and we can say, and say it L'nout egotism, that when undertaken it is well done. I,.leeently enquiries have reachr.d us as to whether the testimonials we have published from time to time, well-known patent medicine were true. We

irLa Hot honestly ansv:er this question, but Nve decided we woulo. Accordingly the " Saturday Night" rviewed several prominent Birmingham people 1.8"." statements had appiared in our paper. As a th"th Wt. are pleased to say that we not only believe all at is there said, but we also unhesitatingly endorse 4111- er's Safe Remedies. div.head: INTERESTING WEDDING AT THEL WALL.
div.p: INTERESTING WEDDING AT THEL WALL.

IA wedding took place at Thelvvall on Taesday, the contracting parties being the Rev. Jenkyn Jones, vicar of St. Asaph and vicar choral of the Cathedral (a son of Mr. and Mrs. Jenkyn Jones, Brenig Villa,Tregaton band Miss Adela M. Pickmere, Remuera, Auckland, New Zealand (niece of Major Pickmere, J.P., of Cedar Lawn, Thel wall. The interesting ceremony took place in all Saints Church at 12 noon, in the presence of a large num- ber of spectators. Flags were displayed at several of the larger houses in the village, and red baize had been laid down from the churchyard gates to the principal door of the sacred building. The bride, who was given away by Major Pickmere, on whose arm she entered the church, is the daughter of Mr. and Mrs. R. Pickmere. She wore a cream satin duchesse dress trimmed with lace and orange blossom, and carried a handsome bou- quet of orange blossom and stephanotis—a present from the bridegroom. Her bridesmaids were Miss Edith Picktnere and Miss Sybil Pickm ere (cousins), and they were attired in dresses of white Chinese silk trimmed with lace and blue ribbons,with hats to match. Their bouquets were composed of sweet peas and maidenhair fern, alsol presents from the bridegroom. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. Canon Fletcher, vicar of Wrexhatn, who was assisted by the Rev. T. P. Williamson, vicar of The!. wall, and the Rev. IL Holbech, rector of Whittington, Salop. The Rev. D.W. Davies, vicar choral, St. Asaph, officiated as groomsman, and the Rev. J. Daniels, senior curate of Carmarthen, was best man. Mr. W. B. Cook occupied his accustomed post at the organ, and as the wedding party entered the church he gave an excellent interpretation of W. H. Richmond's "Ave Maria," while at the conclusion of the service he played Mendelssohn's well known Wedding March and Richmond's Grand Marche Heroique. There was a full choral service. The hymns sung were " The voice that breathed o'er Eden," to music which had been composed by the organist, and " 0 perfect love," No. 578 A and M. At the conclusion of the service in the church, the wedding party returned to Cedar Lawn where they assembled in front of the principal entrance and were photographed by Mr. Birtles, of Sankey-street, Warrington. A special photo- graph was also taken of the bride and bridegroom, who later on in the day left for Buxton, where the honeymoon will be spent. The wedding breakfast was set out in the billiard-room, which had been most elaborately and artistically decorated for the occasion, under the superintendence of Mrs. Pickmere. The tables were adorned with choice flowers and ferns, while above theist were four fairy bells composed of a light paper material, surmounted one with the rose, another with the shamrock, a third with the thistle,and the fourth with the leek. The following is a list of the invited guests :—The Rev. the Dean of St. Asaph ; the Rev. Canon and Mrs. Fletcher, Wrexham ; The Rev. H. and Mrs. Holbech, Whittington, Salop; the Rev. T. P. and Mrs. Williamson, Thelwall ; the Rev. R. B. and Mrs. Faulkner, Ightfield, Whitchurch ; the Rev. D. W. Davies, St. Asaph; the Rev. Henry Jones, St. Asaph ; the Rev. J.Daniel, Carmarthen ; Mr. Alderman Greenall (Mayor of Warrington) ; Dr. and Mrs. Palin, Wrex- ham ; Mr. E. T. and Mrs. Pickmere' and Miss Pickmere, Moseley, Birmingham ; Mr. E. div.head: WESLEYAN METHODIST CONFERENCE.
div.p: WESLEYAN METHODIST CONFERENCE.
THE REV. OWEN WATKINS ON THE ADMISSION OF WOMEN.

An exciting debate arose on Monday at the meet- ing of the representative session -of the Wesleyan Conference which was held at Birmingham regard- ing the presence of a lady as the representative of • the Third London district. The Rev. Owen Watkins (Warrington) drew attention to the presence in the conference of a lady representa- tive elected by the Third London Synod. He submitted that the constitution of the conference provided for 240 ministers and 240 " laymen." He submitted that such an innovation could not come about in that way. He contended that it was not respectful to the conterence, arid it was not respectful to the Methwlist Church. He moved that the lady elected to the conference by the Third London District be allowed to take her place, and that such admission be without prejudice to the case, and that a committee be appointed to consider the whole question, and report, and that no further election ot ladies take place until the conference has decided the whole question of the admission of ladies as representa- tives to the conference, whatever their views might be. They could not settle this question off hand. It was grave departure from Methodist usage. Mr. Price Hughes, in a vigorous sreech, contended that a committee could not throw any light on the ques- tion, and he did not see why the conference could not decide it at once. Why should they agitate the connex- ion for a twelvemonth upon a subject on which they had all made up their minds ? Everyone knew how opposed he was to agitation. If the question must be discussed why not discuss it now ? He wished the incident could have been passed over without notice. He did not think there was any good in debating it at length. There was nothing so awful in the admission of a lady. At this point, amid considerable excitement, several delegates appealed on a point of orCer. The president, having decided in favour of Mr. Hughes, the latter pro- ceeded to say that if the conference intended to slam the door in the face of women let them do it now. (Hear hear.) His contention was the vote of the L-gal Hun- dred took no notice of anything except the Legal Confer- ence to admit laymen did not contemplate the inclusion if women, it did not exclude them. (Loud cries of " Time.") The Church owed much to women, as for instance the Roman Catholic Church, the Quakers, and the sisterhoods in the Church of England. Ultimately it was resolved that the lady should r, tamn or place in the Conference for this year, without pre- judice, and that in future no nomination of a lady representative should be received until the Conference should have determined by legislative action upon their admission and until such legislation should have been sutnaitted to the district synods. 'file President (the Rev. Watford Green) addressed the Conference. After dealing with Connexional matters, the President referred to the passing of the Parish Councils Act as a new force put into their hands which they sheuld'use for the good of the community at large. Bey must seek to take their full share in the social and reli4ious life of tie age. A letter was read from Dr. Dlle expressing friendly sentiments towards the Confer- ' cnce and Wesleyans generally.

div.head: 'I HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 28,1894. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: 'I HE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JULY 28,1894. THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT WARRINGTON.

The Warrington Liberal Club Committee have de- cided to have a special trip to Ilawarden on Thurs- day, August IGth, this being the occasion of a special fete to be held at the residence of the Right Hon. W. E. Gladstone, in the grounds of Hawarden Castle. Special interest will be manifested on this occasion, by the fact that it has already been an- nounced that the ex-premier will return to Hawar- den in order to be present at the fete. An excur- sion to Hawarden is always popular amongst Liberals, and it is expected that the fete of this year will attract even larger numbers than usual. There is, I hear,every promise of the excursion from Warrington being a great success.

The Warrington cattle and horse faiis were- held last week as usual in Winwick-street, much to the annoyance of the inhabitants and passengers of that locality. It is a positive disgrace to the town to hold such fairs in the public streets of Warring- ton, for the filth in the streets in consequence is simply disgusting. Added to this is the danger of being knocked down by the quadrupeds when pass- ing through the streets. A person unacquainted with Warrington, and passing along the Cheshire Lines Railway would almost tancy he was passing an old world town, when he saw the cattle and horses pat up for sale in the public streets. It is getting quite time that a more suitable place was provided so that the dealers can carry on their trade without being a nuisance to the public..

It is not at all satisfactory that the Warrington Battalion of Volunteers should be represented at Bisley by only one member, namely, Corporal Plinston.. It is unfortunately the case that the local corps has not,for some years past at all events, figured prominently at the great annual shooting competitions, and undoubtedly the main reason is the lack of a suitable shooting range within easy distancefrom the town. As is well known the Warrington Volunteers are obliged to journey to Widnes or Altcar in order to practice,and with such ar unsatisfactory state of things, it is not surpris- ing that first class shots area rarity amongst the Warrington Volunteer corps. Ihave no doubt, that with proper encouragement and opportunities the Warrington corps would soon turn out a fair pro- portion of marksmen who would worthly uphold its reputation at Bisley.

An old inhabitant of the town passed away on Saturday week in the person of Alderman Ashton. In the earlier part of his career he had a pretty close connection with the railway, and I hear that it was his dying wish that he should be borne to his grave by a number of railway guards. This wish was carried out, for although it was a difficult matter for the guards to getaway from their employment, Mr. Starkey, the station master at Bank Qtlay station was able to provide six bearers at the faneral on Wednesday last. Alderman Ashton was him- self a guard for a long period, and at a time when the trains were more like stage coaches than those of the present day. Like stage coaches, the train 3 would stop in those times to pick up passengers along the road, and there was not as much hurry and bustle as now-a-days.. Alderman Ashton was also stationmaster of Arpley station before the pre- sent railway bridge over the river was-constructed. His death therefore takes away another link which bound the present period to that of the time of the formation of our present railway system.

I wonder whether the Tories in the Town Council will adhere to the rule they have found it conveni- ent to follow in recent elections rendered necessary by aldermanic vacancies in the Town Council. They have protested loudly that length of service should be the ground upon which a new alderman should be elected, forgetting their conduct when they refused to elect the late Councillor J. Greening to this post of honour. It happens this time that the oldest councillor is Councillor Bolton, who, however, is not a persona grata with a certain class of the Tories. It will therefore be curious to watch the action of the Tories in the matter.

I notice that the gates which Mr. F: Monks has presented to the town have arrived, and operations are in progress to place them in their position. There is the greatest interest taken in them now that they have arrived, and during the operations large numbers of people have been watching the workmen as they proceed with their work. The gates will no doubt give Sankey-st. a fine appear- ance when they are put together, and nothing will then reinain to be done but the laying out of the plot of ground in front of the Town Hall. If this is done in a proper manner, that part of Warrington. will be a credit to the town.
RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS,

On Tuesday afternoon Mr. J. Mcrntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting: oF the above Board, at Dutton Workhowie, when there were present— the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner,Dr. Gastaldi, and J.Hanby Messrs. J. Brandreth, H. E. Heywood, S. Yarwood, J. M. Williams, J. Stokes, T. Baxter, C.C., T. Lewis, T. Handley, J.P., W. Pickering, A. R. Norman, S Woodward, C. T. Whitley, J. Ashton, clerk and G. Ashton, deputy clerk.

THE GUARDIANS AND THEM SCHOOL. ir:SES ENCPUIHY OFFICER. The Local Government Board writing on the ifich inst. in reply to a communication containing particulars of the proposed appointment, without remuneration, of Mr. T. Cooke, relieving officer for the Runcorn district of the Union, as enquiry officer for the district. The 'letter stated Um': the Board had no authority to sanction the appointment of such an officer unless some remuner- ation was assigned to himrso as to constitute him a paid officer under their regulations. At the same time the Board drew attention to having had no reply to the enquiry contained in the Board's letter of April 10th, as to the payment of school fees. The Board enquired if they were right in assuming that school fees were being paid under section 2 of the Elementary Education Act, 1891.—The Clerk said he had written to the Board.saying that the school fees were paid under section 2: of the Act referred to.---Mr. Brandreth,. alluding to the first portion of the letter, recommended the payment of Is. to Mr. Cooke for every fresh case which he investigated. Mr. Danzig had told them that such a course was fol- lowed by some Guardians.—The Rev. J. Hanby asked if Mr. Coske would then be considered a paid officer, to which Mr. Brandreth answered in the affirmative. Et tter some little discussion Mr. Brandreth's motion was seconded and carried.

THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT ACT, 1894: The Clerk reported the receipt of a print of an, order from the Cheshire County C)uncil postponing until March 31st, 1895, the operation of section 25, of the Local Government Act, 1894, so far as it related to the taking over of the powers of the respective highway boards in the various unions. VISIT TO THE WORKHOUSE BY THE LADIES' COMMITTEE.

The Clerk read a letter from Miss Best, ot Aston Lodge, Preston Brook, thanking the Board for the compliment paid her by asking her to become a member of the Ladies' Committee to visit the Workhouse. She was sorry to decline the office, but she was forced to do, so owing to her leaving Aston in a few months. Had she been remaining in the district she would havebeen:glad to serve on the Committee.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner reported having called the Committee of Ladies together. Four of the ladies attended, and three were absent. Out of the number selected, two had resigned. At the meet- ing of the Committee, the ladies elected Mrs. Maitland Wood as their president for the year.—The subject of filling up the vacant seats on the Committee was then brooched, but was finally adjourned until the next fort- nightly meeting, on the proposition of Mr. Heywood.— The Rev.J.W.N.Tanner further stated that the ladies had made a thorough inspectiAm of the Workhouse- which occupied them for two hours. They were afterwards provided with tea.

div.head: M.ERUN
div.p: M.ERUN
THE: REV J KIRTLAN., AND THE. PARISH COUNCILS BILL..

After the usual Monday night service at' Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel, the Rev. J. Kirtlan gave his views upon.the Parish Councils Bill, which will come into operation during the present year. He said that tke Bill would make great changes in the villages of the country, and it was therefore- im- portant that they in Sankey Bridges should be fully acquainted with its details. The Parish Council would have control•and management of almost all the business of the parish. The number of members would in BOMB cases be only six and in some cases as many as 15; He would also state hereethat women had also aright to sit upon the Councileand every householderr would have a vote. There would be no plurality of votes.. (Hear, hear.) No man would have a number of votes simply because he had property. One of the things the Council would have charge of was the lighting. There was great difficulty in the villages in consequence ef,want of light. If the people had light in the towns' they re- quired it still more in the villages,. and he looked for- ward to the time when the villages would- be. lighted with electric light.. The Council would also have in hand the provision of baths- and washhouses- which he coissidered very important.. Another very important matter was the provision of cemeteries and burial grounds.. He did not wish. to say one word. to arouse sectarian jealousy, but they did not know what Methodists had to suffer inseam of the villages on these grounds. The provision of these places of sepulture would be, under the control of the Council,. and it was therefore very im- portant whom they placed. upon it. Then there was the matter of libraries and, reading rooms.. There were also many other things which he could not speak about that night which deeply touchecithe happiness and well-being , of the parishes of the country. He would mention how-! ever the power of the Parish Council. to secure allot- ' ments. By this, people would be able to secure land sufficient to have a good garden,. and. he able to cultivate it for the good of their families.. The control of the overseers of the poer was a very important matter. By this means, the poor people in the workhouses would be better looked. after, and their lives made more com- fortable. What he wanted to say .that night was, that as a church they ought, without any rivalry with other churehes,to take their own part in connection with this movement. For instance, if there were six, or if there were 15 members of the Parish Council of Sankey, they ought to. be able to nominate some of their own number for that parish council. It would be very important to thorn as a denomination and as Non. conformists that they should. be prepared. He hoped that they would have a fair representation upon the first Parish Council. Many of the congregation, of course, would be out of it, as they lived in the borough,but still those would sympathise with the others. Mr. KIRTLAN asked if any member of the congrega- tion would like to say anything upon the subject, when Mr S. BLYTRN said that he was glad that Mr.Kirtlan had brought the matter before them, as they as a congrega- tion were a very important body in the district. He was glad that the measure had been passed as it was a thoroueli workingmen's measure, as there was no pro- perty qualification necessary for the parish councillor:l. He hoped that they would get workingmen and Metho- dists upon the Parish Council for that district. The liev.J. KIRTLAN observed that workingmen would be able to attend the meetings after they had finished their work, as the law required that they should be held not sooner than six o'clock in the evening. He hoped that the congregation would think well over the matter. The elections took place in November. In the mean- time, they mieht form a committee who could work in unison with their friends at Penketh, so that they would. be prepsred when the time came. The meeting then terminated.

div.head: FINANCIAL STATEUENT.
div.p: FINANCIAL STATEUENT.

Mr. Brandreth preseuted the report of the Finance Committee from which it appeared that the amount voted for the payment of accounts was £395 4s. 4.d. There was £BO to be given to Runcorn for relief, which was rather less than previously. £3O to Frodsham, and £2O to Budworth for the same purpose. Another amount was £lBO to Mr. Thomas Davies, contractor, for the new tramp ward erected for the accommodation of females. He moved the adoption of the report which was seconded by Dr. Gastaldi and carried.

div.head: GUARDIANS AND THE COUNTY RATE BASIS
div.p: GUARDIANS AND THE COUNTY RATE BASIS

The Chairman intimated that he had received a. circu- lar letter from the Guardians of the Wirral Union who asked their support by sending representatives to the forthcoming Conference at Crewe when an appeal would be made against the new county rate basis. The letter cited two points of importance which would . lan- dealt with at the Conference. Continuing, the Chairman observed that the Assessment Committee of the Bard had me:, that morning and after some consideration had come to the conclusion that there. was a great deal of injustice in the present system of fixing the basis. They had therefore appointed Messrs. H. E. Heywood, A. Thomas, and J. Mclntyre to attend the Conference.— Mr. Handley proposed that the recommendation of the Committee be accepted and that the gentlemen named should attend the gathering.—Mr. E. Aaron . sEoonded, and the resolution was carried. THE CHILDREN'S -ANNUAL TREAT.

Mr. Cunnah, master of the Workhouse, reported that he had received the SUM of £l6 ss. id. towards the cost of the children's annual treat which would take place on the Ist August when they would journey by train to Rhyl. He had also received a large quantity a choice flowers from the Rev. G. D. Wray.—The Guardians passed a vote of thanks to the latter gentleman for his kindness.

div.head: CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION AT GOLBORNE PARK.
div.p: CONSERVATIVE DEMONSTRATION AT GOLBORNE PARK.

A monstre demonstration was held in Golborne Park on Saturday afternoon under the auspices, of the Gol- borne portion of the Newton Division Conservative Association, prior to the demonstration the members assembled at the Golborne Workingmen's Clubto witness the formal opening of the new wing by the Hon. T. W. Legh, M.P..' for the Newton division. Mr. T. D. Grimke Drayton, JP., presided, and there was a crowded atten- ance. The chairman briefly alluded to the altered ap- pearance of the premises, and said it was-entirely the work of the Conservative workingmen of Golborne. Councillor T. T. Brown proposed a vote of thanks to the Hon. 'l'..W. Legh, .for opening the new, wing. Mr. J. Laycock.seconded the-resolution, which was cordially adopted. The Hon. T. W. Legh, MX., in reply, said he was gratified to be present to open thethandsonte addition to the club, because it was evidence of increased pros- perity and activity in the Newton Division generally, and in GolbornediStriotiuparticular. A:monstre procession, including the members of the Primrose League, and accompanied by two brass bands, was then formed, and proceededto Golborne Park. Mr. T. D: Grimke.43rayton,..LP:, presided, supported by the Hon. T.. W. Legh, M.P., Mr. T. Bromley-Davenport, M.P. for Macclesfield Division, Sir Edward Stanton, Councillor Brown, Mr. J. Robinson, Mr. W. Holland- Ocre-n. Alderman Hilton (Wigan),, Mr. F. Silcock, the Rev. JL Anders (Haydock), and a number of ladies, in- cluding Lady Gerard (ruling councillor of the Gars wood Habitation of the Primrose. League) and Mrs. Grimke- Drayton. After a few introductory remarks from the Chairman, Mr. Robinson proposed a vote of "'unabated confidence in the Unionist leaders andrecording appreciation of the action taken by the House of Lords in rej-cting the Home Rule Bill ; and further, in the interest of all classe; and for the prosperity of the country generally, praying for the early return of Lord Salisbury to power," and Mr.F. Silcock seconded the motion.

The Hon. T. W. L.egh, who, on rising, was enthusias- tically cheered, said he and his friend, Mr. Bromley- Davenport had sat for their respective constituencies for or la months,, and he would ask all present were they better for this term of Radical rule. Prom what he could gather, there were few satisfied with the present condition of things, but after a deal of trouble lie had, however, discovered one party who was satisfied with the present condition of things. That party were the Gladstonian members of Parliament for Lancashire. They were so pleased and delighted that they had recently celebrated the event by entertaining that distinguished statesmen Mr. Bryce and his successor to dinner. The cause of their pleasure was that Mr. Bryce had been so successful in Jobbing Radicals on the county bench in Lancashire. If theßaii- cals were given sufficient freedom heMr.Leg,hrlooked to, the time when prisoners in Lancashire would cease to-si plead guilty and not guilty like other people, but would I plead that they were either Radical and Tory, claiming-I to be re-tried by magistrates who were sound on the. Newcastle programme. The Radicals had certakiiy passed a budget. Much was being made of this "popular - budget," and the reason was sufficiently simple tone, clerstand. It was based on a principle which had, been advocated years before Sir William Harcourt was-born. The principle upon which it was built meant that- the. possession of property and riches was more or-lass a crime, and that taxes should be exacted as the penalty for economy or success. Thus Sir William Hare,ourt- had been able to wreak his vengeance upon his political opponents. Referring to the evicted tenants' bill, he said in his opinion a more iniquitous measure. was never brought before the British Parliament. It was a.proposal to put dishonest men in the place of honest, men, and ' public money was going to be voted that these worth-. ; less people might be put hack to the positions to which they were unjustly supposed to have a right. it would be a crying shame to this country if ever such a ' measure became law. As to the miners-eight hours bill, ' he believed Sir William Harcourt had- no inter,tiors of passing it, and he did not believe he wanted it to pass, because many of his colleagues were-opposed to it. nisi. measure, however, was, he thouglat, in the sane boat as the direct veto bill, and stood ,about as =itch ettanct ef becoming law. He looked forward to thatime—pro- bably in the near f uture—wher, the Conservatives would be returned to power—men who were in every way qual- ified to administer the affi.:irs of the country, (Ap- plause.)
