div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
MONDAY.

In the House of Lords on Monday a number of Bills were advanced a stage further. Lord RIBBLESPALE, replying to the Earl of ROME, said simultaneous muzzl- ing might be the simplest mode of stamping out rabies, but it would be attended with great difficulty,and could only be carried out if there was a very strong public opinion at the back of the authorities. At preAent he did not think there was any case for such a measure, and was of opinion that the local authorities might be trusted to carry out the law.

In the House of Commons,Sir J. T. HIBBERT informed Mr. T. HEALY that the amount of arrears due by Irish landlords to the Crown for quit rents to March 31st last was £14,275, including recoverable arrears. Mr. AsquiTs informed Mr. S. Sluts that up to the present no sufficient evidence had been forthcoming to warrant police action in reference to massage establishments, or show the necessity for an amendment of the law. Mr. J.CHAMBERLAIN resumed the debate on ColonelSautmEn- soN's amendment to the motion for the second reading of the Evicted Tenants' (Ireland) Bill. He said they must all feel that such a thing as a final settlement was almost impossible, and that every interference with the ordinary course of law invariably brought with it a new crop of grievances and a new agitation. In the present case their caution ought especially to be exercisedr because this was a bill containing provisions so extra- ordinary as to be justly said to establish a new prece- dent. He ventured to say that there was not a district in the whole of England and Wales—not a town in Eng- land or Scotland—in which the annual number of evic- tions did not enormously exceed the proportion with which they were now called upon to deal. He would without hesitation vote against the second reading. Mr. HFALY, amid loud cheers from the Irish Nationalist members, concluded a vigorous speech with an eloquent appeal to the House to read the bill a second time. The debate was continued by Mr. MACARTNEY, Mr. T. W. RUSSELL (who regretted that he was unable to give his vote for the bill), the SOLICITOR-GENERAL, Mr. HAYES- FISHER, Mr. DILLON, Sir E. ASHMEAD-BARTLETT, Mr. 'tumult and Mr. JOHN MORLEY. The bill was read a second time by a majority of 32.

div.head: TUESDAY.
div.p: TUESDAY.

_ In the House of Lords on Tuesday the Chimney Sweepers' Bill was read a second time, the Industrial Schools Bill was read a third time and passed, and the. Uniforms Bill was brought from the Commons and read a first time. In the House of Commons the Lords' amendments to the Great Western Railway (No. 1) Bill were considered and agreed to. Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE in- formed Mr. HERBERT LEWIS that copies of the Local Government Act in the Welsh language would be read on an early date. Mr. .Ascturrn replying to Mr. TOM- LINSON and Mr. D. Tnomes, said the Government, as a Government, did not take any part in the Miners' Eight Hours Bill. He was himself a strong supporter of the bill, and would put down an amendment providing that the penalty for contravention of the Act should not fall on the employer alone with the object of making it a more practicable workable measure. Mr.SHAW-LEFEVREI informed Mr. JEFFREYS that the Parish Councils Act would probably come into operation between the 10th and 17th December. Sir WILLIAM HARCOURT informed Mr. J. A. PRASE that he would endeavour to give as much notice as he could of the consideration of the Miners Eight Hours Bill, but he could not name an). particular period. Mr. S. BUXTON, in answer to Mr. MACDONA, said the South African Republic had released the British subjects already impressed, and if any others had been impressed it had been under a misapprehen- sion, and the Government hoped they would soon be released. Mr. SHAW-LEFEVRE moved the second read- ing of the Equalisation of Rates (London) Bill, on which a debate ensued. WEDNESDAY.

In the House of Commons on Wednesday the debate on the motion for the second reading of the Equalisation of Hates (London) Bill was continued. As on the previ- ous day, the discussion was almost entirely confined to London members. Mr. GOSCH.EN said there was no pre. cedent for a grant in aid from certain parishes to certain other parishes unaccompanied by precautions in regard to expenditure, and he asked what security there was that the money would be spent in improving sanitation. Mr. SHAW•LEFEVRE moved the closure, whereupon Mr. Ginns's amendment was negatived without a division, and the bill was read a second time.

_ On the motion for the consideration of the Church Patronage Bill as amended, Mr. CARVELL WILLIAms rose to move his amendments, but, Sir F. POWELL intimating that he was unaWe to accept them, the bill had to stand over.

THE. P.S.A. AT THE Y.ALC.A. • -- PUBLIC MEETING. A.public meeting of the P.S.A. which is held in connection with the Y.M.C.A. was held on Sunday afternoon at the Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel. There was an excellent attendance, the body of the large chapel being crowded while a good number was also in the gallery. The singing was led by the united choirs of Bold-st. Wesleyan Chapel, Sankey Bridges Wesleyan Chapel, Friars Green Mission' and the Brick- st. Mission, in addition to an orchestral band under the leadership of Mr: W. Brough. Mr. Peter Harrison acted as organist. After opening with the singing of a hymn, Mr. William Roberts read the 146th Psalm. Miss J. Jones of Bolton then sang "The Holy City," in an excel- lent manner. Mr. C. E. PAREER, who occupied the chair, next ad- dressed the meeting. He said that he was very glad to be among them that afternoon and to stand side by side with those who recognised the strong, man Christ Jesus, as their hero. They had a great work and .a noble work to do in Warrington, and he thought that if they would do that work permanently,.they would have to encircle the whole.life with religious influences. The truth was coming gradually to the churches that it would not do merely to touch one side or one phase of the nature of the young men and women. They required healthy influences which would touch the intellect and the body as well as the soul. The truth had been gradually breaking that they must claim the whole man for the sake and in the name of Him who had redeemed the whole man. He had just returned, from a visit to the United States, and he had been " wandering s to and fio " in that country. Be found that while their American cousins were very far behind them in most things,, there was one work in which he thought they were distinctly ahead of the Englistapeople. This was the work among the young people. He thought that perhaps the success they had achieved was from the fact of the number of- young men's associations and social clubs in which they could meet together. In America, the work of the Young Men's Christian Association was much more developed, and more capable of vigorous work than here. He visited Montreal in Canada, and found there a building of this kind which cost somewhere near£4o,ooo; and it was in the centre and in the best position of the town. In connection with it were a gymnasium, baths, cricket clubs, and many other institutions. He thought it would be well for Englishmen to take hold of this idea. He was glad that the Y.M.C.A. of Warrington was en- gaged in the special work on Sunday afternoons- and he wished them every success. The Chairman's address was followed by a selection, "March tr iumpha nt," by the band,which was performed in a masterly manner. The Rev. J. Kirilan then engaged in prayer, and after another hymn had been sung, Mr. KENT made the announcements in the course of which he explained the objects of the. P..S.A. He said that they did not wish to take aeybody away from the Sunday schools. Those at the head of the P.S.A. had received too much good from the Sunday schools to wish to do that. They wished to bring in those who attended nowhere. He was glad that the P.S.A. movement was growing in various parts of the country. There was no jealousy between the various P.S.A.'s whatever. They of the Y.M.C.A. had a big brother in the Wycliffe P.S.A..' and they rejoiced to know of its success. With regard to the meetings which were held every Sunday after- noon at the Y.M.C.A. building, he might say that they were somewhat similar to the present service, hut they had no orchestra, and no ladies were allowed in the meeting except once a quarter. He appealed to every-. one present who was not a. member, and who did net attend eny Sunday school, to give their names to the Secretary at the close of the service, as the subscription was oniy a Denny per week. The next item on the programme was an anthem " What are these," (Stainer), by the choir who very efficiently performed their task. Mr. T. WoRTHINGTON, of Wigan, was the speaker for the afternoon, and gave a most telling address upon " Thomas." He said there were many Thomases now- a-days who wished to have proof of everything before they would believe. After all, he thought Thomas was a pretty decent fellow, and there were many places where Jesus Christ had not yet been. There were many places where He had not been in Warrington, or they would not have so many wretched housee,which required pulling down. Jesus Christ was not in the Corporation of the town, or there would not be so many public- houses. (Applause.) They could never get altogether out of the sinrll of a publiebouse in Warrineton. If He were in the Corporation, the Watch Committee would carry out the law properly. Every prliceman would then know that promotion depended upon carrying out the law, not winking at it. Ile was clad of what had taken place in London on the previous week, where masters and men in the coal trade had agreed that there should ba no strikes for two years. He thought that the churches had net taken sufficient notice of that step. He looked forward to the time when Jeans Christ would influence everything in England,ancl then England would be indeed hanpv. Aqer Mr. Worthinron's addre;s. Miss Jones again sang " Glory to Thee, Mc Goa " (G mood), with great feeling and power. A collection was tin n taken, after which the meeting was bronglit to a close in the usual ii anncr.

div.head: SHOCKING FATALITY AT LONGFORD GAS WORKS.
div.p: SHOCKING FATALITY AT LONGFORD GAS WORKS.

John Kelly, 42 years of age, and who lived in Foundary-st. met with a shocking death whilst following his employment, on Monday morning. The deceased who was in the employ of Mr.Pilking- ton, carting agent, went in company with another man named iloulding to the Longford Gas works with two horses for the purpose of drawing waggons of coal from the London and North-Western Railway siding into the works. They were engaged in drawing a waggon of coal when deceased stumbled an d fell across one of the rails; two wheels of a waggon passed across his thighs and abdomen, killing him almost instantane- ously. An inquiry, relative to the death of the deceased, was conducted by Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, in the Parade room, Irlam•st., on Tuesday. Mr: .J., Lyon Whittle, town clerk,represented the Corporation, and the secretary of the Gas Department, Mr.. Taylor, was also present. Patrick Kelly,6s,Foundry-street said that the deceased was his brother, and lodged with him until Saturday night when,in consequence of the deceased failing to pay for his lodgings he was turned out. He was 4(7/ years of age. Witness saw him early on Monday: morning, and he then appeared eo be under the influence of drink. He was addicted to drink. Charles Houlding, horse driver, in the employ of Mr. Pilkington, stated that the deceased was employed by the same gentleman. On Monday morning he and Kelly were engaged at the gas works, running waggons from the London and North-Western siding into the shed. A chain was fastened to the waggon, which was drawn by ahorse. Witness was at the horse's head when, hearing a cry, he stopped and ran back. He found deceased ly- ing across the rails. The wheel of the waggon had passed over his thighs and abdomen. He died in a few minutes. The deceased had been working at the gas works about five weeks. It was the duty of the deceased to uncouple the waggons.—By the Foreman : Had he anything to uncouple the waggons ?—No.—ln answer-to the Coroner witness said the deceased had had some drink, but was able to do his work.

David Lewis said he worked at the. Longford Gas Works. He saw the dezeased running by. the side of the waggon to catch up to it as he was -a .little behind. When he had reached the front of the waggon deceased seemed to have caught his foot and tripped himself. He fell on the rails,and the waggon.ran over him. Houlding. was at the other aide of the waggon, .driving the horse. Witness shouted to him, and. he stopped his horse. The
deceased was picked up alive, b‘u‘t died soon after- wards.

James Parkinson, foreman at the-works, said that df,ceased's duty was to uncouple waggons. Witness. saw deceased early in the morning, and he appeared to have had drink, as he was talkative. HQ wa s,however,, capable to attend to his work. Witnesss did not see the accident.

Mr. ‘A 'little (town clerk) said he would consult the gas manager to see whether he could devise a betterr means of uncoupling the waggons than at present. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death."

div.head: HOW SANDOW TREATED A FOUL WRESTLER THE "BEAR'S
div.p: HOW SANDOW TREATED A FOUL WRESTLER THE "BEAR'S

Sandow, when in ,Venice, had an encounter with st• wrestler named Muller, whose unprofessional brutality in a match whichnnsueagaveSandow occasion long to remember him with keenest-dislike.. He was, in truth„ a terrible antagonist, being known to resort to infamous. tactics—such as seeking to break,his opponent's fiug_er or limb—to get the better of an adversary and win the match. even through a foul. Sandow, though aware of 111uller's vicious habit,, was not loth to try odds,with. him, and the match , was duly, brought on before-an; immense and highly, wrought-up audience. Sandow entered the arep.a and confronted his adversary with-his usual pluck and coolness. Afterca few minutes' strugvli- ing and a few feints,. Muller saw that he was not likely to throw his oppnnent,. and he then attempted to, play his old game, .which Sandow- -for the time being foiled. Muller persisted, however,.inhiStactics,and endeavoured to get Sandow at a-disadvantage, seizing hold of wrist, arm, or leg in turn, ,with the avident design of breaking or disabling it% . That Sandom-was wary, and fomfurther while succeeded in checkmating his purpose, until, with both hands„ Muller fastened upon Sandow's right fore- arm and tried to snap, it at the wrist, and at the same time, with a su.prerne effort,. he forced two fingers. of his right hand.an inch deop-into Sandow's flesh., cruahing the veins till they, burst„and causing him intense. pain. This dastardly, act, so foully committed, caused Seadow, for the first,-auil only time-in his life when wrestling, to lose his temper, though, net his presence of mind. With all his strength Sandow,. by an alert naovement,, jerked back his left arm, and,, closing upon Muller,.threw both arms around his.body-,. between the waist and the chest, and drewsliii opponent-towards him in a vor,?; bear's hug until Muller's face blackened and blood gushed from his mouth, and he frill upon the floor as if:he-were dead. The clefencewas-the-a:A of a minute, but- it.left Muller not dead, hut with. Four broken ribs, from!which it took him a long :time to recover, while Sandow was disabled for four. months,. the -reins being torn in,,his arm and the nerve.. fibres, greatly lacerated. Ever,. though years.lia.ve, pass,ed, Sandow spealQ eL the circum- stances.with,the keenest regret and r.o. Little reticence, though it . was. Muller's own perfidy- that provoked 'Sandow, to aa.aainister the merited tat unrestrained chastiseineek

It is hard to understand the deter- t -"t1 and hitter opposition that has been offered :f eted Tenants Bill except on the theory t ,andictive desire to still further harass and 4jtlstli°l the Irish tenants who, some years ago, es much in the interests of others as 111iselv, :g,Tainst the exactions of an unjust 83.8t,,r0. There can now be no good end ' ' it'vec-it even, we should think, from the Point of view, by withholding from evicted tenants an opportunity of ert i: 'l'lttatie.o-- the it,Tr cultural point of - -• , ~- wr •,em , '' 7s-i a' tliere is certainly nothing to be said for a - Ilmi'tiv- policy. In the report of the Evicted Commission we are told that " the ' 'sett 6,6ditioy. of (.•veted firms on many of the .4,plorable. The land has gone to Yield. once cultivati d and fairly produc- : r;clf.alst:' ""k" covered k% itli furze and weeds. by Ow ipdustry of the tenants ' t gittnlib""; "h in.luntain are returning to their ( c 41 on- COltliion ." It is sure v riot with the object tj"Le PlL.Petnatino. such a state of things as this that ' T .. °ties throw obstacles in the way of the wh.aefrnmont 13ill l'" The-i on tie score of politics i 3 there to be said for an unconciliatory The evicted tenants are regarded by irtlen as the " wounded soldiers " of their

agrarian struggles, and Nationalists of all shades of opinion are inflexible in their determination to stand by the tenants till a fair measure of justice is meted out to them. To refuse all conciliation is to keep open a running sore which will indefinitely retard the pacification of Ireland. That, surely, is not he highest aim of Tory statesmanship. On the ground of injus- tice to landlords there is nothing tobe said against the Bill. A landlord is not bound to accept a tenant he does not want. He can compel such a tenant either to purchase the land, or to give up all his claims. The bill is in no way unfair to the tenant who now holds a farm from which a pre- vious tenant had been evicted. If the present tenant wants to stay he eonnot be dispossessed against his will, but it is stated that most of them will be only too glad to leave and to pocket the ' compensation that will be given them. It is sug- gestive of the unchanging nature or Toryism that in spite of all the cogent arguments that could be and were adduced in support of the Bill, the Tory members voted on Monday with absolute unity against the suffering and dispossessed tenantry, and in favour of the vindictive and anti-social methods of the Irish landlords. On Tuesday it was the same Toryism that was displayed over the the Bill for equalising London rates. What would be said in Warrington, or any other Eng- lish town or city outside London, of a system which imposed on the working-class districts a sanitary or lighting rate twice or thrice as heavy as a similar rate on the wealthy residential quar- ters? Yet such is the system that prevails in London, and it is against the slight rectification of this system which is proposed by the Equalisa- tion of Rates Bill that the Tories have mustered their forces this week.

THE business of Parliament has The Peers and now reached an interesting stage. the Budget. Last week the Budget Bill passed its third reading in the House of Com- mons and it is not likely that it will be subjected to any further modifications. It is true that there are members of the House of Lords, including Lord SALISBURY, who seem disposed to contend that the hereditary legislators can alter and " amend" a finance Bill just as they are wont to deal with otker Bills. It is, however, not probable that they will venture to translate their words into actions. If they do they will give great satisfaction to those who aro, eager for the reform or abolition of the Upper Chamber, for in no other way could the crucial question of the relative positions and powers of the House of Commons and the House of Lords be more effectually raised. For many years now the Lords have only had the right of saying " Yea " or "Nay" of a Budget Bill—that is to say, of either rejecting it as a whole or accepting it as a whole. A power to alter and amend, to add to or eliminate from, has neither been recognised nor exercised. As a matter of fact the "Times" newspaper seems to be on per- perfectly safe ground when it says that "a Money Bill cannot be touched in the House of Lords." It will be a strange example of fatuity on the part of the Marquis of SALISBURY and his followers if they are so reckless and headstrong as to attempt to " touch " the present money Bill. It has been said that there are members of the Government who are averse to entering into a quarrel with the House of Lords, but if any attempt is made by the irresponsible legislators to recast the Budget in a form different from that decided upon by the House of Commons the least bellicose of Ministers will be compelled to take up a militant attitude. There may be differences of opinion as to the extent to which the Peers should be de- prived of their present legislative powers, but there can be no question as to resistance being offered to any encroachments by them upon the prerogatives of the House of Commons.

THE news that there is to be ThSeetCtoleaml eTnrta.clepeace in the coal trade,for the next two years at all events, will be re- ceived with general satisfaction. A very few weeks ago it seemed as though the state of ten- sion that then existed between mine-owners and miners would almost inc vitably result in another disastrous strike or lock-out. But wiser counsels have prevailed. Representative .coal-owners and representatives of the colliers have met round a table in friendly consultation and have found that their differences could be peacefully adjusted. The agreement that has been come to is in the nature of a compromise. Both sides concede something, though it must be said that the most substantial concession has been made by the miners. They agree ts accept a reduction of ten per cent in their wages to come into force on the Ist of August this year and to remain in force till the Ist of January 1896. The employers, on their part, agree that no further attempt to reduce wages shall be made between now and the beginning of August in 1896; that is to say, they will allow the principle of the "minimum wage" to operate for the next two years. In January 1896, but not before, the miners will be at liberty to put in a claim for an advance of wages to the extent of fifteen par cent. upon the rate of wages of 1888. The question as to whether the advance, or any part of it, should be given will be decided by the Conciliation Board which is to remain in existence till August 1896. So far as outsiders are con- cerned the great point in this compact is the fact that there will toe no general stoppage of industry owing to a dearth of coal for at least two years to come. Further than that, at the end of the two years the present agreement will form an excellent foundation upon which to base a permanent understanding. If by the present concession of a ten per cent, reduction the miners succeed in securing the recognition of the "living wage' principle they will, on the whole, not have made a bad bargain.

At the Warrington County Court on Thursday,flis Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes, gave his decision as to making a vesting order in the CP.S3 of Tunstall and others v. Butterfield. His Honour said he had already made an order declaring the Nounger de- fendant Butterfield, to be the trustee for the elder defendant, and also an order that the defendant be fore-closed. The remaining question,as to whether he should make a vesting order, he must refuse. Mr. Cobbett, solicitor, had asked him to put his reasons in writing and that he would do.—Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, said he saw Mr. Cobbett on Tues- day, and he told him he had come to terms with Messrs. Peace and El:is, solicitors for the lessors, so that there would be no necessity for 11i Honour to state his reasons to Mr. Cobbett.—His Honour con- tinuing said he could not find any authority directly on the point. He thought it was a case in which that court should not make sth,.ii an order. RUNCORN COUNTY COURT.

There was a sitting of this Court on Tuesday last, his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes being present. There were no cases of public interest, the list containing three adjourned, four default, and 91 original plaints.
THE REVISION OF WESLEYAN MINISTERS' STATIONS :
RUNCORN.

It has been suggested during the revision of the second draft of stations that the Rev. W. Arrowsmith, of Run- corn, should be appointed from the second to the first position in the St. Heleas Circuit, and that the Rev. E. Lloyd Jones should be second minister at Runcorn and the Rev. W. George vice. A MUSICAL BARD IN RUNCORN POLICE COURT.

Frederick -Haynes, a travelling musician, and well- known in Runcorn, was brought up at the Police Court on Friday morning before Mr. P. Speakman, charged with being drunk in High-street, on the previous night. Evidence having been adduced, the prisoner was fined 55., or in default seven days in goal.

div.head: DISORDERLY BRICKLAYER AT RUNCORN.
div.p: A DISORDERLY BRICKLAYER AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court on Tuesday morning before Messrs. John Brundrit, and F. J. Norman, Joseph Basnett, of Irvvell-lane, bricklayer, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Egerton-street, on (he pre- vious night.—P.C. Ellis proved apprehending the man and gave evidence as to his condition and behaviour.— Fined ss. and 53. 4d. costs, or an alternative of seven days in gaol with hard labour.
RUNCORN PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL.

The Rev. Thomas Bramhall began his ministrations at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday evenin, a large congregation being present. The sing- ing was especially enjoyed and the remarks of the rev. gentleman appreciated. A. special anthem was sung by the choir in good style, Mr. William Gittenr, jun., ably conducting them. Mr. Jones, of Widnes, acted as organist in an efficient manner. The collection was devoted to the trust fund. DEATH OF A SMALLPDX PATIENT AT RUNCORN.

The woman named Esther Ogden, who was on Satur- day removed from a boat to the Infectious Diseases Hospital, at Runcorn, suffering from smallpox, died on Tuesday. It is stated that her life was despaired of hen admitted to the hospital, and that she has died from a complication of congestion of the lungs. Satisfac- tory progress is being made by the patient who was re- moved there some three weeks ago.

div.head: WIDNES ATHLETES' SUCCESSES.
div.p: WIDNES ATHLETES' SUCCESSES.

At Rochdale on Saturday, H. Barber, Widnes, won the first prize in the half-mile hurdle race, and P. O'Connor, Widnes, secured first place in the mile handi- cap. At Prescot, P. J. Kenyon, J. T. Bouch, and G. Wright, all of Widnes, secured first, second, and third prizes respectively in the mile handicap. At Tranmere. F. W. Sherratt, Widnes, secured first prize in the mile (novice) bicycle race ; and W. Jackson first and second in the two miles and mile bicycle races respectively.
COLLIER'S BREAD is the best money can buy.—Advt. THE PROPOSED BRIDGE IN HALTON-ROAD.

On Wednesday evening a meeting of the Highways and Buildings Committee of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners took place in the Town Hall, and after some consideration it was decided to recommend the Commissioners to sanction the expenditure of £lOO for the construction of a bridge across the Bridgewater Canal, near the crane, Halton-road. It is understood that Mr. Posnett, on behalf of the promoters of the scheme,will provide a bridge, lithe Commissioners will only place it in position.
RONCORNIANS' TRIP TO OVERTON HILLS.

The annual picnic in connection with the Holy Trinity, Band of Hope, R:incorn, toilt place on Saturday after- noon, the spot sel, ced for the event being Overton Hills Frodsham. Nearly 100 members were conveyed thither in buses, belonging to Messrs. Yarweod. They enjoyed a tasty tea, after which amusements of many kinds were indulged in. The return journey was com- pleted in safety, and before dispersing to their several homes, the members expressed a wish that such another pleasant day would be spent next year.
COLLIER'S Is. BUTTER is lliS gem in the market.—Advt. SUCCESS OF A RUNCORN VOLUNTEER AT SISLEY.

Success has attended Sergeant Hervey, of the local Company of Volunteers, who accompanied Sergeant Cooper to Bisley for the purpose of participating in the meeting of the National Rifle Association. In the com- petition for the St. George's Vase Sergeant Hervey suc- ceeded in notching 66 points, being only ten behind the winner of the coveted trophy, and a good distance ahead of the remaining competitors from Cheshire. The shoot- ing of Sergeant Cooper has also been very commendable, he having kept close at the heels of his companion- at-arms.
RUNCORN CHORISTERS' EXCURSION.

Southport, the popular Lancashire seaside resort, was this year selected for the annual outing of the youthful members of the St. Michael's Church choir, Runcorn. Starting somewhat early on Monday morning they had a pleasant ride to their destination in the company of the Rev. A. J. Jameson, who did his utmost to please the young members under his charge. They partook of dinner and tea and amused themselves in many ways. The return journey was made in good time, home being reached at about nine o'clock, after a very pleasant day had been spent. div.head: SUNDAY SCHOOL TREATS AT WIDNES,
div.p: SUNDAY SCHOOL TREATS AT WIDNES,

On Saturday, the scholars, teachers, and friends, of the Oakland-street Wesleyan Sunday school, had their annual treat. Shortly before two o'clock a procession was formed, and headed by the Widnes Subscription Prize Band, paraded the town. They then prA,ceeded to a field kindly lent by Mr. Johnson, of Hale Gate Farm, were a variety of games were indulged in. About one thousand persons partock of the splendid tea provided. The return journey Was commenced ab.)ut eight o'clock. —The scholars, teachers, and friends in connection with the United Methodist Free Church also had their treat on Saturday. Headed by Gossage's Band they pro- ceeded to Hopgh Green, where a field had been placed at their disposal by Mr. Longton. The return journey was commenced shortly before nine o'clock. About 500 scholars, teachers, and friends connrcte.l with the Brunswick ‘Veslevan Sunday S ;hoot, Runcorn, spent a very jally day on Friday last at Overton. The occasion was that of their annual treat,and they started from Runcorn Station shortly after one o'clock by special train for Frods,harn, being accompanied by the Rev. W. Arrowsmith, Mr. John Simpson, senior superintendent ; and Mr. E. Taylor, superintendent. In consequence of pressing duties at the conference, the Rev. T. Wilkes was unable to be present. On reaching Frodshain they made their way to Overton Hills, being favoured with beautiful weather. Here they amused themselves in divers ways until tea tune. The meal was provided in capital style by Mrs. Parker, and was keenly relished by all. Other sources of pleasure were then resorted to, many of the scholars engaging in racing competitions for priz?s, consisting of nuts, swects, Szn. Subsequently they returned home perfectly safe, everyone being very much pleased with the afternoon's outing. COLLIER'S BLACK BLENDED TEA. 2W.per quatter lb.—Advt
TEN MILE CYCLE RACE AT RITNCORN.

On Wednesday afternoon a ten. nub handicap was rim off on the old Aston course, Runcorn, by the ineml9ers of the Runcorn Cycle Club. There were seventeen entries, hut probably in consequence of the heavy state of the roads, only six turned up to compete. The race was made up of three laps round the course making in all ten miles. The competitors were Messrs. J. C. Craw- lord, F. Hindley, E. Lawson, G. Whinyates, T. J. Chrirnes, anci C. Johnson. At 715 the riders Were started, Crawford receiving 3 minutes limit, Hindly minutes, L wson 4. Johnson, and Chrimes 3, whilst Whinyates stirted from the scratch. Crawford and Chrimes uniorturiately came to grief after completing the first lap, but luckily received no personal injury, their machines we,e slightly damaged. Lawson gave up before finishing the second round and the three that remained ended the race hs follows :—Johnson 40 min- etes • Whinvate?, 7 mintiteF 20 F-•;enurlF, ; HinC.ley third. The Liwe ococipi,ci by U. Whinyates in covering the dis- tance beats all previous records over the same course. The Drizs for presentation to the successful competitors are one gold and two silver medals each of which will bear a suitlEe inscription.
THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, J ULY 28, 1894.
ANOTHER DONATION TOWARDS THE RUNCORN TECHNICAL
INSTITUTE.
The Technical Instruction Committee have received a donation of £lO from Mr. J. W. Lightburn towards the cost of constructing the Runcorn Technical Institute.
'THE LICENCE OF THE WIDNES THEATRE.

On Thursday, at the Widnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. G. Pilkington and Councillor %V. W. Gossage, Mr. Joseph Garibaldi Kiddie made an application for the re- newal of the licence of the Alexandra Theatre. The police offering no objection,the licence was granted.

A DESTRUCTIVE PRISONER AT WIDNES. At the W'idnes Petty Sessions, before Mr. G. Pilking- ton and Councillor W. W. Gossage, Julia O'Brien was charged with having wilfully torn to pieces three rugs, valued at 18s., which were sunpliel to her while confined in the cell at Widnes on the 25th inst.—She was sen- tenced to one month's imprisonment.

div.head: WIDNES WIFE DESERTER.
div.p: A WIDNES WIFE DESERTER.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday,before Mr. G. Pilkington and Councillor W. W. Gossage, a man named Peter Woodward, no fixed abode, was charged with having deserted his wife and child, and left them chargeable to the common fund of the Prescot Union. It appears that defendant deserted his wife in Northwich in November last year. She came to Widnes and sub- sequently went to the workhouse,putting the Guardians to an expense of over £3. Prisoner was sentenced to one month's imprisonment with hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD TECHNICAL CLASSES.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD TECHNICAL CLASSES.

The following is a list of the successes gained by the students at the recent science and art examinations : machine construction and drawing 2nd class advanced: James H. Seel, George A. Williamson, John Wilson.— Elementary pass : John Baker, J. H. Williams, W. C. Cooper,HarryTurton.---Building construction—advanced 2nd :—Wm. Sillis, Harold Davies, W. H. Wiswall.—Ele- military pass :—Win. Kershaw, David B. Williams.— Applied mechanics, advanced 2nd :—W. H. Wiswall.— Elementary pass :—Percy Buckley.—Steam: Elementary pass : W. H. Wiswall, E. J. Harrington.—Model draw- ing :—E. W. Rosser, J. Peacock.—Freehand element iry: —A. Poole Ist class, Eleanor Davies, Carrie Abel, Ger- trude Done, John Peacock, 2nd class. RUNCORN FREEMASON'S ANNUAL EXCURSION.

On Thursday morning a party of about seventy mem- bers of the Ellesmere Lodge of Free and Accepted Masons journeyed by train from Runcorn to Llandudno on the occasion of the annual outing in connection with the Order. Many of the brethren were joined by their wives. They arrived at their destination in perfect safety and spent some time rambling about the sands and the pier. They subsequently partook of a substan- tial dinner at the Marine Hotel and when the repast was concluded, many of the most interesting places of Llan- dudno were visited, some of the brethren driving in con- veyances. Tea was afterwards served at the same hotel and was much enjoyed. Finally the party returned to Runcorn, every member having passed a very pleasant day. ALLEGED CRUELTY TO ANIMALS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions on Thursday, Michael Small, master carter and farmer, Barrows' Green, Widnes, was summoned for hawing worked a horse in an unfit condi- tion. Inspector Luff, Royal Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals. Warrington, stated that on the 11th inst. he saw the defendant in charge of a horse attached to a cart. He noticed that the horse was lame and on examining it he found that it was suffering from contracted tendons aad ringbone. • He thought the animal was in pain. Police-sergeant Fretwell corrobor- ated. Mr. J. W. Kriowles, solicitor, called several wit- nesses, including Mr. Richard Eimondson, veterinary surgeon, St. Helens, who said that the horse was not in pain. The bench said it was a suspicious case, and one that the inspect)r was jastified in bringing before them, but, in view of the evidence for the detence the sum- mons would be dismissed. ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT RUNCORN.

The anniversary services in connection with the Sun- day school of the Free Gospel Mission, Ashridge-street, Runcorn. were conducted in the Mission Hall on Sunday when powerful sermons were preached by the Rev. W. Brimelow, Bolton, President of the Conference. There were large congregations, the members of which highly appreciated the re.narks of the President. Special musical selections were rendered in good style by the scholars assisted by the choir, under the efficient leader- ship of Mi. M. Moorfield. On Monday a service of song entitled " Whiter than Snow" was gone through. Mr. T. Handley J.P. presided over the proceedings, and in his opening address spoke in praiseworthy terms of the vast amount of good work which was being carried on b; the Mission in various quarters. The collections showed an increase of £2 on those taken the previous year. RIINCORNSCHOLARS TRIP TO OVERTON HILLS.

The annual excursion of the scholars and teachers con- nected with the Mill Brow Wesleyan Mettodist Sunday school, Runcorn, took place on Thursday. M Inv of the parents of the scholars also j.,ined the trip,and the whole party, which numbered more than 300 startNl from Runcorn station for Frodsham at. a varter p ist two. On rcaching Frodsham they made; their way to Mersey View, Overton Hills,and after indulgi.;; in various kinds of sports, participated in an excellent tea, supplied by Mrs. Parker. The Rev. W. Arrowsmith, Mr. Frith and Mr. Pope, both superintendents of ,the selio)1, did their best to ensure the comfcrt of the scholars, and worked assiduously to please them. The teachers did likewise, and after the return journey was completed the excur- sionists expressed themselves as highly pleased with the day's prooßedings.

div.head: BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL PICNIC.
div.p: BETHESDA CONGREGATIONAL SCHOOL PICNIC.

About 150 scholars, teachers, and friends, connected with the Sunday school of the Bethesda Congregational Church, Runcorn, had their annual picnic on Wednesday when they enjoyed a very pleasant drive to Clifton. The children were conveyed thither on lurries, belonging to Mrs. Stubbs, and the adults in waggonettes supplied by Messrs. Booth. On arriving at Clifton they repaired to the farm owned by Mr. Stokes, and engaged in all kinds of field sports, Mr. Stokes himself interesting the child- ren to a great extent. Mr. W. H. Cl:adwick, superin- tendent, was present, and did his utmost, with the teachers, to add to the pleasure of the scholars. Tea was partaken of and keenly relished, after which sweet- meats were distributni. The party was afterwards safely conveyed home at about nine o'clock, all very pleased with the outing. A WARRINGTON EGG DEALER IN TROUBLE AT WIDNE S.

At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday,before Mr. G. Pilkington and CGuncillor W. W. Gossage, Patrick Sexton, egg dealer, Warrington, was sum- moned for working a horse when it was in an unfit state on the 11th inst. The case was proved by Police-constable Ft etwell and Police-constable Evans who found the horse's foot very much in- flamed, with spavin inside the hock. The defend- ant admitted that he knew the horse was lame when he left Warrington in the morning. Defend- ant's brother was recently fined at Warrington for working the same horse while unfit. The Bench said this was a bad case, and fined the defendant 20.=. and costs.

div.head: SUTTON WEAVER.
div.p: SUTTON WEAVER.

A RUNAWAY HoasE.—At about five o'clock on Monday evening a man named Charles Logan, employed by Messrs. Gore and John Percival, of Parkside Farm, Aston,was driving a milk shandry along the Chester-rd., Sutton, when the horse bolted. Logan was thrown out of the cart and severely cut about the head and face, as well as sustaining serious injury to his right shoulder. The runaway animal was caught whilst running in the direction of Halton station and was led back to its owners. Dr. Selby, ""of Frodsham, was summoned and whilst this gentleman was coining Sergeant Benfield rendered "first aid." Logan was subsequently attended by the medical practitioner named, and was afterwards conveyed to his home.

div.head: WESTON.
div.p: WESTON.

THE COMMISSIONERS AND TRE INADEQUATE WATER SUPPLY.— Tile deputation appointed by the recent rate- paver' meeting, and consisting of Messrs. Vose, E. Aaron, Nesbitt, Kirkham, and J. Collier, had an inter- view on Tuesday evening with the Water Committee of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners at the Town Hall. The committee was presided over by Mr. Nleadowcroft, and the remaining commissioners present -were—Messrs. James Pritchard, Edwin Imison, William Handlv, J. W. Lightburn, and B.Taylor. The attention of the committee was drawn by the deputation to the interrupted supply of water to the village and explained the nature of the grievances of many of the ratepayers who could not sometimes get water from their taps until eleven and twelve o'clock at night. For the rat eight or nine days, however, with few exceptions, the supply was quite sufficient,and all that could be desired,and the deputation thought that if the supply was maintained there wculd be no reason to complain further. The com- mittee replied that they were sorry the supply was sometimes of a intertnittent nature, and would do their utmost to maintain a good supply. The deputation having been thanked for their attendanc,, and also the committee for the way in which they had received the deputation, the interview closed.

div.head: II ELSBY.
div.p: II ELSBY.

FORTHCOMING VILLAGE FAIR AND FLOWER SHOW. by reference being made to our advertising columns it will be s:.en that "a vil!age fair," together with a grand baz tar, and an exhibit;oa of poultry, flowers, fruit, hmey, vegetables, butter and eggs will take place on the 3rd and 4.qf August at Llelsby. The fair will be held near the railway station, and the bazaar in the National schools. The event promises to be very successful inas- much as there is a long prlz3 lit which should attract plenty of exhibitors, and an admirable programme of entertainments has been drawn tip. The services of talented artist s hay,- teen nlist d rte occasion,wlio will be capable of catering for almost all sections. Atten- tion might be drawn to the fact that cheap bookings have been arranged for the benefit of those who wish to travel by railway on Saturday from WarringtdniChester Macchester, Liverpool, and other places.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.

Before Messrs. G. Pilkington and W.W. Gossage. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—The following persons were dealt with for the above offence :—Sarah Ann McGuire. Kent-street ; Thomas Steadman,Warrington-road ; John Brawley. Willington-street ; George Jones,South-street ; Martin Hollein, Catherine-street ; and Thomas Crow, Catherine-street.—A warrant was issued against Bridget Murphy, Nelson-st., who failed to answer a summons. FINED FOR DRUNKENNESS. —Mary MUITIIV,I2, San key. street ; Mary Dodd, Nelson-street ; Edward Doyle,Crotn- well-st ; Thomas Devonport, Weston ; Mark Ryan,Hale- wood ; and George Lowe, Liverpool-road, Farnworth. UNFRIENDLY NEIGHBOURS.—EIizabeth Ashton, 14, Chatham-street, was summoned for using threats to Elizabeth Heyes on the 22nd inst. She was bound over to keep the peace in her own recognizance of £lO. THROWING WATER OVER A GIRL.—Ann Jennion, 33, Moon-street, was summoned at the instance of Michael Carroll for assaulting his child, Elizabeth, on the 20th inst.—She was bound over to keep the peace for three months, in her own recognizance of £lO and a surety of £5.

DRUNK ON LICENSED PuEmisEs.—Aaron Walker and John Dwerryhouse, Cronton, were summoned for being drunk on licensed premises, on the 14th inst.—P.C. Dodd stated that on the 14th inst. he visited the Black Horsa beerhouse, kept by Martha Houghton, and saw both defendants drunk. He drew the landlady's attention to them, and she refused to serve them.—Fined 10s. and costs.

STONE Timm', G.—Robert Thomas Jones, Warrington- road: George Harrison, Catherine-st. ; James McQuirk, Victoria-st., and Peter Gallagher, Victoria-st., were each fined for throwing stones in the streets. THEFT OF COAL.—James Cafferty, aged 13,0 f 68,Pear- st., and Thomas Curley. 13, of Pear-st., were charged with stealing 681bs. of coal, value 9d., from West Bank Dock, the property of Hutchinson's Trustees, on the 23rd July ; and Catherine Cafferty, mother of the boy of that name, was charged with receiving the same.— Mr. Routledge, manager, spoke to the coal produced being similar to that on the works.—P.C. Wood stated that at 12 30 on Monday he was on duty in West Bank, and saw the two boys carrying the sacks of coal pro- duced. He noticed the woman meet them,and take the bag from her son. On seeing witness she ran back into the siding. He searched herhouse and found more coal in bags. Superintendent Keighley stated that when they got hold of the parents they desired the Bench to make an example of them.—Curley was fined 10s., Jas. Cafferty was discharged, as they believed he was sent by his mother, and Catherine Cafferty was committed to prison fora month.

div.head: FRODSIIAM.
div.p: FRODSIIAM.

THE PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES' AND THE RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.—At the fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Rural Sanitary Authority on Tuesday afternoon, at Ditton Workhouse, under the presidency of Mr. John Mclntyre, the minutes of the Frodsham Parochial Com- mittee's last meeting, held on the previous Friday even- ing, under the chairmanship of Mr. A. Thomas, J.P., were read and submitted for confirmation. Tne minutes show that the Inspector had applied, on behalf of Mr. J. J. Crosfield, of Netherdale,for a certificate of occupation, the water supply to such house being described by the analyst "as a first-class water, and fit for domestic use." —The certificate was granted.—Several accounts were produced and passed for payment for repairs and improveinents to the main sewers. With regard to the notice served upon the owner of the Ship-street pro- perty, it was decided that, as the notice had now -almost expiaed, the Clerk write to Mrs. Scragg's solicitors and point out that the sanitary arrangements must be car- ried out forthwith.—The • superintending engineer reported that there had been 96 connections made with the water main to supply some 185 houses, about 50 houses being actually now connected with such main. which was considered satisfactory. After some discus- sion it was resolved that the committee charge for the water supplied to the various householders as and frcm the 15th of August next, at the rate already made known or at such other rate as will be sanctioned and approved by the Local Government Board. —The minutes were approved by the authority. VOLUNTEER CHURCH PARADE.-0a Sunday morning the members of the I Company ,f the 2 id (Earl of Ches- ter's) Volunteer Battalion Cheshire 11:ezirnent, stationed at Frodsham, attended the' Parish Church for divine service. They were accompanied by the Volunteer Band, and were commanded by Captain H. Harrison, Lieut. Ashton, and Colonel Aslston. SAD ACCIDENT TO A PLEASURING PARTY.—An accident of a somewhat alarming nature, and which might pos- sibly have been attended with much more serious result, occurred on Monday near the Overton Hills, Fr,dsliam. It appears that a party of school children were on their ways to the Hills referred to above for the purpose of picnicing. They were scholars from Alvanley Schools, and were attended by the Rev. E. P. Alexander, and their schoolmaster, Mr. J. M. Harnainan. The children were being conveyed in three lorries and two shandries, but when Toot Hill was reached, the breechin strap of the horse yoked to the last lorry broke and as the animal had now no power over it, the conveyance rushed down the hill. The second lorry was pulled out of the way but the one ahead was unable to -do s';) in time with the result that the runaway dashed into it and was thrown on its side. The cries of the frightened children brought some farm labourers to their aid, and they were extri- cated from their dangerous position. The assistance of Dr. Selby, of Frodsham, was requisitioned, who had the injured pleasure-seekers taken home. Nearly thirty children were on the lorry at the time of the occurrence, of which number about twelve were more or less inju red . Others were shaken, but not sufficiently to prevent their participation in the picnic. The horse was cut so severely that it was obliged to be shot.

div.head: FRODSHAM PETTY SE9SION3.
div.p: FRODSHAM PETTY SE9SION3.

WEDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Alfred Thomm, and T. Rigby. DISOBEDIENCE OF A SCHOOL ATTENDANCE ORDER.— Mary Ellen Blythe was summoned for disobeying a school attendance order by neglecting to send Arthur Jackson to school at Frodsham on June 25th.—The magistrates now made an order for the boy to be sent to the Maccles- field Industrial School for four years.

.„. GRAVE CHARGE AGAINST A FRODSIII3I MAN.—James Corker, of Miin-street, Frodsha in was brought up on a warrant charged with having inflicted grievous bodily harm upon John Ray, of Frodsham, by biting. and wounding the latter on the 21st. inst.—C wing to the non appearance of the legal adviser of the prisoner, only formal evidence was given in order to justify a remand. From this it appeared that the two men were near the Commercial Hotel on the prey bus Saturday night when they began to quarrel. During the progress of the dis- turbance it was alleged that Corker bit Ray through the lower lip and wounded his head. —The case was ad- journed tor a month, the prisoner being granted bail in his own recognizince of £5, and a surety of that amount.

div.head: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: NEWTON-LE-WILLOWS BOWLING CLUB.

A bowling handicap was played on the Newton Green on Saturday atternoon, the first prize being given by Mr. James Smith. There were 32 entries, and the brothers T. and W. Fairclough were left in the final, and they agreed to divide the first nrui second prize, the third prize fell to Mr. J. William- son, and thc fourth to Mr. Jos. Aitken.

ST. PETER'S Cliuncla CHOIR, NEWTON. - On Wednesday afternoon the boys belonging to the choir of above church to the number of about 20, had their first annual picnic at Daresbury at the residence of Mr. Whitley, a late resident at New- ton. They left Newton about two o'clock, and the day being fine they had a most enjoyable out. The Rev. 11. Monk was in charge of the party.

EARLESTOWN FOOTBALL CLUB. On Tuesday evening the playing members and committee of the club, and a few friends had their annual convivial evening at the Griffin Hall, Earles- town. About 2.0 sitt down to a capital knife and fork tea prepared by the host Mr. Thomas Hamer. After tea the evening was spent in a sociable manner, songs being given by Messrs. A. Levers, J. Williams, S. Swann, W. Clare and others.

div.head: DEATH OF A PUBLICAN AT PADGATE.
div.p: DEATH OF A PUBLICAN AT PADGATE.

The death occurred on Saturday night of Mr. Samuel Clare, who had been the landlord of the king and Queen Inn for the past 26 years. Deceased had been ailing for a long time, and his death was not altogether unexpected. lie was 57 years of age. lie has left a widow and three sons and two daughters to mourn his loss. The late Mr. Clare was a well-known thldfellow, having been initiated into the Con,4it ution Lodge (Warrington District) over 30 years ego. The deceased was a member of the Warrington Licensed Victuallers' Association, which body was presented at the funeral, which took place on Wednesday afiernoon at the Warri rig- ton Cemetery.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
THE CHEMICAL AND COPPER WORKERS' UNION.

At an executive meeting of the Chemical and Copper Workers' Union, held at the clubhouse, St. Helens, Mr. P. J. King, president, gave notice of his intention to resign that office. It was decided to call a general meeting on Sunday next, to consider the situation.

div.head: FIRE AT THE WATERLOO FOUNDRY.
div.p: FIRE AT THE WATERLOO FOUNDRY.

Between eight and nine o'clock on Tuesday night the St. Elelens Fire Brigade, under Superintendent Ruther- ford, was called to the Waterloo Foundry, where the roof of a shed near one of the largest boilers was found to be on fire. The flames were soon extinguished, and little damage was done.

div.head: LORD SALISgURY AND Sr. HELENS CHURCHES.
div.p: LORD SALISgURY AND Sr. HELENS CHURCHES.

The Marquis of Salisbury has forwarded £5O to the Rev. M. F. Binney, vicar of Sutton, St. Helens, on be- half of the building fund of All Saints' Church. Hii; lordship has also forwarded a similar sum to the Rev. J. W. Willink, vicar of S. Helens, towards the restoration of the parish church.
SWIMMING AT Si. HELENS.

At the Boundary-road baths, St. Helens, on Tuesday night, the monthly handicaps of the St. Helens Swim- ming club were held. The races were very exciting, J. Martlew, with four Feconds start, won the two lengths by the touch from Willie Sister; and C. Pennington, who was given five seconds lay Sha.rrock, won the three lengths race. Sharrock did not compete.

div.head: FOND OF GINGER BEER.
div.p: FOND OF GINGER BEER.

At St. Helens on Monday, two boys named Michael Lyons and James Mara, both of Bold-street, were charged with stealing two bottles of ginger-beer from a shop in Duke-street on Saturday evening. Both boys pleaded guilty.—Mara, who had been up previously for theft, was fined 53., or seven days, and Lyons was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. TESTIMONIAL TO THE MAYOR.

The presentation of the portraits of the Mayor of St. Helens ( Alderman A. Sinclair), the cost of which has been defrayed by public subscription, has been fixed for Wednesday, the Ist of August, at the Town Hall. The portraits have been painted by the Hon. John Collier, and are intnided as a public recognition of the services of the Mayor to the town during his fifty years' connection with it.
Low DEATH-RATE FOR ST. HELENS

The medical officer of St. Helens (Dr. Robertson), reported to the Health Committee on Wednesday, that during the Past fortnight the death-rate had been 15.0 against 18.7 in the previous fortnight, and 33.70 at the same time last year. The town was comparatively free from zymotic diseases, no deaths having occurred last week, and only five in the previous week. There had only been nineteen notifications of infectious disease.

div.head: COAL TRADE.
div.p: THE COAL TRADE.

Mc ssrs. Richard Evans and Co.,Limited, of St.Helens, Haydock, Golborne, and other places have sent an in- timation to thc shareholders in the following terms : " Your directors have very carefully considered the question of declaring an interim dividend, but, having regard to the continued depression in the coal trade, they do not consider themselves justified in declaring an interim dividend this year." IN BAD COVPANY. At St. Helens, on Monday, Margaret Ford and Ellen Davies, well known characters, were remanded cn a charge of stealing a silver lever 'catch frcm Martin Churchill. Peter Woods was also remanded on a charge of receiving the watch. When arrested Ellen Davies said "We had been drinking with him all day on Sat- urday. Maggie (meaning Ford) held him down while I took the watch." Ford said the watch was handed to Woods, but the latter denied it. The watch has not been recovered. ST. HELENS EX-FOOTBALLER AND THE LICENSING BUSINESS.

At the Police Court on Tuesday, Mr. J. 0. Swift, solicitor, applied to Alderman Nl`Bryde and Mr. W. J. Thomson, on behalf of Alexander M`Geachin, formerly a celebrated three-quarter in the St. Helens Recreation Football Club, for a tenvorary authority to sell intoxi- cating liquor at the New Church Tavern, Ashcroft-st. It was stated that Nl`Geachin was the son-in-law and sole executor of Mr. James Fairbrother, the holder of the license, who had died.—The application WAS granted.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT THE GAMBLE INSTITUTE.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT THE GAMBLE INSTITUTE.

A labourer named Bernard Flynn was engaged on Tuesday, in excavating for the foundations of the new Gamble Institute, Corporation-street, St. Helens, when a quantity of earth fell, and his legs and a part of his body were buried. While in this position a large stone and other delleis fell upon his head, and injured him severely. He was got out, and taken on the ambulance to the Providence Hospital, where he was attended by Dr. Bellew, who found that he had three ribs broken and severe contusions and bruises on the head and body. Another man, named Edward Carney, had a narrow escape of being injured.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL VACANCY AT WEISTON.
div.p: COUNTY COUNCIL VACANCY AT WEISTON.

Mr. Muspratt, deputy returning officer, sat at the boardroom Whiston, Prescot, on Tuesday, to hear and decide objections to the nomination papers of Mr. William Gamble and Mr. William Gibbings, candidates for the Whis'on Division of the Lancashire County Council. The proceedings were private, but at the close it was stated that Mr. Holland Owen. on behalf of Mr. Gamble, had made several objections to Mr. Gibbings's nomination paper. The objections were not entertained, and the election will take place on Monday. Mr. Gib- bings did not take any objections to the five nomina- tion papers of Mr. Gamble.

div.head: DEITH FROM SC:ILDS.
div.p: DEITH FROM SC:ILDS.

The death was reported to the police on Saturday morning, of Francis Bradley, aged five years, son of a chemical labourer, who resided at Marshall's Cross. Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest on Tuesday, at the Griffin Inn, S. Helens, on the body of Francia Bradley, aged five years, son of Francis Bradley, a chemical w‘.rk -r. of Marshall's Cross. On Tuesday, the 10th inst., the child was rocking in front of the fire, on which was a pan of boiling water. The mother went to stop him, but before she got near enough he cuught the handle of the pan, bringing the water over him.—A verdict of " accidental death " was returned.
SUBSIDENCE OF A RAILWAY BRIDGE.

Throughout the whole of Sunday and Monday a gang of men, under the direction of Mr. Vernon, per- manent way inspector, Edge-hill ; Mr. Gregson, chief traffiz inspector, and Permanent-way Inspector Taylor, Edge-hill, were engaged laying new girders across the railway bridge at Peasley Cross-lane, St. Helyns. In consequence of colliery operations in the district, the road and the bridge in question have continually sub- sided, and very frequently the railway company hare to raise the bridge to make the buttresses higher, so as to keep the line level. The company recently resolved to practically reconstruct the bridge by placing new gir- ders across, which would be easier to raise than those which have formed the bridge for many years. The work was one of considerable difficulty on account of the heavy traffic over the bridge. During the period named the traffic was worked on a single line under the management of Acting-Inspector T. Manning.

div.head: SUPPOSED SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: SUPPOSED SUICIDE AT ST. HELENS.

The body of a man was discovered on Monday after- noon, in an old stone delph, off Howard's-lane, near Springfield. Eccleston, St. Helens. Mrs. Ashcroft, of Back Bolton-street, St. Helens, who was on a visit to some friends in the neighbourhood, white walking near the delph, saw the body in the water. She raised an alarm, and Police-convtable Simpson dragged the body out and conveyed it to the Griffin Inn, Eccleston. As there were no marks of violence on the body, and nothing but a small portion of tobacco in the pockets.it was supposed to be a case of suicide.—At the Griffin Inn, Eccleston, St. Helens, on Wednesday, Mr. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest on the body,which was discovered to be that of John Hale, collier, aged thirty- five. Margaret Hale, the widow, said she and her hus- band last lived at 27; Higher-Parr.st., St. Helens. He was out of work, and they had to go out of the house three weeks last Monday, which was the last time she saw him alive. There was no reason why he should take his life, but he had said in hospital, when he was suffer- ing great pain, that if he could get out he would drown himself. After other evidence, the jury returned a ver- dict of "Found drowned," there being no evidence to show how deceased got into the water. MEETING OF RAILWAY MEN. On Sunday afternoon a large gathering of railw ty ser- vants was held in the People's Palace, St. Helens, Mr. T. Humphreys occupying the chair. Tile meeting had been called by Mr. Thomas Manning (a local railway servant) in connection with the Northern District of the Railway Servants' Universal Interchange Privilege Ticket Move- ment, and addresses were given explaining the objects of the movement. by Mr. R. Bradshaw, chairmin of the district, and Mr. J. Meade, secretary. It was stated that the inevement had been in operation for twelve months nHi good results. A number of steatnboat companies had granted their is quests te, the extent of half fares for adults and q tarter fares for children under fifteen years of aee. Detailed arrangements had been e, complt t- 1 fer the issue of interchange privilge ti•k •ts between the Gr, at Northern Cempany and the Mioland Company. To the con re pendence sent to the maiieers of other con parries courteous and encouraging replies had been received. Appeals were made to the railway servants for them to use every endeavour to prevent abuse of the privilege. The following resolutions were passed unanimously :—" That this mass meeting of railway men tenders our sincere that ks to the several manaeers, who have interes'ed neinselves on our behalf and ask them ti use their 1, fluence to bring ab mut the universal interchange of privilege tickets as spf eddy as possible. In the event of the same belies granted we pledge ourselves tn protect the same from any abuse whatever ;" and " That this mass meeting of railway men of St. Helens expresses satisfaction at the several concessions obtained by the northern committee, and hereby pledge ourselves to render them all the help and assistance in our power, and also to elect a delegate to , represent us s•n th n,r!hernc,onvoittee." Mr. R. Fowles was elected cies gst •, and the following were appointed to form a local committee to represent the various de- partments i—Lecal, Mr. T. Humphreys; signal, Mr. T. Manning ; permanent way. Mr. John Fairclough ; coach- ing, Mr. A. Merrill ; sheeting, Mr. J. Jahnson ; =Mc, Mr. H. Hardy ; and goode, Mr. Jones.

div.head: BORTONWOOD MAN'S VISIT TO Sr. HELENS.
div.p: A BORTONWOOD MAN'S VISIT TO Sr. HELENS.

At St. delens on Wednesday, Margaret Ford and Ellen Davies, of Sandfield-crescent, were charged under remand with stealing a silver lever watch from the per- son of Martin Churchill, a collier, of Burtonwood. Peter Woods, a young fellow, was also charged with receiving the watch knowing it to have been stolen. Prosecutor and the two female prissners were drinking together on Saturday night in the Liverpool Inn, Liverpool-road. Churchill did not know when he lelt the public-house, but he found himself in Brook-street, a distance away, about nine o'clock. He then missed his watch. Pris- oners were arrested on Sunday. Davies said Churchill gave her the watch instead of money, and then wanted it back again.—Ford and Woods denied having seen it. —All three prisoners were committed to the assiz2s for trial.
SPREE OF A FISHDEALER.

At the St. Helens Police Court, on Monday,a fish sales- man named William Dutton, living in Crab-street, St. Helens, was charged with stealing 135., the property of his employer, John Henry Nickson, a fish dealer. Prisoner was sent out on Friday last with another man with a cartload of fish, and after selling fish to the amount of 13s. he told the man he was going into the next street to get a newspaper. He went awav,and did mat return until arrested on a warrant. Mr.J.P. Mearns, who prosecuted, said Mr. Nickson had been defrauded by his men from time to time, and had taken the proceed- ings against prisoner in order to put a stop to the practice.—Prisoner said he intended to return, but got drinking. He would refund the money in a couple of days.—Mr.Mearras asked for a small fine only —Prisoner was bound over in £2 to come up for juidgn,tnt when called upon.

div.p: EA.RLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
VIADUCT INSTITUTE BOWLING CLUE.

In connection with the above club, a bowling handicap was played on Saturday afternoon. Owing to the recent rain, the green was in a sodden con- dition. There was a large entry, and bowling was up to the average. The first prize, a silver cruet, given by Mr. W. Melling, was won by W. Marrow, junr., 2ad prize, copper kettle, 3. McAteer,3rd prize set of jugs, G. Houghton. The prizes were pre- sented to the winners on the green, by the president Mr. Jos. Emmett.

div.head: COLLINS GREEN COLLIERY EXCURSrON.
div.p: COLLINS GREEN COLLIERY EXCURSrON.

The annual excursion of the employe; at the above collieries took place on Saturday to Black- pool. A couple of special trains left Collins Green shortly after six o'clock, conveying upwards of 1,000 passengers, to the favourite Lancashire sea- side resort. The weather was fine during the greater part of the day, and the excursionists enjoyed themselies to the fullest extent, Visits to the pier, winter gardens, the tower and other places of in- terest were paid, and bathing was indulged in by many. The return journey was calpleted shortly after nine o'clock.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S SUNDAY SCHOOL.

On Saturday the scholars attending the above school, who have participated in the weekly con- tribution for a picnic, left Earlestown about 9.30 in four conveyances belonging to Messrs. Maginn Bros., of Warrington, for Hale, which they reached about 11.30. The " Childe a Hale" was made the headquarters of the party, and after lunch, the children rambled about the village, and down to the river side, where they paddled about in the water for some time. Tea was served in the large room attached to the hotel, after which a visit was paid to Hale Hall Park, by the kind permission of Col. Ireland Blackburne. There were one or two smart showers, but op the whole the day was favourable for the outing. The party left Hale about 7 o'clock and reached Earlestowa about 9.30.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLARS.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLARS.

The usual weekly session of the Hope of Earles- town Lodge of Good Templars, was held in the Co- operative Hall, Earlestown on Monday evening when there was an exceptionally large attendance of members,presided over by Bro. Joseph Anderton C.T.—After the lodge had been formally opened, 13, candidates were initiated, and several others pro- posed for membership, Bro. W. If. Dale secretary gave a report on the" Musical Instrument fund " ; showing further contrlbutions,and satisfactory pro- gress. Other items, including date, and place, for Lodge pic-nic, were laid over to the next session. An open meeting having been arranged for, the attendance was considerably increased, the room being crowded in every part. A spe,.:ial musical programeie had been provided, for which Bro. G. Clarke, assistant secretary was responsible. The following items were rendered in a satisfactory and creditable manner,the choir of 20 voices,trained by Bro. Edwards, performing the part remarkably well :—Glee " The village choristers," organ solo, Bro. W. Willis, solo "The lost chord," Bro. 0. Sdwards, part song "The sleighing song," choir, solo," The echo boy,"Sister Mrs. Willis, solo," Angels ever bright and fair," Sister Mrs. Wakefield, duet, " Lord of all power and might," Sisters Holliday and L. Barr. Solo," The old clock,"Bro. o.Edwards, recitation, " I'm a Templar," Bro. G. E. Warburton; solo and chorus,"Hark the Vesper hymn is stealing," Miss Barcroft and choir. Bro. Clarke in a few re- marks thanked the friends present, and referred to the unprecedented success that had marked the Lodge's progress during the present quarter, 49 new members having joined. He urged non-members. to unite and help on the good work in Earlestown A very successful and encouraging meeting was afterwards brought to a close.

div.head: (O OD TEMPLIRY.
div.p: (O OD TEMPLIRY.

The usual weekly meeting of the Earlestawn Ebenezer Lodge, took place in the Co-operative Hall on Tuesday night, Bro. J. Taylor presiding. There were six admitted to membership, after which the lodge was thrown open. A first class programme was proceeiled with. for which the Tem- perance Mission Lodge of Warrington. was respon- sible. The following took part, Bros. Sinister, Littlefair, Nurse. Mortimore, ~mith, Tomlin and Bradley, Sister Nurse, and juvenile Sister Nurse. Alter the programme a coffee supper was provided for the visitors and members to which about fifty sat down. A vote ot thanks was tendered to the visitors and the meeting closed about 10 p.m.
SUGGESTED ALTERATION OF COUNTY COURT DISTRICTS.

A letter has been —r-e-ce-i-Ced -by Mr. J. W. Green solicitor, St. Helens, from the Lord Chancellor respecting the memorial of the Haydock tradesmen praying that Haydock might be transferred from the I%;e4lrerins I w t°lit County Court district into that of S reported some time ago that Mr. Green had communicated with the Lord Chan- cellor upon the subject, and in reply,the Lord Chan- cellor has now written that as far as he can ascer- tain there has been no case of any difficulty arising through the district of Haydock being attached to the Warrington court, and he does not think the Committee to whom Platters of the kind are referred are likely to advise a change. It is understood that Mr. Green, acting on the instructions of the Ilaydock tradesmen, will again move in the matter by asking the Hon. T. W. Legh, 11,P., personally to approach the Lord Chancellor.

div.head: GOOD TEMPLAR'S DISTRICT MEETING.
div.p: GOOD TEMPLAR'S DISTRICT MEETING.

The quarterly meeting of the District Council of Juvenile Templars of South West Lancashire was held in Raffles' Memorial Rooms, Liverpool, on Saturday. There was a good attendance of super- intendents and representstives f• 0111 all parts of the district ; Bro. E. Newman, D.S.J.T , of Earlestown presiding. The reports of the various temples showed the Juvenile Order generally to be progress, ing, there being 1,063 juvenile members in 30 temples and 167 adult honorary members. Bro. A. Newell, P.D.S.J,T., reported on the projected dE- monstrations to be held in Liverpool on ..ieptember 4,5, and 6th to celebrate the 22nd anniversary of the Juvenile Order. Bro. Newell moved and *Bro. li,rkus seconded and it was unanimously resolved by standing vote, that an expre.ssion of sincere con- dolence be sent to Sister Mrs. Browne, G.S.J.T„ of London, recently bereaved by the sv.dden death of Bro. Browne. A general discussion was earnestly tak,n op cn the qaestion of betting and gambling, the following rei,o'.ution being unanimously adopted : " This District Council of Juvenile Templars having during the past 22 years carried on an active crusa,te against the vice of gambling, hereby strongly protests against any encourage- ment of betting, &c., and respectfully :urges upon I ,cal authorities to take steps for its suppres- sion." Thanks were accorded the friends for their arrangements and a very useful and encouraging session closed for tea about six p.m. A united ; gathering of temple Superillteiadeatt NYLti, aftr- wards held.
