LIMITED. LLANELLI'. SOUTH WALES.
BEFORE Tlik MAGISTRATES.

THEFT OF A HORSE AT WARRINGTON. At the Warrington Borough Police Court on Tuesday morning. Henry Hankinson, a middle-aged man, well known to the police, was charged with stealing from the stable of James Newton, Orford-lane, some time between 11 p.m. on the 20th inst and 4.30 a.m. on the 21st inst, a horse, bridle and loin cloth value in all £l2. The Chief Constable in his statement to the magistrates said that the complainant was a contractor' and had his premises and stables at 15. Orford-lane. The prisoner was a fustian cutter of Culcheth but now called himself a stone mason. He was a man under police supervision, and had recently been set at liberty. At eleven o'clock on Friday night the complainant saw his horse safe in the stable. At 430. the next morning, a horse was missing together with a bridle, and horse cloth. Information was immediately given to the police and telephone messages were sent to various plases. Every inquiry was made during Saturday, Sunday and Monday. At mid-day on Monday, Mr. Newton and D. S. Monaghan proceeded in a trap to Manchester, and from inquiries, they got some valuable information. They went to Salford, and ascertained that the prisoner arrived there about six o'clock on Saturday morning, and that he went to the house of Alice Walker, at 47, Hampson-st., who kept stables. Permission had been given the prisoner to put a horse up in the stables, but at eleven o'clock the same morning he took it away again. From further inquiries made, it was found that the prisoner bad sold the horse for 50s. to a coal dealer at Salford named William Charlton. Detective Monaghan went to Charlton's premises and found the stolen horse, bridle, and cloth at seven o'clock. The complainant identified it as his property and the horse was sent by rail to War- rington. About eight o'clock Detective Monaghan got the assistance of a Salford detective, and in walking along Ellen-st. they met the prisoner, and took him into custody. He was identified as the man who had engaged a stall at Walker's stables, and also by William Chatlton as the man from whom he had bought the horse. Mr. Charlton also handed to D.S. Monaghan a receipt for the money paid to the prisoner for the horse. Prisoner was brought to Warrington and on the way he told Monaghan "It will be a seven far me this will." On being charged with the theft he replied " yes, it is right." Evidence in corroboration of Mr. Hunt's statement was given by Messrs. James Newton, J. Jones, 16, Anderson-street, Salford, William Charlton, 58, Oldfield-st. Salford, and D.S. Monaghan. Questioned by Mr. Fleming as to whether he did not think it strange for the prisoner to accept 50s. for a horse valued at £l2, the witness Charl- ton said that a man named Parkinson who was with the prisoner told him that the horse was all right. He did not consider the horse worth £l2 as it was full of sores. Mr. Hunt said he thought it only fair to say that Charl- ton bore a very good character, and assisted the police in every way to capture the prisoner. The prisoner on being asked if he had anything to say replied," Be as lenient as ever you can with me." He was committed to Liverpool Assizes for trial.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
FiIUDAY. —Before Alderman Harrison (chairman), Alder- man Wright, Councillor H. Roberts, Dr. Gornall, and

Mr. S. Wright. SHOCKING ASSAULT ON A WlFE—Benjamin Crompton, of 12, Platt-street, was charged was having on the 19th Inst. unlawfully assaulted and beaten his wife, Emma Crompton. The complainant, who appeared with her face badly mauled, stated that the previous day the prisoner sent for a woman to take some of his ciotliesta the pawnshop. The woman came but refused to take them whereupon the prisoner laid the blame on witness. He knocked her to the floor and struck her several times in the face with his fists. Two neighbours gave evidence as to finding the complainant lying on the floor suffering from wcunds in the face.—Sergeant Chantler stated that he arrested the prisoner the previous night, ard charged him with the offence. He stated that he would say nothing about it then. From papers found on the pri- soner there was no doubt but that he was a betting man. The complainant was a very respectable woman. The prisoner had practically no defence, simply stating that he wanted a few shillings and was unable to get them from his wife. He was srnt to gaol for one month hard labour, a sf paration order was granted, and the prisoner was ordered to contribute 10s. per week towards his wife's maintenance when lie came out of gaol. MAKING A FALSE ATTESTATION.—ItiChard Disley, last from Liverpool, was charged with having been in the Army Reserve (King's Liverpool Regiment), and after- wards fraudulently enlisting in the Lancashire Artillery, stating that he had never been in her Majesty's service. Two military officers proved the case. P.C. Turner who apprehended the prisoner on Wednesday morning ap- plied for the usual reward which was granted. The prisoner was sent to gaol for one month. A SUSPICIOUS TRANSACTION.—George Connolley, no settled abode, was charged with being a convieted thief found upon the enclosed premises of Wm. Plinston, Back Aikin-st., at 12.40 that morning, for the purpose of com- mitting a felony. Mr. Plinston stated that whilst he was in bed at the time stated one of his windows was opened, and a glass near the window was broken. He heard the fall of glass and went downstairs, and found the window thrown open. Tbe prisoner, who had occa- sionally done work for witness, was found lying down riear to the back-kitchen window. He thought the "catch "of the window must have been pushed back with a knife. The Chief Constable stated that the pris- oner would no doubt find a piece of hoop-iron in the complainant's yard,which would be handy to push back the catch. The magistrates committed the prisoner to gaol for one month bard labour. A SLEEPER Our.—John McCue, no fixed abode, was charged with sleeping on the enclosed premises of Bewsey Forge, and having no visible means of subsistence. Sergeant Lawrence deposed that from complaints he had received, he went to the works at four o'clock that morning and found the prisoner asleep. He was lying near to a shed from where they had had a r6bbery cf tools. Tne prison( r had been brought before the magis- trates previously on a similar charge. He was sent to gaol for 14 days hard labour. OVERCROWDING A FIOUSE.—John Hewitt, 5, Rose-yard, was summoned for having on the 11th- inst. taken lodgers without being registered.—lnspector Powell stated that in company with P.C. Bruen he visited the defendant's bnuse on the d ite named at two o'clock in the morning. On entering the house he found a woman sleeping on an old bed downstairs. Upstairs he found the defendant, his wife, and a daughter aged 15 sle‘-ping in one bed. The house was in a filthy c• ndition. The defendant was reported to the sanitary committee for a similar offence in April, 1889, and he was then cautioned by the committee. The house was only adapted for two I persons, and at the time of the visit be found four ' sleeping in it. PC. Bruhn gave corroborative evidence. A -fine of 10a. including costs -vas imposed.

CRUELTY TO & HORSE.—Robert Mason, Worsley-st., Pemberton, was charged with cruelly illtreating a horse at Warrington on the 9th inst. Inspector Luff deposed that on the date named he saw the defendant in charge of a grey mare, drawing a load of potatoes. Witness saw that the mare was very lame and stopped it. On examining it he found that the knee was broken and that there w:is a sore where the skin had been broken. The tendons were also strained, and the animal was totally unfit for work. The horse was drawing a load of about one ton, and the defendant had about 13 or 14 miles to go. Sergeant Cheney gave corroborative evi- dence. Defendant was fined the costs, 103. SATURDAY.—Before Mr. J. Burgess. ANOTHER WINDOW BREAKER.—Ann Donnallan was charged with wilfully breaking several panes of glass, value 33. 6d., the property of Richard Bond. Knutsford- road, on Saturday the 14:h Of July.—P.S. Chantler said that he arrested the prisoner at her house on Friday, the 20 Ii inst. and charged her with the offence, to which she replied "I did it in a fit of temper."—Prisoner was fined 20s. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment.. - -

- - MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Harrison, Messrs. J. W. Hayward and S. Wright. DRUNK AND DISORDHRLY.—The following were dealt with for this offence : Jos. Warburton, hawker, Edels- ten's-yard (23rd appearance) 10s. and costs; Jos. Dig- nail, hawker, Sharp-st., 5. and costs; Michael Milligan, iron worker, Dallam-lane, Si. and costs; Julia Shields, Filling's Court, Diahst.. ss. and costs; Bryan Scully, labourer, 6, Old-road. ss. and costs. ASSAULTING THE POLICE.—James Carrington, rivetter, Friar's Green was charged with tieing drunk and dis- orderly in Mersey-st. on Saturday night, and also charged with assaulting P.C. Fish at the same time and place. Prisoner was further charged with doing wilful damage to a window to the amount of one shilling.— P.C. Fish deposed that on Saturday night he received a complaint of the prisoner's conduct in Mersey-st. He proceeded there and saw the prisoner drunk, and also saw him fall against a window which the prisoner broke. Witness took him into custody whereupon he became very disorderly and kicked witness on the legs.—P.C. Smith gave evidence as to going to the assistance of P.C. Fish, and spoke of the prisoner's disorderly conduct.— P.S. Chanties also gave evidence. A fine of 10s. and costs or 14 days' imprisonment was imposed. SLEEPING IN A. STABLE.—Two youths named Patrick Roberts, 108, Pierpoint-at. and Bernard Hennigan, 12, Buckley-st., were charged with being rogues and vaga- bonds found sleeping in a stable belonging to Jos. Quinn, , without havir'es any visible means of subsistence.—P.C. Evans proved the case. As they had previously ap- peared before the magistrates charged with a similar I offence they were committed to gaol for seven days' hard labour. A WARNING TO BOYS.—Hugh Je kes, 12 years of age, residing with his parents at 14, Arpley-st., was charged with throwing stones to the danger of passengers in Museum-st., on the 1.5.11 inst.—P.C. Barnett stated that he saw the defendant throwing stones on Trinity schools on the date named.—The magistrates fined the defend- ant 2s. 6d. PUGNACIOUS WOMEN.—Jane Cartledge, 8, Silver-square and Elizabeth Travis, 12, Morris-yard were both charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting in Morris's-yard on the 17th inst. P.C. Foster proved the case and said he separated the two defendants. 'I hey told the magistrates that "it was over the children" that they had fought. The magistrates ordered them to pay the coats 7s. each and to be bound over to keep the peace in sureties of £5 each. A BUTCHER AND His HORSE.—John Coggins, butcher, 50 Ashton-street, was charged with driving a horse and trap to the danger sf passengers in Bewsey-street on the 17th inst. Sergeant Cheney deposed that on the after- noon of the date named he was in Bewsey-street in com- pany with Sergeant Lawrence when he saw the defen- dant driving a horse and trap at a furious rate, He con- sidered that the horse was going at the rate of 14 or 15 miles an hour. There were a few children near Wycliffe schools at the time, and a fatal accident occurred there sometime age through furious driving. The defendant appeared to be showing the horse to another butcher who was in the trap with him. Sergeant Lawrence gave corroborative evidence. The defendant denied the charge and called as a witness, Mr. Plinston of Bewsey-street, who stated that the defendant was trotting the horse and showing it to another man. He considered that the de- fendant was not driving furiously. The magistrates imposed a fine of 2s. 6d. 'PITCH AND Toss."—Thomas Foster, (18) 2, Appleton- street and James WheTan (17) 3, Appleton-street were each fined 57,. and costs for playing at a game of chance called " pitch and toss " in Appleton-street on the 15th inst.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. R. Garnett (chairman), and Mr. J. H. Fleming. A DEsEntrEa.—James Conway was charged with being a deserter from Her Majesty's 2nd limg's 14' verpool Regi- ment; since the 16th inst. Prisoner pleaded guilty. P.C. Wood who apprehended the prisoner the previous night was granted the usual reward. The prisoner was com- mitted to Strangeways gaol to await an escort. A BOY'S TaF.rr.—Frederick Pierpoint, 41 Ellen-street, a respectably dressed boy about fourteen years of age, was charged with stealing from the roof of some dwell- ing-houses, about 4.40 that morning, a quantity of lead the property of Messrs. Tunstall.—Mr. Pemberton on behalf of Messrs. Tunstall said they did not wish to prosecute under the circumstances. The defendant was therefore dismissed with a caution. A LODGER AND HIS LANDLORD.—AIfred Maloney, who had for a sh,rt time been residing at 1 Neston-street, Liverpool, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Bank Quay bridge the previous night, and also with assaulting Edward Jordan. P.C. Evans gave evidence as to the drunken condition of the prisoner on the pre- vious evening. Eiward Jordan stated that at 9.30 p.m. on Monday he went home to prepare himself for work. He found the prisoner there in a drunken condition. Witness asked him what he was doing there, and the prisoner told him to mind his own business. Witness told him to go out, whereupon the prisoner struck him in the eye, greatly discolouring it. Be did not wish to press the case against the prisoner as he had known him for many years, he having been a lodger at his house. The magistrates fined him 103. including costs. THIIRSDAY.—Before Major Ridgway (chairman), and Councillor J. Fairclough. A SUSPICIOUS CHARACTER.—Thomas Newt.n.Winwick was charged with being found in possession of a ladies' umbrella, supposed to have been stolen. P.C. Barnett (27) stated that he met the prisoner in Buttermarket-st. on the previous night with the umbrella in his possess -n As he failed to give a satisfactory accunt of it, lie was brought to the police station, and when searched a gill glass, three plates,and a brass rule were also found upon him. He said that the rule had been given to him hy a lad who had picked it up in the market.-1 he prisoner was remanded until Monday on the application of the Chief Constable. The umbrella has the letters F.A.R. engraved on the handle in oh i English character.

SERIOUS CHARGE AGAINST A BLACKSMITH.--tienry Wright, a blacksmith, of Aston-by-SW[on, was charged with having trespassed in pursuit of f2aine on land occu- pied by William Wilkinson, farmer, Aston-by-Sutton,on the 12th inst. The prosecutor was represented by Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, and the defendant by Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins, of Warrington.—Mr. Knowles said that at ahout ' four o'clocit•on the morning of tile above day James loin- linsos,a gmekeeper employed by his client was watching the district in which the defendant resided when lie saw the Latter leave his dwelling and wall( in the direction of Aston Heath with a gun. The gamekeeper kept the de- fendant in view and saw him enter a field owned by Mr.' Robert Wade. The defendant was then f, r a moment lost sight of behind a hedge and shortly a fterwulla Tom- linson saw smoke issu:. from the barrel of a gun over Mr. Wilkinson's land. The keeper hurried towards the spot and taw Wright get over a fence into Wilkinson's field. After looking about tor a few moments Wright came back and when aecostrd by Tomlinson said he had shot at a rabbit on a public footpath ard thinking that it had run into the field he had gone there to lock for it.—James Temlinsonganneke'per. sursported the statnnent made be Mr. Knowles. In reply to Mr. Jenkirs the, keeper denied the existence of ill-feeling La tween himself and tile defendant. He was nnt aware that Mr, lVade had authorised Wright to shoot over 1.i4 land and no sueli authoriifbad been read over to him by the defendant's daugl.ter.--Mr. Jenkins in defendin,, characterised the case as a most trumpery one. Wriaht was a highly res- pectable man, and did certain work for Mr. Wade who allowed him the privilege of shooting a few rabbits,. The defendant had shot the gun but he was on Mr. Wade's

div.p: WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT.

Mom)Ay.—Before Messrs. J. Tinsley and S. R. Armitage. A QUARREL AT RIXTON.—James Jury, an Irishman, was charged with committing a breach of the peace by fighting at Rixton on the previous day, and further with having assaulted Joseph Hinton on the same occasion. P.C. Ryder said he saw the complainant lying on the floor with his head covered with blood. He was sur- rounded by a crowd of people. He said the prisoner had kicked him on the head whilst he wagon the ground. Joseph Hinton, the complainant, stated that he was in the prisoner's company on the previous afternoon about six o'clock, but subsequently separated from him. As he was coming along the road later on he was knocked down by somebody, and prisoner kicked him on the head whilst he lay on the ground. Prisoner, in his defence, stated that he went into a public-house, where the complainant and a number of others were seated. One of complainant's mates wanted him to fight, and he refused, and the landlord turned complainant and his companions out. He stayed in the house half-an-tour, and when he went out there were a number of people fighting, and someone who was lying on the flaor got hold of his legs. He jerked his foot loose, but did not kick anybody. Prisoner was bound over to keep the peace. DRUNKENNESS.—For this offence at Rixton, Joseph Roberts was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.

TUESDAY.—Before Mr. James Tinsley. A SLEEPER OUT.—Maria Barker, no fixed abode, was sent to gaol for seven days for sleeping in an outhouse at Orford, early that morning. P.C. Williams proved the case.

Browne, of Warrington, appeared for the defence.—P.S. Garner stated that at half-past 10 p.m.on the day riamed,he visited the Fleece Hotel and found the defendant drunk. On charging him with it the defendant said " I am all right sergeant " and then took him into the " snuggery " and asked him not to report it because of his wife and family. A CABDRIVER'S CLAIM.—A cabdriver named Peter White claimed from the proprietress of the Patten Arm, Fl-tel (Mrs. Kiernan) the sum of Bs. for loss of time and wages due. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, appeared for the defendant. The complainant stated that he was in the employ of the defendant 7 hours. Be was told by Mr. 51aginn that Lie would find work if he went to the hotel. The; defendant's daughter engaged him. At 9.30 p.m., when he had finished his work, the defendant offered him a shilling,which he refused to accep*. Mr. Browne, for the defence, called Mrs. Kiernan, who said that the plaintiff returned to the hotel drunk, and only brought 2s. as a fare to oolston. She offered him is. fid, which she considered was a fair wage for half-a-day's work. She usually paid cabdrivers 18. a week.—His Honour said he would allow the plaintiff Is. 6d. for the half- day's work.

div.head: ST. HELENS MAN " PRESSGANGED."
div.p: A ST. HELENS MAN " PRESSGANGED."

At the Kirkham Police Court, on Wednesday, a case was heard in which Patrick Rowe. a labourer, residing at 25, Liverpool-street, St. Helens, sought to recover ..£l4 7e. 61 from Frank Oakes, master of the full-rigged three-masted sailing-ship ArLaurin. for wages due.—Mr. H. L. Riley, solicitor, St. Helens, who appeared for plaintiff, stated that the proceedings were instituted under the Merchant Shipping Act, to recover wages for a voyage at sea, a voyage which had been completed at Fleetwood.—Plaintiff then entPred the box, and stated that up to S,turrlay, April 7, 1894, he was employed as a fireman at Kingman, State of Maine, U.S.A. He had been under a doctor a short time pre- viously, but seemPd te get no better, so on the 7th April he went down to Bangor, a coast town some forty miles off, for medicine. He stayed there the ,following day (Sunday), and on Monday met a friend named Tracey, Who asked him whether he would like to go on a sailing ship. Plaintiff replied in the negative to each question hut Tracey took him into a saloon kept by " a friend of his." 'There, he allezed, whether with Tracey's know- lrdge or not, he was drugged. The following day ("rues- day, the 10th) he woke up and found him- self on board the sailing ship M`Laurin, of which defendant Frank L. Oakes was captain. He was quite nnabie to eat the reugh stuff the men had to put up with,which was biscuits and rotten salt horse. He certainly complained more of the fond than of the treatment he otherwise pers uvally received on boarl There was not a man in the crew but was hit or kicked more or less. He (plaintiff) was only hit once, by the first mate, but the first and sPeond mates and the boat- swain used to threaten him with the :es'. Sometimes he had not an hour's rest in the t wenty-fouro nd he regarded six WPf IE3 on the vessel as bad as 12 month 7; ashore. Sarno of the crew were foreigners (Dutchmen),whom he cauld not understand, hut he found out from the Briti3hers that every ore, of them had been " pressed" liee him- self. One was a Nova Scotian named Ike Spieer, and he was so frightened at the threats of the second mate that in trs hg ti Pet hold cf a block he missed his foot- ing and fell overboard. The captain threw a line to Spicer, who was then fr a-tern, and the be atswain threw a plank. There ought to have been a boat at the stern ready te lower insta but there was none. The two boats the vessel carried were filled with lumber. It would have tak -ra nearly an our to launch one of them, se Spicer was left to drewn, " and there was one man le" to pay 'veers to." The vessel was houndt for China, but first it had to call at Fleetwood to unload its cargo of wood pulp (2.500 te,ne), then to call at Cardiff for a cargo ef coal for China. When they reached Feet- wood nnm of the crew,an American, took his bed beards and swam ashen, goaded to it by s+arvation. fle had mat been paid,ner had a ny of the others ein arrival at Fleet- wood been paid. He was discharged on the 30 h May. Ile did not knew whether he was written down an ab(e- bedied seaman or an oroinary seaman ; the former, the crew said, got .$23 a month and the latter $lB a month. He claimed for four months up the 4th July. Six weeks of the actual voyage would amount to £7 3s, 9 l.—There being no defence, the magistrates—Messrs. B mker. Buckley, Catterallemil Brynint,—.,t once retired, end on their return ordered defendant to pay £lO 2. 61. in- cluding advocates' fees on two occasions (£2 18 6).)

div.head: PHENOMENAL WEATHER IN VARIOUS PARTS OF THE COUNTRY.
div.p: PHENOMENAL WEATHER IN VARIOUS PARTS OF THE COUNTRY.

Telegrams from various parts of the country report heavy thunderstorms on Wednesday, and much damage to crops. During a severe thunderstorm which visited Montgomeryshire in the afternoon five valuable head of cattle, the property of Mr. Davies, farmer, Rhos, Llan- d rinio, near Oswestry, were struck dead by lightning. Rain fell in torrents, and the lightning was most vivid. lit Chester the phenomenal scene of several inches of hailstones of enormous sin lying on the street on a hot July afternoon was witnessed. The early afterooon was close and oppressive. There was a light easterly wind, and the sky soon assumed a threatening aspect to wind-ward. Shortly after four o'clock thunder was heard rumbling in the distance, and just before five, the storm broke over the city. The sky was inky black, the lighting was very vivid, and the thunder peals culminated in an appalling crashlike discharge of heavy ordnance. Rain and hail then fell in an almost solid sheet,and the street channels being unable to carry off the water,the thoroughfares were for the nonce com- plete watetcourses. The hailstones, which were about half an inch in diameter, soon accumulated and grass lands especially showed a surface of wintery whiteness. Lads pelted each other with handfuls of ice gathered from the streets,and the proverbial" oldest inhabitant" was non-plussed ta• find a match to such an atmospheric peculiarity. From the scene presented in Grosvenor Park, wheSe flowers and foliage have been ruined, enormous damage must have been done to the fruit and indeed all growing crops. At the Groves a branch of the main sewer, under the terrific pressure, burst, tearing up the ground for yards around and discharging a large volume of water, rising several feet in the air. Low-lying dwellings in various portions of the city were flooded,and the inhabi- tants put to- considerable discomfort and inconvenience. Fortunately the storm soon passed over in a northwes- terly direction, and the sky afterwards cleared. During a severe thunderstorm at Burulay, extensive canines works in Elm-street, belonging to Mr. Robeit Hirsforere struck by lightening. The building was soon a mass of flame and the -roof collapsed immedi- ately alter the firemen got to work. Tim premises which' were two storeys high, were gutted. The Blackburn district was visited by a thunderstorm of unusual severity, during the height of which the house of Mr. Councillor Hamer was struck, theichief Chimney being demolished. Fortunately no one was injured. A heavy storm, accompanied bylfivid flashes ot lightning and heavy thunder peals, burst over the Sheffield district, and lasted several hours. A house in Nether Edge was struck by lightning and damaged, a bedroom and its contents being partially destroyed. Several persoas were on the premises, but no one wan injured. A house in Grimsthorpe was struck about half-past • six o'clock. The current; after lifting the slates off the roof, entered the house in two differen:: directions. Reaching the kitchen, a huge ball of lire played about the heartlirue, on which a baby was lying, while two other children in the room were paralysed by fright. Their escape was miraculous. Ths storm which raged over Dublin on Wednesday night sud next morning vas the most violent experienced for many years and caused great injury to crops. A boy was killed by lightning near Lisdoonvarna. The thun- derstorm in %Vest Yorkshire. although not reiul'ing in great damage, his caused two deaths. At Thackley. near Bradford, a mill hand was struck by a. flss'i and killed instantaneously. In the same district a farm labourer's wife returning to the kitchen was killed, and insltralforii,a Gordon boy was struck by lightning while delivering messages, and there is little hope of recover. The Leeds and Liverpool callal was obstructed by tNe washing of road metal into the waterway between LetiB and Bradford.

John Davis was sentenced at the Central Criminal Court on Tuesday, to eighteen month,' hird labour for „extensive frauds perpetrated through the medium of the "Exchange and Mart." The Rev. Ernest Fitzroy, formerly incumbent of St., Jude's, Livf rpool,ls under remand Irom the Mars lehooe Police Court on a charge of i,tealing, a black IA; Contain- ing wearing apparel valued at £2, _the property of the Rev. James Newton Beale, of Canterbury. The ',port of the Lunity Commissioners, which was issued on Saturday, shows the numb* r of lunatics, idiots, and persons of unsound tnind-on January Ist to be • 92,067, or 2,245 in excess of the pruvious year's returns. This is the largest increase in he nUmCier of ufficially known lunatics yet recorded. •- •

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.

The Warrington team failed to come to any definite conclusion on Saturday in their match at Arpley. This was the same as the first meeting of the clubs at Liver- only on that occasion Warrington had a very good chance ot pulling off the match, while on the present occasion the result was a very open one indeed. The two Crosfields were again absent from the Warrington team, while on the other hand,the Northern club had the assistance of T. Routledge. a member of the South Afri- can team, who are at present on tour in this country.

The Warrington innings at the commencement had a very ominous look, for the two initial batsmen each returned to the pavilion with the figure 0 against their names, and only a leg bye scored. Not content with this, the visitors sent Smith to the right about when only 18 had been scored. Clarke and Wordsworth how- ever, altered the look of the game considerably ; the latter being especially severo upon the bowling and he was not long in scoring 48, 32 of which were made up of fours. During his innings, a rather curious incident occurred. He had Connor for his partner, and a drive happened to knock Connor's wickets down. Connor was unfortunately out of his crease and was therefore " run out." Parry and Gleave also gave a great deal of trouble to the Northern team,for Parry sent Job to the boundary thrice in one over, and in the next sent Edwards twice. Notwithstanding the inauspicious start, the innings realised the extremely satisfactory total of 158.

The bulk of the Warrington wickets fell to Job and Henson. The patient one took five for 43 runs, and the other three for 34. Routledge claimed a solitary one for 16 runs. The innings of the Northern team was only of 25 minutes duration during which time however Garnett managed to get his leg before a straight ball from Connor and was thus compelled to retire. When Thompson had made five, and Rftitledge 28, the clerk of the weather decreed that enough cricket had been played for the day, and accordingly turned on the tap, with the result that stumps were drawn, and the match aban- doned. This is to he regretted for there would probably have been a very exciting finish to the match had it been fought to the end.

The second teams of the clubs were able to come to a very definite;conclusion at Waterloo, in fact too definite for Warrington. The Northern juniors went in first,and so successful were they that 179 were scored for the loss of only eight wickets. Fracer scored the highest on his side, his score being 43. When the Warrington team went in,they were tretted very unceremoniously,for they were tumbled out after scoring only 62, of which Bibby alone scored 45 ! Five ducks, two ones, a two, a three, and an eight with tw•l byes made up the rest of the score. The players who scored eight was under the circum- stances a very high scorer,and I therefore give his name for the infoemation of the readers. His name was Ash- ton. What the Warrington team would have done with- out Btbby is too awful to contemplate.

The S trikey Bridge Wesleyans met their namesakes of Earlestown at Mill-lane on Saturday and added another success to their already long list. In fact, with the ex- ception of the disastrous match with the Y.M C.A., and Llandudno, they have not tasted defeat this season. The match on Saturday was twelve a side and It;derick was the top scorer on the S inkey Bridges side, with 22. Bailey and Booth each contributed a score runs,and Peers 12. The Earlestow n fielding', was very loose with the result that 16 extras were sccred, and the Sankey Bridges realised 104. Clare was the only Earlestownian to get kto double fizures, and the team as a whole could do little against the excellent bowling of Watkins and Peers, whc, each claimed five wickets. Thirty-eight was the sum total of the Earlestown innings and thus they were very badly beaten. After the match the rivals sat down to a tea when all rivalries were soon forgotten.

The Sankey Wire Mills were also successful on Satur- day, defeating Hough Green for the second time this s-ason. The two Sankey teams in fact have both records to be proud of, and have very rarely known defeat this season. In the match on Saturday, Hough Green could make no stand whatever against the bowling of Hodson and Marshall and were all out for 38. On the other hand, Cook for the Mill men came within five of the score of the Green men,and for the loss of only six wickets they had scored 81. The villagers have a lot to learn yet in cricket. The second team were not so successful as the first, for the Grappenhall St. Wilfrid's second team were the better of them by 44 to 33.

A nuinher of the other junior teams were settling their little differences on. Saturdm. Fairfield had the better of the Arpley Juniors by 41 to 32. Buckley-street were so ne4r eq11.41 to St. Anne's, that they only won by 22 to 19. The Widnes Alberts had to lick the dust before Whitecross, who had a player named Bradley, who took five wickets for three runs, and the result of the match was a win for the wiremen or rather wireboys by 30 to 19. Ellesmere-street Mission nr.t the Bewsey-road Wesleyans but whereas they scored 19, the team .from Bewsey scored 49, which, of course, was a win for Bewsey.

div.head: BASEBALL.
div.p: BASEBALL.

I wonder what the --s-e-c-ia-a-ri and members of the Warington baseball teanythink of the following com- munication I have received. I will give it in full so that they may read, mark, learr . and'inwardly digest it to their heart's content. This is how it runs. "Sir,— By your permission, I should like to ask the Seoretaly of the Warrington Baseball Club—that is if they have one at the present time—whether the club Is doing as well in the Liverpool and District league as they did in their first three or four fixtures as I begin to think that, by the way they were defeating their opponents, they intended to come out with an unbeaten record. But I begin to think that they are loosing now, as I cannot see in the " Examiner " a single line about their doings. Perhaps it might be that the secretary does not like to publish losses, hut I should advise him or some one of the Com- mittee to take this matter into consideration and also try to obtain a league table for the 'Warrington Ex- aminer.' Wishing you every success on Saturday next. —Yours, ONE INTERESTED."

"One Interested," appears to bear out his non de ,plunte, perhaps his inquiring mind will be set at rest by a little information about the way things stand with the Warrington baseball team. I hone the team is as strong as ever, for I can testify that the game is one well worth watching.

div.head: M. TIIIIPIN'S WAR ENGINE.
div.p: M. TIIIIPIN'S WAR ENGINE.

According to a French military paper' M. Turpin's invention i3on he same principle as a rocket which in exploding divides and subdivides almost indefinitely. He makes with picric acid a projectile which in explod- ing bunches smaller prejectiles, and these again do the samp, so that a given space is entirely covered with them. At present, however, this is simply theory.

div.head: TO WARRINGTON FROII
div.p: TO WARRINGTON FROII
SALE OF WORK AT WARRINGTON RECTORY.

On Thursday, last week,a sale of work to secure a portion of the debt remaining on the St. George's Mission, Warrington, was opened in the Rectory garden, by Mrs. Stanton, of Thel wall. The articles for sale were in two large tents, in addition to a small one which contained the flower stall. The following were the stallholders :—General stall, Mrs. Willis', Mrs. W. Woods (Fennel-street), Miss Gray, Mrs. R. T. Fairclough, Mrs. John Walton, Mrs. Fairclough, Mrs. Wilcocks, Misses Percival, Miss Nannie Fairclough, Miss Walton, Miss Jackson. and Miss Wilcocks ; flower stall, Mrs. White aud Miss Cash ; refreshment stall, Mrs. Wm. Gill, Mrs. A. Woods, Mrs. A. Browne, Misses Gill, and Miss Mainwaring. There was a good number present at the opening ceremony. In addition to Mrs. Stanton there were pre- sent the Rector and Mrs. Willis, Rev. H. V. and Mrs. Pigot, Rev. B. Percival, Rev. A. A. Markham, Rev.G. B. Thurston, Captain Buckton, Dr. White, Councillor A. Woods, Mr. J. Walton, Mrs. Darwall, Mr. W. Gill, Mrs. Sharpe, Mrs. Beaman, and Mr. J. Banner. The Rector in introducing Mrs. Stanton, said that he was sure that those present would be interested in knowing something about St. George's Mission. Three years ago the foundation stone was laid by Lady Walker, and the building was opened six months afterwards by Bishop Royston. The building had some excellent rooms, and the work had been chiefly in connection with the Sunday school. There were also Sunday evening services, a men's club and other institutions in connection with the place. It was through the zeal and energy of Mr. Jack- son to a great extent that those beautiful buTlings hail been erected and the work carried out, and they were greatly indebted to him. The work was now in charge of the Rev.G. B.Thurston who seemed quite equal to the task. The cost of the buildings was £1,910 composed of £1,400 for the building and £5lO for furnishing, &c. The receipts up to the present bad been £1,760, .C 1,260 of which had been subscribed and collected,and £5OO had been received in the form of a loan from Mr. Wm. Gill. They therefore required £175 that day to wipe out the debt and pay the expenses of the sale of work. Ile hoped that they would be able to realize that sum. He would like to read out some of the subscriptions which had been received. The patron of the parish had given £5O, the late Lord Winmarleigh, £4O ; Sir Andrew and Lady Walker, £5O; the late Sir Gilbert Greenall, £220 ; Mr. Mortimer, £150; and Mrs. Beaman, £l5O. They were greatly indebted to Mrs. Stanton for the many kind- nesses they had received from her, and he had great pleasure in asking her to declare the sale open. Mrs. Stanton said that she knew that very good work had been done at the mission, and she hoped it would be very successful. She now declared the sale of work open. A vote of thanks was passed to Mrs. Stanton on the motion of Councillor A. Woods, after which the business of the sale began. During the afternoon, the Blue Coat School band played selections of music on the lawn. A tennis tournament was held at which there were CO entries. The arrangements were in the hands of Messrs. Stanley Wright, F. Taylor, A. Browne, A. Woods and If . Fairclough (secretary). The decorations were in the hands of Mr. H. Hayes. Just before dusk, a fire balloon was sent up from the grounds. The sale will be con- tinued to-day, when the final of the tennis tournamenl will be played. The sale will be opened by Mrs. Beamont at three o'clock. I The proceeds of the first day's sale amounted to £96.

div.head: HAYDOCK BANKRUPT.
div.p: A HAYDOCK BANKRUPT.

On Friday the public examination of Tnomas Twiss, builder, Owl's Nest. Haydock, was continued by Mr. A. B. Potter, the assistant official receiver, at the Warrington Bankruptcy Court, before Mr. Registrar Ridgway. Mr. Irvin, solicitor, Liverpool was present to represent Mr. C. E. Percival, Scot- land-rd., Liverpool, one of the creditors. Questions were asked by Mr. Porter with regard to a traf) which the bankrupt had sold to Mr. Hunt, his wife's uncle, and had nevertheless given to Mr. Wane, a cieditor, who had not been scheduled, as security. The bankrupt said that Mr. Hunt knew that he had given the trap to Mr. Wane, and allowed him to do so. He had not scheduled Mr. Wane as a creditor, because that gentlemen did not wish him to do so. He had not compounded with him in anyway. In further examination the answers which Twiss made to Mr. Potter were so indefinite, that Mr. Potter at length said that he simply could not believe a word of his statement. He did no!, appear to pay any attention to the questions put to him. —The Registrar : He does not give his answers satisfac- torily at all. He does not appear to remember anythin,g He seems to be trying to hedge.—Mr. Twiss said that he answered to the best of his knowledge.—From further examination, it was elicited that a portion of the banh- rupt's timber had been taken away by a creditor from his yard, while the sheriff's officers were in his bonee. His foreman had sent it away without his (Twiss') sanction. The timber was to be sawn up, but it had not since been returned. He supposed the creditor was keeping, it as security. He said that he did not remember telling Mr. Percival in Marsh, that if he were sold up he could pay 30s. in the £. He could not remember telling him that Evans and Co. owed him £4OO or £5OO. The Company never did owe him that much.—Mr. Percival was then put into the box, and repeated that the bankrupt had told him what he now -said that he could not remember. Twiss owed him £2BB 10s., but had it not been for the statement he made , to him in March, witness would not have allowed him ! any trust at all.—The Assistant Official Receiver applied ! for a further adjournment of the examination until September 7, and in the meantime inquiries would tic:: made with reference to the reit-meal of goods from the bankrupt's premises. The application was granted.

div.head: RAILWAY SERVANI'S SERIOCS MISTAKE.
div.p: A RAILWAY SERVANI'S SERIOCS MISTAKE.

In the Queen's Bench. London, on Wedne,sclay,llannah Mary Mack, Court dressmaker, recovered from the Lon- don and Brighton Railway Company £lOO damages for assault and false imprisonment. She was the holder of a first-class season ticket on . the. defendants' line, and was admittedly of irreproachable character, but while she was awaiting a train at Victoria S:ation at night a railway servant seized and forcibly removed her under the impression that she was a loose character. She was compelled to go home by another route. The ju ige s•rid the suit was practically undefended. •

div.head: WARRINGTON BOROGGII FINANCES.
div.p: WARRINGTON BOROGGII FINANCES.

Mr. J. Fairhurst, the Warrington borough treasurer, has issued the annual report upon the finances of the borough for the year ending. March 31st, 1894, in a book of 170 pages. The accounts are put in a very plain and concise manner, such as to be easily understood by the reader. The first account in the book is the borough fund account from which the expenses of the Watch and various other committees are taken. We give herewith a summary of the accounts. WATCH DEPARTMENT. The receipts of this department contain an item of £2,299 Bs. 4d .from the Lancashire County Council ,for one- half the charge of the pay and clothing of the Vallee for the year ended September 29, 1893,and the total receipts of the department were £2,452 ss. 4d. Against this,the expenditure was £5,079 35., which includes the Chief Cr)nstable's salary of £3OO, constables' wages, £4,082 13s. 11d., and other incidental expenses of the police force, £329 151. 43. The rest of the expenses were comparatively small, the highest item being the maintenance of the prisoners, £6B Bs. MAINTENANCE OF PROPERTY. This portion of the borough account gives as receipts £ll9 45., and expenditure £24 84. 31. Among the receipts were £6O from the overseers of the poor of War- rington, a year's rent of offices, and Town Hall, and £5O from the volunteers as rent for the premises cast of the Town flail. The expenditure contains no item of pnblic interest.

CEMETERY DEPARTMENT. The cemetery fees for the year were £1,239 3s. 4d. of which £l7l us. 6d. consisted of church burial fees,l payable to the Rector and others. The debit side con- tains £743 as interest upon the debt, and instalment of a principal sum of £17,000. The registrar's and assistant's salary amounted to £l3O, and gardener's and labourer's wages to £2809a. The total expenditure upon this de- partment was £1,549 2s. 2.1. BOROUGH ANALYST'S DEPARTMENT. - It is stated under this head that Mr. J. R. Gornall, borough analyst received £5O for a year's salary. Mr. R. Norman, inspector of the department £5O, and appa- ratus 84e., £4 17s. 6.1. Then follows the Contagious Diseases (Animals) De- partment the expenses of which only. amount to £8 lei. ed. MUNICIPAL ELECTION EXPENSES DEPARTMENT. The cost of the municipal elections for the year was £179 153. 6d. and the total receipts towards this was the formidable sum of a is., which was the amount of the fine which Mr. Chandley had to pay to resign his office as alderman of the tyirough. ' TOWN HALL, BANK PARK, AND BATHS DEPARTMENTS. There were no receipts from the Town Hall department. The only am)unt received from the the Bank Park De- partment was 14s. from the sale of pigeons, and the baths receipts have been £587 us. 23., which is a very' satisfactory amount. The Town Hall keeper's and cleaner's wages were £lll 14s. and the total cost of the Town Hal was £617 19s: ill. The gardeners, labourer's, and park keeper's wages were £519 17s. BJ., and the park has cost the borough £823 163. 6.1. in all. The sum of £143 was required for the interest and payment of instal- ment upon the loans taken up for the extension of the baths. The bathkeeper's and assistants' wages were £l9l Os. Bd., and the total cost of the baths for the year was £925 6s. id. SCHOOL ATTENDANCE DEPARTMENT. The salaries of the three school attendance officers were £3ll 7s. ed. The maintenance of boys at indus- trial schools was £215 184. 3J., and one girl There is also a donation ot £2l to the Ship" Clio." The expenses of deputations to the Ship "Clio," of which we hear so much, was £l2 2s. 4d. .
VARIOUS DEPARTMENTS.

After the accounts of the school attendance depart- ment, follow a numbcr of various amounts of expendi- ture, The sinking fund and interest departiwnit rt - quired £1,032 13s. 91; parliamentary expenses &part- ment 1-;14 ss. 61; open spaces department £3B 7s. 61.; and miscellaneous department £1,076 14s. 2,1. This last department contains the cost of deputations, post- ages, hire of convoyances,Stc. The heaviest item is that of paintin,,, stationary, and advertising, wtl.di amounts to £551 19s. 11cl. £956 us. 93. was also traßsferred to the Museum and Library Department as the proceeds of a 11d. rate. The amount in hand on the Borough rate fund ac- counts was £956 11s 9d. The next account, is the Improvement Rate Fund account which contains the accounts of the market and other importanL branches of the municipal finances. The receipts from this rate we...T :224,651 16s. 4d.

MA KET DEPARTMENT. The t)tal receipts ot the market were £3,927 4s. 4d., and the experials—w'lich iriniudo wages to inspector arid assistants, £3OO ; paintina :ind repairs, £419 13s. 6d.; and scaven,ing,E2oo—were £1,636 14.4.2 d. Closely allied to the markA is the Weights and Measures Department with the receipts of 4-?,323 is. 10d., and expenditure of £152 14e. Sel.
FIRE ENGINE DEPARTMENT,

This dem.rtnjr-i-t.;s—r-ocieipts amount to the modest sum of £3 53., £5 1.45. of which ia the money repaid by Coun- cillor Heaton for the supper to firemen. The firemen's wages were £lO6 9s. 86., and the total expenses of the department were £736 12e. 51. STREET 331PIZOVEMENT, Sec. The amount required for the rent, taxes, and main- tenance of property was £1,074 10s. 10d. Li2hting cost £2,261 16s. ; and the ztreet, improvements £205 103, 51. The sinking fund and interest required to. pay off the interest upon loans for the various improvements in the town, and also to pay off the instalments was £3,051 os.2d
SCAVENGING DEPAIITMENT. The scavenging of the town entails an expense of £3,211 15s. 3d. Wage is the mast important item, for it amounts to £1,807 95. 67].

lIFA.LTH AND HOSPITAL DEPARTMENTS. These departments realised an income of £537 7s. 7d., and the expense was £3,284 Bs. 11d. Interesting items of expenditure are Dr. Gornallis salary as medical officer of heilth, £150; Mr. R. Norman as inspector of. nuis- ances and of the Canal Boars Act, £168; Mr. James Powell (assistant), £9l; men's wages for disinfecting, £72 13s. 103. ; disinfectants, £123 3s. • printing and advertising, £149 18s. 31.; Aiken-street hospital, £2,155 Os. 4d. ; Rope hospital, £2,125 12s. 7d. ,

NIGHT SOIL AND LONGFORD DEPARTMENTS. These departments provide an income of £3,616 45., of which £3,040 4. 21. is derived from the sale of con- centrated maeure. The night toil department's wages were Mr. J. Church (insrector), £9B 16a.; night soil- men's wages. £1,353 2. 3d. ; di:to, extra men employed during coal dispute, £ll4 2s. 31. ; coopers' wages, £173 7s. 5. ; and carters' wages, £442 us. 10d. Cartage is a large item with £921 6-. 3d. At Longford, the salary of Mr. Dras, the manager, was £200; mechanics' and lab- ourers' ways. £1,281 9s. 6 I. ; extra men during the coal dispute, £46 12. ld. ; and the cost of th 3 intercepting de; tots was £751 is. The total cost of these departments was £9,2574a.

div.head: HIGHWAY DEPARTMENT.
div.p: HIGHWAY DEPARTMENT.

The expenditure in this department was wares, £2,192 7s. 93. ; flagging and stone breaking. £615 4s. 91.; sewering, £698 4s. 5d.; setts. £1,713 3s. 8 L ; cement,.£ss9 lls. sd. ; cartage, £1,201 03. 93. These and other items make a grand total of £10,692 17s. 43. The receipts of the department were £6,160 2s. 61.
GENERAL SEWERS RATE ACCOUNT.
.• ..... _ _ The income from this rate was £2,704 us., which left a balance in hand of £947 10s. 9 I.

MUSEUM AND LIBRARY FUND ACCOUNT. The income on this account was £1,266 19i. 9.1., and it is interesting to know that £39 181. has been received during the year in fines awing ti keeping the library books over the stated The expense; comb £126 3s. sd. below the receipts, and th principal items are Mr. Madeley (librarian), £170; other salaries, £427 10s. 10d. ; picture purchase account, £150; books, periodicals, etc., £269 7s. 10d. TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION ACCOUNT. The receipts were £1,624 14.2. Bd., which leaves a ba- lance in hand of £166 83. The income was composed of the grants from the County Councils of Lancashire ani Cheshire, £B3B 11. 6d. ; fees, Sic., from the School of Art,, £337 ls. 81. ; ditto from the School of Science, £332 us. 4d. ; ditt from the Continuation setools, £3O 8. The principal items of expenditure were, Mr. Madeley (sec.),£s3 ; exrenses of the School of Art, £528 14s, id. inducing £2O) Mr. Aylward (head master's) salary; ditto of School of Science, £697 53 4.1. ; ditto of Continuation school, £4B 6s. 11d.
MISCELLANEOUS ACCOUNTS.

A large number of accounts now follow. The Bathsl Extension account sat z that the balance still owing is £1,005 184. 3.1., and that Messrs. Joseph Gibson and Son had received £1,750 on account of contract, and Messrs. Tleimas and Taylor £653, balance of contract for machitirry. The Fire Envine Renewals fund accouit has a balance in hand of £.3.3 91. 2d., after expending £262 10s. to Merry weather and Sun for the new steam tire engine " Captain." Tle Linzford Deps-, Exteusicn account lots a dele.:it of £829 18,. 3 1., and among items of expord,ture are, iron shed, £558.; sinking of a well, £5OO 144. ; and the

building of a chimney shaft at Howley Depot, £155 114. 6i. The Picture Purchase account shows receipts of £2lO 163. 7d. ; expenditure nil. The receipts of the Nice Superannuation account amount to £856 18s. 4d., and the payments only amount to £52 163. 7d. ; £5O ss. 4d. of which was the amount of the pension of P.C. Singleton. The Private Street Improvement Expenses account' show a deficit of £6,493 4s. 6d. The amount received from persons on account of constructing streets and Passages was £5,262 18s. id. The Sewers Construction account shows a deficit of £363 103.81. as also does the Street Improvement Loan accsunt of the large sum of £35,950 18.. 91. This large amount is chiefly due to a sum of £25,640 165., which was spent in the purchase of property in various parts of the town. The Walker's gift account shows a balance on the right side of £77 17s. 3d. THE GAS WORKS ACCOUNTS. After a lengthy statement of the Sinking Fund account upon the various departments, we get to the Gas. Works accounts. The salaries for the Gas Wm ks, am4unt to £1,004 193., and the amount spent in coal and cannel £12,882 Bs. 11d. The amount realised from gas was £35,542 64. 5d., and the working for the year shows a balanca of £9,403 17s. 50. The Gas Works Extension account also shows a balance of £720 74. 7d., and the Gas Works Reserve Fund account, of £517 Bs. 31.

WATER WORKS ACCOUNTS. The balance in hand on the year for the Water Works was £10,086 4,=. 2d., the water rate realising £14,583 Bs. id. The amount spent in salaries was £715 45., Appleton reservoir cost £ts3 16. 55., and Winwick pumping station, £837 19s. I.od. The Water %%orks have a capital account of £4,698 153. sd. SUMMARY OF ACCOUNTS.

The total expenditure of the bcrough for the year was £222,678 64. 2d., which leaves an adverse balance of £34,754 19s. 4d. Near the end of the book, is a list of the bonds and annuities, but as a number of the bond holders have complained of the publicity given to their names in pre- vious years, only the initials are given, and the bond- holder can therefore trace his or her name, without the general public becoming acquainted therewith. AsSBSSABLE VALUE AND RATES OF THE BOROUGH. An interesting table is given of the various assessable values and rates in the borough from 1857 to the present time. The assessable value of the, borough in 1857 was £54,321, and since then it has steadily grown until in the present year it had amounted to £154,022. In 1857 the Improvement Rate was only 23. now it is 33. Bd. ha the £. There was no Sewers rate until 1858, when it was 21. in the £, which is the present rate. It has been 4d. on'five occasions, viz., 1887, 1888, 1890, and 1692, and 1893. The Poor rate has‘been very changeable. In 1857 it was 2s. 11d, in the £. It is now 23. Bd. It his never been lower than 2s. in the £ which it was in 1878. The total rates of the borough were 43. 11d. in 1857 against 63. 61. at present. The rates have been below the 1857 scale on two occasions only, viz., in 1878 when they were 4s. BJ., and in 1884 when they were 4. 101 On the other hand the present scale has been surpissed on two occasions, in 1862, 63. 101 , and in 1881. 63. 8.1. It has been equalled on one occasien,lBB2. The rates are very heavy at present, and no one denies that, but still the averages of the various periods ao not show very much difference. The average rates for ten years from 1857 to 1867 was 53. 101. in the £; from 1867 t 3 1877,5 a. 10.1. ; from 1877 to 1887, 53. 81L and eight years from 1887 t.) 1894, 63. 9.1. At the close of the book is an abstract of the accounts of the Grammar School for tha pat year. Copies of the Borough accounts can be had on applica- tion at the collector's office at the Town Hall.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTiiOItITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTiiOItITY.

The usual fortnightly meeting of the Authority took place on Tuesday afternoon in the Workhouse, DintoD, Mr. John Mclntyre presiding, There were also present the Revs J. W. N. Tanner,and J. Hanby Messrs. H. E. Heywood,J. W. Williams,J. Brandreth T. Baxter, C.C.,J. Stokes,E. Aaron,J. Weir, T. L3WIS, W. Pickering, S. Woodward, J. Ashton, clerk, G. Ashton, deputy clerk ; J. Farrington, nuisance in- spector; and Dr. Adam,,, medical officer of health. A WARNING TO SANITARY AUTHORITIES. A circular letter was received from the Local Govern- ment Board urging Sanitary Authorities to (xereise the utmost vigilance to contrJlany cases of diarrlice might, be auspicious tither in character or amount dur- ing the present and forthcoming season ; and with a view of facilitating action in this direction the Board would give favourable consideration to any appficatiun that might be addressed to them for their approval to add diarrhcea to the li of notifiable diseasss, until the termination of the present quarter. Etch :Sitiitary Authority woukl doubtless consider how tar it was de- sirable in the first instance, at least, to limit notification of cliarrt,ce r to at acks -occurring over one year of age. This course was suggested by the Board, because there were signs el recrecescence oi cholera on the continent. It was coosidered that to place diarrhoea am ingst notifiable diseases would largely increase the expenditure of the authority and it was finally resolved on the pro- position of Mr. Heywood, seconded by Mr. Woodward that diarrhoea should not be added to the list of notifi- able diseases. THE CONSOLIDATION OF THE AUTHORITY'S LOANS. Mr. Brandreth in submitting the report of the Loans Committee said that it was questionable whether they would be able to consolidate the loans at all as they were borrowed on the rates of the various townships. They could not exactly do so by making a charge on the whole union. The loans were borrowed for Overton,Frecisham Frodsham Lordship, and Weston, at 3 and a per cent. ,so that it was a difficult matter to consolidate them. Then they would have to ask the consent ct the Local Government Board -before they could effect a change. Mr. Heywood inovd, aud Mr. Brandreth seconded, that in the-cases where 3 and 31 per cent, was paid, the matter be referred to the Par c,ctrial Committees of those townships for consideration after which a report should be made to the Authority.—This proposition was agreed to.

THE "OFFENSIVE TRADE" AT CLIFTON. Dr. Adaans, the medical officer of tealth,reported that in accordsnce with instructions, he had visited and in- spected the premises in the tOwnship (if Clifton where a process of trade for abstracting oil from livers of cod fish, and .fish offal, was carried on by, he was informed, Mr. Jecob Commits of 91, Aubrey-street, .Everton, Liver- pool. He certifel that such process of trade was, an "offensive trade under the meaning oh the Public Health Act, 1875.—The Clerk said that the authority possessed urban powers and that if an "offensive trade' was established, the person who established it was liable to a penalty of £5O, and £4O per day for carrying it on. —Mr. Stokes said that in hot weather when the livers were brought in casks they fermented to such a degree as to buret the barrels,and he La :I himself seen evidences of this having been the case. The smell was the most offensive he had experienced; and a few days previously some people whom he had engaged for the purpose of haymaking, were compelled to tie hankerchiels over their heads and noses or they would not have been able to have finished their wotk.—Eventually on the proposi- tion of Mr. Woodward, it was decided to instruct the clerk to write to Mr. Col:Edits drawing his attention to the fact that the trade was an offensive one and ask him for his reasons for not consulting the authority before establishing it. Further that he be requested to abate the nuisance at once. FINANCE: IiOW LANDOWNERS' PROPERTY IS IMPROVED AT

Mr. Brandreth subtintted the statement of the Finance Committee, which showed that the present balance in the treasurer's hands was £174 10s. 2d.. and the ac- counts which the ccinmittee had passed on for payment amounted to £2lB 4s. He moved that the report be adopted.—Mr. J. M. Williams, in seconding the motion, referred to an account amounting to £35, which was for a sewer road from Overton to Frodshain Lordship. This sewer extended over a hundred yards, and the ratepayers of Frodsham had to .pay the account for the benefit of [ha Nlarquis of -Chohnondeley.—Mr. Williams considgred th it it was unjust to impose upon them the cost of works of this description, which improved the landowners' Property. - The sewerage, gas, and water schemes passed through land which belonged to the Marquis of Cholmondeley, but for all that his land was improved as fa rming land by 2d. or 3d. per yard, com- pared with £2 or £2 109. per acre, that gentleman did not contribute anything towards the CO4. A farmers had recently informed him (Mr. Williams) that he had .paid £35 or £37 for the sanitary rate for previous sewers being laid in the same locality, whereas his farm was nearly two miles away, and be did not benefit by the improvements at all. On the other hand, land had been let for building purposes within ths last few years at increased rates.—Mr. Heywood said they had sent a petition to the House of Commons ssking that landlords should pay the cost of sewers.—The Clerk remarked that almost all other Sanitary Authorities had done the same t hing.—Tne Chairman observed that.a Bill dealing with this grievance had been introduced, but it had not met , wiqi much success.—The financial rep ,rt was then • adopted.

div.head: Zettero to tbt ebitor.
div.p: Zettero to tbt ebitor.
FREE EDUCATION.

Sir,—A great deal has been said in Warrington lately on the subject of school accommodation. and I under- stand that an inquiry is soon to be held on the subject. It may be opportune, therefore, to set forth a few facts on the above subject as bm fly as possible, so that in the event of school extension,free education may be brought within the reach of many who deserve it, but who can- not at present get it. It should be known to everybody that every person in England who sends his child to school has a right to free education. Where fees are levied without his consent he can at once have the grievance remedied. The managers of any particular school may not be bound to admit children free ; but where free education is refused, complaints should at once be made to the Education Department, and free education demanded for the child in question. The Department will act as soon as possible on this complaint. It is the duty of the Department to secure free schools, not only in a school district as a whole, but in any part of a school district. Parents cannot reasonably be asked to send their child- ren some distance to a free school, and they may reason- ably refuse to be called on to seed their children across a dangerous thoroughfare,or to send their elder children to a different school from the infants. Where a parent asks for free schooling, any attempts to inquire into his means are, under the present laws, as impertinent as they are offensive. The right to free education is inde- pendent of the income of the parent. Free education means no payment for fees, books, or any other purpose whatever. Parents whose children are paying no fee in their present standard may demand a free school if fees are charged in the higher standards. The school must be free from top to bottom. Parents desiring free education and finding any diffi- culty, should write to the Right Hon. A. H. D. Acland, M.P.,Vice-President, and the letter need not be stamped. It is desirable that those who write should say what are the number of children for whom they want free education. I may add that parents will succeed best in their demand for free education, if they combine. One or two children may be forced into some less suit- able free scheol. Collective action by a large number of persons will probably result in freeing the school they now are in, and thus securing the benefits of free educa- tion without any disturbance of the school course of the children. Thanking you in anticipation for the insertion of this letter, I am yours truly,
G. D. M.
NEWTON POSTAL ARRANGEMENTS, &c.

Sir,—l am glad to see from correspondence in the" E- xaminer "that the latest act of folly of the Newton Com- missioners is being taken up in the manner it is. And as I consider no one should stand aside I am wishful, therefore, to contribute my share in exposing the con- duct of our local rulers. I was hoping,as we are to have wards and a new representation in November next, and as the present Board is only on sufferance till then, that no new scheme would be launched. Our Earlestown friends have managed with the present postal arrange- ment for many years, and why they could not manage a few more months I am at a loss to know. Do they think because Newton has, at the present moment, only one representative,that they are to erect a new building at Earlestown for their own use solely, and make Newton pay its share of such a building ? I tell the Chairman and the other Commissioners that they will be fought inch by inch in this matter. I have no per- sonal feeling against Mr. Emmett or any of the- Commis- sioners, but who will deny that ever since Mr. Emmett has been Chairman, town's matters have:gone on badly, and I see no reason why certain things should not be boldly put before ths public. I will endeavour to put a few of them as a "refresher." (1) Lord Newton a few years ago kindly signified his intention to give a Park to the town, (not to Earlestown only) which would be convenient to both ends of it. The Chairman and his friends said we will not have a Park, but we will have a Public Hall instead. Newton said we are not selfish,you need a Hall,and we agree to £4,000 or £5,000 of the ratepayers' money being spent, and we will forego our portion of Lord Newton's generous offer i which could go for the site. The Chairman and his ' friends took it as a matter of course, without any remorse of conscience, and in addition to this spent £5,000 more without consent and removed the offices. (2) The Chairman and his friends arranged for £6OO per annum additional to be taken from the ratepayers' pockets for water, and this additional amount has gone into the coffers of the Railway Company. Was not this a splendid thing for the Company? (3) When a vacancy occurred on the Board two years ago the Chairman and friends filled it up with Mr. Col- lingwood, whe had only been a few hours in the place, and who knew nothing about the town or its require- ments. This action was denounced at the time by nearly every ratepayer. (4) The Chairman and friends opposed the division of the town into wards, tooth and nail, and then when they found the division could and would be made with- out. them, the Chairman said " I was always in favour Of the wards." (5) The Chairman made a great effort to thrust Mr. E. T. Evans on Newton as one of its representatives, knowing at the sarne time that Mr. Evans Wal put in by the Earlestown vote, and that nine-tenths of Mr. Evans' interests were at Earlestown and one-tenth at Newton. (6) When another vacancy on the board recently occurred the Chairman and his friends elected Mr. Smith, another stranger, without consultation with anyone, and then made a public announcement that Mr. Smith was a Newton Commissioner. _

(7) The Chairman and friends during the last few years increased the rates by 25 per cent. I could give many other instances but think these will at present suffice. I suggest that the ratepayers consider and ponder over these statements, they are not new but at this junctionkiwill bear repetition. See'np.., the town will be properly represented at such an early date all these points would have been allowed to pass into oblivion, if the new building for a post office had not turned up, and the undue haste and pres.!ure with which the matter is being pushed forward in the circum- stances, is unprecedented. Thanking you in advance for inserting this letter. —I am, yours respectfully, RATEPAYER No. 3. Newton-le-Willows, July 25th, 1894.

div.head: SCENE IN A THEATRE.
div.p: SCENE IN A THEATRE.

It is difficult to determine whether the extraordinary incident in the Theatre Royal, Glasgow, when one of the audience rushed upon the stage to pretect the heroine during the performance of "La Dame aux Camelias" was an unconscious compliment to Dumas or to Mdme. Sarah Bernhardt. The incident is net with- out parallel, for there is a well-known stcr; of a sailor who was so affected by a piece which he was witness- ing that he let himself down from the gallery by a rope, and, storming the stage, rushed to the rescue of suffer- ing innocence. He knocked the villain down amid the cheers of his comradu,and was only appeased when the manager appeared and hurriedly endowed the heroine with a large fortune in "property " bank ne,tes. Pro- bablv the earliest story of the sort is that of am Quixote and the puppets,which Cervantes is sald to bave borrowed from real life.

div.head: LORD COLE RIDGE AND THE VACATION
div.p: LORD COLE RIDGE AND THE VACATION
OF SEATS.

Lord Coleridge offered himself voluntarily for exami- nation as a witness on Thursday, before the Select Corn- mittce of the House of Commons, on the subject of the vacating of seats as raised by the recent case of the Attercliffe election. Lord Coleridge, in reply to the Home Secretary, said he applied for the Chiltern Hun- dreds on June 18, four days after his father's death. and _ . .

signed the application, " Bernard Coleridge." He had not at that time furnished any information to the Lord Chancellor ai to his succession to the peerage. Ic was a week later before he got any reply to his application for the Chiltern Hundreds. He made the application be- cause he believed that 'although on his tather'46cloatli the seat was not vacant, he could only remain A memter of the House of Commons under disabilitie.l. He had no doubt that if he sat and voted he would be proceeded against for penalties. He had special rea,ons tor delay- ing to ask a writ of summons to the Upper Howe be- cause he wanted first to obtain a settlement of the question whether he might still continue to practice at the bar, and meantime he was anxious to restore effective repre- sentation to his constituency.

div.head: LATEST NEWS. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LATEST NEWS. IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT.
THURSDAY.

In the House ef Commons on Thursday evening Mr. AsnuiTß, questioned on the subject of experiments as to the effect of coal-dust in producing explosions in mines, I said the Royal Commission had expressed a decided opinion that no further experiments were required and that the matter was ripe for legislation, and in that opinion he fully concurred. Mr. WASON asked the PRESIDENT of the BOARD Of TRADE whether he would endeavour to bring about a reconcilia- tion between employers and workmen in the Scotch coal trade. Mr. BRYCE said the Board of Trade had no power to intervene against the wishes of either party. They regretted that their powers had not been enlarged owing to the Conciliation Bill not being passed into law, but would, if there was a reasonable prospect of success. gladly place their good offices at the disposal of both parties. Mr. ASQUITH spoke to the same effect, and added that he proposed next year to introduce a bill to amend the Coalmines Regulation Act, and hoped that such amendmont would tend to prevent strikes. After the Speaker had ruled out of order Mr. BARTON'S proposed instruction to the Committee to empower them to divide the bill into two bills, and in the first place to rep9rt the portion relating to lands of which the land- lord remained in occupation, the House went into Com- mittee on the Evicted Tenants (Ireland) Bill. A number of amendments were defeated by majorities varying from 54 to 76. In answer to a demand from Mr. BAL- FOUR for a statement of the real object of the bill, the SOLICITOR GENERAL said the intention and purpose of the bill was that it might, if the tribunal thought fit, embrace every case of a tenancy of a holding in Ire- land which had been determined since May 1,1879. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN said the bill went altogether beyond the title and the order of leave, and he thought that in such a case a bill was usually withdrawn. The Chairman (Sir J. GOLDSMITH) decided that it was too late now to say that the bill should not be proceeded with. After a warm discussion Mr.MORIALY said the Government would consider the matter, and if some alteration of title was necessary it should be made. Debate was adjourned at midnight.

In the House of Lords the Earl of ROSEBERY formally moved the second reading of the Budget Bill. The Earl of FEVERSHAM complained that the whole of the Budget resolutions were now included en bloc in one bill, so that no part could be rejected without rejecting the whole. The bill, he said,was a confiscatory measure, and would do a vast amount of injury to the landed interests of the country. The Duke of DEVONSHIRE said it would be impossible for the House to amend the bill without en- suring its defeat. His Grace criticised the graduation proposals,and said that when once the principle was ad- mitted that the Stee had the first claim on a dead person's estate it was difficult to see why the limitations were not capable of indefinite extension until absolute confication was reached.

Lord FARRER supported the principle of graduated death duties. The Duke of RUTLAND and the Duke cid ARGYLL claimed that the House had a right to amend money bills. The Lord CHANCELLOR said he never doubted that the Huse could reject a money bill, but whether having regard to the practice of the last two hundred years, it would be constitutional or proper to do so was anoth.3r matter. Lord HALSBURY said the bill seemed to be intended as a demonstration against the owners of land. The bill was then read a second time.

div.head: ANNUAL OUTLNO OF POOR CHILDREN FROM RUNCORN.
div.p: ANNUAL OUTLNO OF POOR CHILDREN FROM RUNCORN.

On Wednesday afternoon the third annual treat to the poor children of Runcorn took place,Overton Frodsham, being again the rendezvous. The children, who numbered in all 620, left Runcorn Station by special train for Frodsham at about one o'clock, being accompanied by the Mill Brow Ragged School Drum and Fife Band, together with several clergymen, Improvement Commissioners and their wives, and other ladies and gentlemen who have kindly rendered their assistance since the annual event was started three years ago. On reaching Frodsham the children were marshalled into processional order and be- ing preceded by the band,marched to the grounds which surround Mersey View. Here they passed away the time until five o'clock in many and various ways. Some ran races for sweets, nuts, toys &c., whilst others in- dulged in divers games. Donkey races were also en- joyed,and in some instances afforded considerable mirth. The ladies who were present very kindly assisted in pre. paring the children's tea, and attended to their require- ments in such an assiduous manner at to deserve the highest praise. The meal, was immensely enjoyed by the children, who ate the good things provided sor them with evident relish. Tea over they again betook them- selves to the play grounds,and the purpose of participat- ing in further sports. Whilst the children were again in the midst of pleasure some 120 ladies and gentlemen were hospitably enter- tained to tea by Mr. S. Taylor, chairman of the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners. Mrs. Parker, of Mersey View, catered for this contingent in the most satisfactory manner, and the repast was enjoyed by all who partook of it.

At the conclusion of this portion of the programme, the Rev. J. Holden expressed the great pleasure it gave him in pr:posing a vote of thanks to their host, Mr. Taylor, for so kindly inviting them there that afternoon. The Chairman of Commissioners did not care to have his good deeds spoken much of in public,but agreed in good works more than words. (Applause.) The rev, gentle- man concluded by saying that Mr. Taylor had been thoroughly interested in that day's proceedings, and his kindness to all of them was a very clear evidence of this. He called upon all present to give their host a hearty vote of thanks for his hospitality. (Laud applause.) Mr. J. B. Holland, in seconding the vote, said he had been present at the respective gatherings since the inauguration of this annual event, and he knew how delighted Mr. Taylor always was to be in their com- pany, and to do his best towards making the poor chil- dren happy. He (Mr. Holland) often met Mr. Taylor, and could say without fear of contradiction that there was no man in Runcorn who took a more kindly interest in the poor of the town than Mr. Taylor. (Applause.) The Rev. Arrowsmith supported the motion with exceeding gritification. For three years he had been Mr. Taylor's neighbour, and had been privileged with a great deal of personal intercourse with him. He could confirm everything that had already been said of him, and might add that so far as the good of Runcarn was concerned, no effort or trouble was to great fur Mr. Taylor if he could only further the well-being of the town. (Applause.) His friend never considered any expense too great if he could only bring joy and comfort to other penp!e ; and it had ni,t been his privilege to meet a kinder-hearted and more benevolent man than Mr. Taylor. (Applause.) Dr. Gastaldi likewise spoke in support of the proposi- tion, and concluded by saying that everyone in Runcorn would wish Mr. Taylor a long life, and he ilth, strength, and wealth to enjoy it. The vote was accorded with enthusiasm.

Mr. Taylor after thanking them for the kind manner in which they had spoketi of him, said he felt proud to be with them that day. It must certainly be very pleas- ing to everyone to be able to take part in that day's entertainment, and to see the children enjoy themselves in the manner they had done. He had looked forward— and he was sure he could speak the same for those who assisted in the Aged Persons and Poor Children's Treat —with the greatest pleasure to this event. The occa- sions upon which the two entertainments he had referred to were held stood out as two red letter days in every year. The treat that day could not fail to make a good impression upon the minds of the little children —an impmssion which the children would never forget. They would see that someone cared for them, and bestowed upon them that kindly attention which unfortunately they so very rarely received. He was pleased to tee so many friends from Runcorn pre- sent, and it must certainly be a source of gratification to the organisers of the treat to find so many ready to engage in the entertainment. Mr. Taylor then went on to speak of the efforts which the Rev. Mr. Holden had put forth to resuscitate the aged persons' treat, and of the interest that had since been manifested in it, inas- much as they were rv,w ab!e t) succeed the above treat with a similar one to poor children. Mr. Holland, their worthy treasurer, felt content that day on account of the fact that he possessed sufficient funds in hand to liquidate the expenses. (Applause.) In conclusion,Mr. Taylor proposed a vote of thanks to all ladies and gentlemen who had taken part in the arrangements. Thsy had all of them worked unanimously, and with determination. (Applause.) The proposition was seconded by Mr. Lightburn, who coupled with it the names of Messrs. J. D. Jone,, W. B. Frith, T. Cooke, and W. Millington, all of whom had worked so energetically as secretaries. The motion having been unanimously carried, Mr. J. D. Jones returned thanks on behalf of his fellow secre- taries and himself for the kind ackn )wle dgment of their services.

Suhsecpeatly the whole party made their way back to Frodshatn station headed by the band. E t!:b before leaving the grounds, was presented with a bun. On arrival at the station they hoarded the train and reached Runcorn at about 8•30. • They then repaired to the back of the M ',Hut place where cheer after cheer was raised for their benefactors after which they dis- persed to I,heir several dotniciles.
