div.head: VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLESTOWN.
div.p: VIADUCT INSTITUTE, EARLESTOWN.
ANNUAL lIEEIING.

The 25t1 annual general meeting of the members of this Institute was held in tt e large reading room on Wednesday evening. There was a large attend- ance of members—Mr. J. W. Emmett presided, and he was supported on the platform by Messrs. C. W. Emmett, D. Barcroft, Joseph Emmett, J. Edwards, J. Smith, and T. Ormand (secretary). All the members having been supplied with the printed statement of accounts, Mr. W. Gilmour moved and Mr. R. Eaton seconded that it should be taken as read, which was carried.—Mr. Gilmour said there was an item in the balance sheet which he had not seen there before It was in the general accounts, and was £8 15s. 7d. "Committee men out of pocket." He would not raise the question, but he had been asked about it several times. It had been said "you ask for subscriptions from the public to present various prizes, and for the first time there is an item in the balance sheet, showing that the committee men were taking nearly £9 away for expenses. There might perhaps be a ' satisfactory explanation, but he would rather see it put in some other way. Mr.W.Sutton said it looked rather suggestive, the item of expenses out of pocket for committee men. He understood there was no distribution of prizes at Horwich. The Chairman said it was quite true they did not go to any distribution of prizes at Horwich, they went there as he understood to see if they could pick up any- thing that would be of service to their Institute, and in order to see whether they were up to the times or not. If they found anything that they were lacking, no doubt , they reported to the Committee, and the deputation ' would perhaps be able to give a good account of them- selves to the General Committee. With regard to the item of £8 15s. 7d., he might tell them that it was only thought fair that some expenses should be allowed the Committee. Last year the Committee were invited to attend the distribution of prizes at Wolverton. Previ- ously they had borne their own expenses, and they did not feel they were justified in putting their hands into their pockets, to bear the expenses any longer, and they thought it was only fair some expenses should be al- lowed them, and he believed the Committee voted a cer- tain amount for the expenses of these who attended the distribution of prizes, and the same remarks applied to Crewe, and it amounted to about 3s. 81. per head for visiting these places. In former years, the balance sheet had not been drawn out quite as accurately, as in the current year. In the previous balance sheets there was an item of sundry expenses, which he need not say much shout. Perhaps some of the expenses might be included in that item, and their Secretary thought it only fair that every item should be shown as it was ex- pended. He (the chairman) considered it only fair, as lots of things could be put in sundries which some would rather not see, and it was for them to say whether the Committee were worth the expense they had incurred. He would advise them to be liberal with the Committee in the trifling expense they incurred, which only amounted to 3s. BJ. per head. Mr. Gilmour said the reason he put the question was because mazy of the members knew he had been on the committee, and he had been both to Wolverton and Crewe, and whatever expense he incurred, he never received a halfpenny from the Institute. It was con- sidered an honour for anyone to be invited to Wolverton or Crewe, to see the distribution of prizes, and he thought it would injure them as an Institute, to see the item put in the balance sheet in this way. It had already been put to him that their committee were tak- ing the money for expenses to go pleasuring. He did not want to-do away with these kind of visits, as it tended to cement the Institutes, but there was no neces- sity for any out of pocket expenses for the committee. The Chairman did not quite agree with Mr. Gilmour with regard to out of pocket expenses. They lived in an age of progression and liberality, and he thought the Institute could afford such a small amount once a year in this way. He was in their hands, however, and if they said the committee were not to have it, they would not get it. Mr. W. Davies agreed that the friendly intercourse between the Institutes should be maintained, but did not think the committee should go and represent that Institute, and pay all their own expenses. Mr. W. Sutton was quite satisfied with the explanation but he thought the meeting should pass a resolution how much the committee should have. He never knew of a Society where the committee voted its own expenses, he thought the general meeting should vote a certain amount to the committee, and then it would take the responsibility off the committee. He concluded by mov- ing that the committee receive £lO per year for their expenses, which Mr. J. Bircroft seconded. The Chairman said there was a minute on the books that each man should receive 53. for every visit he made to Wolverton, Crewe or Rugby. Mr. Gilmour thought the motion of Mr. Sutton would be going to extremes, and thought 23. 6J. per head wculd be ample, and that the expenses should only be paid to bona-fide members of the committee. - Mr. J. Gee moved as an amendment that each com- mittee man be allowed 53. per visit for attending the prize distributions at Wolverton, Crewe or Rugby. Mr. R. Eaton seconded, and the amendment was carried. The Secretary then read the report of the committee, which was as follows : "In accordance with our usual custom we have the pleasure to submit for your consideration an eoitome of ' the work accomplished during the year to the 30th June last. But whilst doing so we are reminded that this is our 25th annual report, and marks an epoch in our existence. With an experience such a term of li!e gives, it is at times necessary to ask whether we are accom- plishing all that might fairly be expected from those whose ideas are cosmopolitan and whose principles are based on a deep and bread foundation. During the quarter of a century that this work has been going on many changes have taken place,but it is with more than ordinary satisfaction that we record the fact that the President, who listenesl t) the first annual report, is still the President, and is spured to be with us when the 25th annual report is read. He is here not only in his official capacity. but because his heart and soul are in the work we, as your representatives, are pledged to carry out, namely, the mental, moral, and physical development of the members who place us in office. We can assure you that to faithfully and impartially perform those duties to the satisfaction of some 1,200 members is not only a most onerous work, but one of great responsibi- lity. We would not, however, for one nsoment attempt to shirk that responsibility,for we believe that the majo- rity of yotnalthough at times perhaps not agreeing with everything we do. are assured that all is done which can be to consolidate the educational influonce it is our pleasurable duty to know is attached to this Institute. In the statement of accounts, a copy of which has been supplied to each memt-er, we have given such explana- tion for receipts and expenditure as would, we think, warrant our passing it by without comment. We cannot, however, do so for two reasons. The first of which is that our receipts from visitors' fees are £7 less than for the year ending June, 1893. co ask for an explanation for such a decrease is natural,but not far to seek, as the wet Saturdays we suffered from at the commencement of the season militated against good gates, and affected our finances come little, but more particularly those of the Cricket club, to whom as you are aware, we give two thirds of all visitors' fees. Secondly, you will no doubt have observed that the receipts from the bowling greens are steadily increasing. In 1892, they were £l4 ss. 51.4893, £l9 3s 10q-1., 1891, £25 189. 114. The interest which is taken in these laudable excitements is a source of considerable gratification to your committee as they are strong exponents of the doctrine of muscu- lar christianity ;in fact physical and mental develop- ment overlap each other to such an extent that to attempt to disintegrate them would be to wreck that which you are most anxious to obtsin, a sound and well developed mind in a strong and healthy body. Before , dealtstg with the examination results, the majority of , which are now to hand, it is our duty to explain that the department of Science and Art, after strong pressure , being brought to bear upon them by a large number of educational bodies, with respect to the injustice they were unwittingly doing to many capable students, by raising the standard in the Elementary stage, of the science subjects particularly, and failing those ca ndi- • dates, no matter how near they might be of the number ' of marks required for an elementary pass, have modifies] their regulations to this extent ;in th elementary stage , the candidates are recorded under three categories " pass,'" " fair " or "fail." To secure a pass,6o per cent ,is required of the marks obtainable. The student who obtains more than 40 par cent, but less than 60 per cent , will -be recorded as " fair." No grant, however, is paid for those students who only obtain " fair " but it is eminently satisfactory and encouraging to a candidate to know that although he did not obt tin a first in the elementary stage, yet his paper was a fair one and did not come under that much hated word " fail." The department however, still enforced a fine for thes:, stu- dents who do not obtain 25 per cent of the number of mark; required.

Laundry 12 examined all passed.—Dressmaking 15 examined 14 passed.—Needlework, E, 2 examined 2 passed, needlework intermediate, 1 examined 1 passed, sick nursing 8 examined all passed. Cricket. —From the commencement of the cricketing season up to date, 26 matches have been played by the Ist and 2nd teams, of which 13 have been won, 5 drawn and 8 lost, which compares very favourably with last year's records, as the clubs they met are stronger and consequently to be occasionally beaten is no disgrace.— Bowls.—The Secretary of the bowling club informs us that at present they occupy the third position in the competition for the Legh Challenge Cup, having won 4 of the 6 matches played, a most creditable performance when you consider the quality of the clubs played against. For a number of years the arrangement and classifica- tion of the books in the library was anything but satis- factory, and as a great number of new books have been added each year for several years, the old catalogue was almost, if not practically, useless, as it did not contain much over one half of the volumes we now possess. Your committee therefore decided to have all the books renumbered, properly classified, and a catalogue based on the best modern principles, prepared, and instructed the Librarian and Secretary to compile such a catalogue. They commenced to do so at the beginning of March, and after a long and arduous task, for the whole of the work had to be done in the evenings, it is our pleasure to announce, that it is in the hands of the printer, who hopes in the course of a few weeks to have it ready for issue. An approximate idea of the labour involved in its compilation may be gathered from the fact that it will take at least eight weeks to print it. To facilitate the use of the books they are arranged in six classes via :—A, Theology and Philosophy, B, History, Biography, Voyages and Travels, C, Poetry, and the Drama, D, Law, Science, Art and Technology, E, Miscel- laneous Literature, F, Fiction. Each book is entered under the name of the author and also under the title, and if a work has any particular reference to a special subject, under the name of that subject also. If the reader knows the name of the author of the book he wants, he will turn to that name, and at once see all the books of that particular author we have in the library, or if the title only is known he will find it under that head. In conclusion everything has been done to render the books as accessible, and as acceptable as possible, and if the new catalogue adds to the pleasure of the reader, and increases the number of borrowers thel committee will be well repaid." 1 The Chairman said they would agree with him that the report they had just heard read, was a capital one,l and it was satisfactory to hear that there had been such a large increase of passes for last year. It only showed that their young men who were attending the classes could obtain passes, and first class passes too, if they only studied a little better than they had done in previ- ous years. (Hear, hear.) At all their prize distributions he had tried to get them up to that mark, as much as possible, and he was glad to hear that there was such a large increase in percentage of passes. With regard to what their secretary said about their 25th annual meet- ing, he must confess, until the secretary reminded him of it, he was not aware that the Institute had been going for a quarter of a century. He had no doubt some of them in that room would remember their begin- ning. They began by having penny readings, and they were remarkably well attended, and they had not only readings, but concerts also, and Alec Skeen° was one of the first artistes they had, and he not only did good ser- vice as an artiste, but in various other was s. Since that time there had been a good many changes,not alone with regard to what had been accomplished. He sin- cerely trusted that the advancement which had been made during the past 25 years might be still improved, until another 25 years had been passed over. (Hear, hear.) They tried as far as they possibly could, in con- nection with that Institute to keep up with the times, if not abreast of them, and he hoped the Committee would continue to do so, as long as he had the honour of being president. (Applause.) - Mr. Gilmour endorsed the remarks of the Chairman, nnd moved a vote of thanks to the Secretary for his valuable report, which was accorded.

div.head: ELECTION OF COMMITTEE.
div.p: ELECTION OF COMMITTEE.

- The Chairman then read out the result of the ballot for the election of six members of the Committee, which was as foilows :—T. Ormand 658, H. Bailey 656, J. Emmett 602, J. Barr 514, D. Barcroft 511, W. Crawford 336.
The followinz were nominated hut were unsuleessful, J. Whitman 353, B. Harrison 337, G. Goff, 293, J. Jud- son 263, F. Forster 261.
AUDITORS.
Messrs. Sephton and Graham were re-elected auditors Messrs. J. Gee and W. Clare jun., were re-elected scru- tineers for the ballot of 1895.

Mr. W. Sutton brought forward a suggestion affecting the bowlers, to the effect that seeing No. 1 and No. 2 greens brought to the funds of the Institute £24 183. 1-1 d he thought it would be only courteous on the part of the Committee to give a prize to these two greens, to be bowled for, say of the value of 303. or £2. Mr. J. Gee disagreed with the suggestion, and thought No. 3 green was as mucii entitled to a prize as N. 1 and 2, as those playing on No. 3 green were as much mem- bers of the Institute as those on the other greens. _ _

Mr. Gilmour thought it would be much better if the question was left in the hands of the Committee. The Chairman considered if a priz3 was given, the players on number 3 green should participate. He had no doubt the committee would take the matter into their consideration and decide upon it. Mr. W. Sutton raised the question with regard to the recreation grounds being used for charitable purposes, and asked if the committee could not be vested with power, to make everyone, whether member or not, pay for admissson to the grounds,on such occasions. The Chairman said the committee had no power under the present rules to do as Mr. Sutton asked,and it would require a special meeting to alter the rules, which he did not think advisable. If there was a special Case in which it was thought the grounds should be engaged for a charitable matter, it should come to him as President, and he would deal with it on its merits. (Hear,hear.) A hearty vote,. of thanks was accorded the Chairman on the motion of Mr. Gilmour, seconded by Mr. J. Bar- croft.

Mr. Ormand in putting the vote sill it would have been a great mistake if they had dispersed without thanking the Chairman for his services at that meeting, and not only that meeting, but during the whole 25 years he had been with them. (ll,?ar, hear.) The Chairman, in acknowledging the vote,said so long as he was president he would try to do as much as he had done in the past for them.

div.p: A PRESENT FOR MR. GLADSTONE.

Mr. M‘Bride, of Buffalo, is at present in Dublin. He WAS the bearer to Mr. Gladstone of a beautiful album containing photographs of many of IrelincPs friends in ArnFrica, including President Cleveland and his entire Cabinet, all the justices of the Supreme Court, the gov- ernors of States, and others.

div.head: TETE COAL TRAM'.
div.p: TETE COAL TRAM'.
THE DISPUTE AT ASH TON'S-GREEN COLLIERY,
ST. HELENS.

Another lengthy conference between representatives of the miners and the management at Ashton's-green Colliery, St. Helens, t.)ok place on Wednesday, and this was followed by a priva,e meeting of miners at the Bull's Head Inn.—Mr. Glover, agent, in explaining the present position of affair?, said the negotiations at not made an proeres, and although they had been discuss- ing the prices in the Higher Delph Mine for four hours that afternoon, no settlement had been arrived at. He advised the men to make another offer,which was rather more conciliatory than the other,and this was ultimately agreed to. If this oriel' is not accep`ed, althottei the dispute only affects the men in the Higher Delph seam, the whale of the men will cease work on Monday night next.—Mr. Glover also addressed the miners on the 10 per ent.r,hluction settlement, and explained the matter fally.—A resolution wastarried unanimously approving of tne settlement.

div.head: UNWHOLESOME FISH.
div.p: UNWHOLESOME FISH.

Mr. 11. Norman, nuisance inspector,made a seizure of unwholesome fish on Saturday. .It was taken to the Town Hall,where it was examined by the Medi- cal Officer of Health, and Mr. Wright, J.P., and by order of the latter it was destroyed.

div.head: MORE POSTAL FACILITIES.
div.p: MORE POSTAL FACILITIES.

On Saturday a new letter box was fixed at the corner of Haydock-street and Lythgoes-lane, in th e premises of Messrs. Furness and Co. The box will be cleared at the usual times on week-days and at 8 p.m. on Sundays. A WARRINGTON MAN IN TROUBLE AT MANCHESTER.

At Strangeways, on Tuesday, Thomas Lowndes, sinker at Gorton, formerly of Warrington, was sent to prison for twenty-one days' hard labour for kick- ing and otherwise ill-treating his wife. Defendant was prepared to pay a fine, but Stipendiary Yates said that men who kicked their wives mu,t go to gaol. He granted the wife a separation order, and ordered the defendant to pay 10s. weekly towards her support. THE CLERGY DAUGHTERS' SCHOOL EXTENSION. The work connected with the extension of the clergy institutions is proceeding briskly under the direction of Mr. Joseph Dolan, builder, Cockh edge, the contractor. Ihe stone work has been let to Mr. Ephraim Aukland, Froghall-lane, and men are busily engaged in making the' alterations at the Mount School. When the additions and alterations have been completed, the work of the college will be considerably facilitated.

div.head: LOCAL SUCCESSES.
div.p: LOCAL SUCCESSES.

Arthur Beech (Tabley) and Walter Williamson (Manchester) pupils at the Knutsford Heath Side Collegiate School, headmaster Dr. Greenwood, M.A., passed successfully in special subjects, at the College of Preceptor 3 examination, held at Manchester in June last.—The following pupils have successfully passed the recent examination of the London Col- lege of Music, at the Liverpool centre :—Practical pianoforte, Julia E. Pigot; advanced senior with honours; L. M. Mullard, senior; Winifred S. Hay- ward and M. Florence Rowe, intermediate; Rose Mainwaring, preliminary.—ln the list, just pub- lished, of the successful candidates at the recent matriculation examination (London University),the name of Mr. T. Y. Zeal, who for years was engaged at the Orford Day Schools, appears in the first divi- sion. Whil,t he was at Orford Mr. Zeal was Placed high in the first class at the Queen's scholarship examination, and entered as a student at the Exeter Training College, where he soon distin- guished himself. Mr. Zeal was for a long period a pupil of Mr. John Cann, headmaster of Orford Schools.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF A WOMAN.

An inqu;s-t-s-%-rii-s-he-l-d--iii-tbe Parade room at the Police Station on Tuesday by Mr. F. A. Jones touch- ing the death of Sarah Taylor, a widow, 44 years of age, of 9, Heaton-at., who died rather suddenly on Monday morning.—Sarah Ellen Taylor, daughter of the deceased, stated that the deceased was the widow of Joseph Taylor, ex-police constable. She had been suffering for a long time from a bad leg, and on Friday last she complained of having fallen. Dr. Hall was called in early on Monday morning, and she died about seven o'clock the same morning. Mary Smith, a neighbour, doposed that the deceased told her that she hurt herself by falling in the yard. A letter was read from Dr. Hall who attributed death to heart disease, but to what extent it was accelerated by the fall he was not prepared to say, A verdict of death from heart disease was returned. the jury being of the opinion that death was accelerated by the accident.

div.head: SALE OF WORK AT THE RECTORY.
div.p: THE SALE OF WORK AT THE RECTORY.

The sale which had been opened on the previous Thursday in aid of St George's Mission on Satur- day was re-openei by Mrs. Beamont. The Rector, said that on Thursday £lOO was cleared. (Applause) He did not think that the building of the mission had proved expensive. They had in Mr. Thurston one who would work efficiently and with energy. Ile wished particularly to thank the donors of small sums, and also the buyers of Thursday. His thanks were also due to the workers. He mentioned Mr. Fairclough and Mr. A. Woods as very representative helpers. Mrs. Beamont,he might say, had purposely remained in Warrington in order to open the sale. (Applause.) —Mrs. Beamont, in declaring the sale open said she had always taken an interest in St. George's Mission.—The Rev. G. B. Thurston having proposed a vote of thanks to Mrs. Beamont for her attendance and services, it was heartily carried,and the sale was resumed.—During the afternoon and evening,performances were given by the Bank-street Ministrels, and a Maypole dance formed an attrac- tive feature. In the evening the grounds were again illuminated with fairy lamps. The amount realized by the day's sale was £lO5, this making a total for the two days of .£205, exclusive, of course, of sundry necessary expenses.

div.head: MUSIC IN THE PARK.
div.p: MUSIC IN THE PARK.

The bandstand in the Park was occupied on Tues- day by Mr. T. J. Down's military band who played the following selection :—March," Hoch Habsburg," Kral; overture, "Poet and Peasant," Suppe ; valse, " The Old Lock," Lamotte ; selection, "The Daughter of the Regiment," Donizetti ; lancers, " 'Talk o' the Night," Williams; Gavotte," Immer ieder," Vandervell ; Nautical Fastasia, "A Voyage in a troopship," Miller; Chorus, " Hallelujah," Handel ; " God save the Queen." The weather was not vety favourable but notwithstanding there was a large number of spectators who much enjoyed the excellent rendering of the various pieces. As the audience was dispersing, Mr. William Diggle, mounting the steps of the stand, proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Down and his band for their services, which, he felt sure,were appreciated by an audience consisting of trom 4,000 to 5,000 persons.—Coun- cillor James Hill seconded the motion, observing that the best thanks of the audience were due not only to Mr. Down, but to his talented daughter and to the members of the band, and he hoped they would soon have the pleasure of listening to them a4ain. The motion was carried by acclamationsbut Mr. Down was engaged on the other side of the bandstand, and not hearing what had been said, he did not therefore,return thanks for the compliment which had been paid to him and his band.

REINSTATEMENT OF THE WARRINGTON POLO

PLANERS. On Saturday a meeting of the Northern Counties Executive of the Swimming Association was held, at the Reform Club, Liverpool. The chief item on the agenda paper was. the application for re-instate- ment of the iVarrington polo team, who were sus- pended through playing Fair Turner in a polo match against the Liverpool Diamond Ton the 27th June at Warrington. It is alleged that Turner on the 27th April last wrestled with T. Cannon, a professional wrestler, for a money prize in the People', Palace, St. Helens, and in so doing forfeited 'Ais amateur status. The club, though warned by Mr. Barker, the secretary to the usociation, per- isted in playing Turner in the match, under pro- test, and on the matter being brought before the executive, the whole of the team were suspended from participating in any league matches. The Athletic Association in the meantime had been acquainted with the facts of the case, and the affair was simply ridiculed by that body, and Turner promptly reinstated as an amateur. On Saturday evening, a deputation, including Turner and the whole of the Warrington team, attended the meet- ing at Liverpool, and explained the circumstances under which the local captain was placed. An apology was tendered and accepted hy the execu- tive. It was eventually decided to reinstate the whole of the team from Monday.

An opet;--air meeting was held on Sunday even- ing, by the members ot" the Warrington Gospel Temperance Mission, on the open space behind the British Workman C ,flee Tavern, Bewsey-st. Mr. John Drury, in opening the proceedings, made a ,t rung appeal to workingmen to stem the evils of strong drii•k. Mr. Adam florrocks stated that, the drink traffie was the greatest cmse to the nation, to the tiorm- of the nation, and especially to the helpless children. lie pointed out that each habit- ual drinker drank in a lifetime 300 barrels of strong drink, which, if rained at £2 each, would amount to £6OO, and then they died paupers, leaving their families in distress and a burden to sober, industri- oo., peoph.. Mr.R.Storey,in an interesting address, said ,trike.s see developing into riots, revolu- tion was in the air, and Parliament was sitting on a safety valve. They tied up the land, they drove the peoplu from•the country into cities, and they licensed 128,000 public-houses to demoralize the population. Mr, H. Taylor, P.C.M., also addressed the !nutting.

div.head: PARR'S BANKING CO , AND ALLIANCE BANK LIMITED.
div.p: PARR'S BANKING CO , AND ALLIANCE BANK LIMITED.
MEETING OF SHAREHOLDERS.

An extraordinary general meeting of shareholders of Parr's Banking Co., and Alliance Bank, Limited, was held on Thursday, at the Bank, Winwick-street, to declare dividends and other business. The chair was occupied by Mr. A. Turner, and the following directors were present : Sir T. G. Frost, Messrs. J. Dun ( managing director),N. Ffarrington Eckerslev, A. J. Fraser, Colonel Gamble, C. 8., A. Hewlett, G. McCorquodale,H. Warren Meade-King,and P. Stubs, in athlition to the following shareholders: Dr. White Dr. R. T. Morris, Dr, Beaman, Messrs. Rowland Young, H. Dean, J. C. Stead, J. High field, J. Robin- son, E. C. Turner, R. A. Farrington, J. A. McGregor, R. Crain, J. R. Buckton, J. C. Parr, T. Handley, Arthur Sinclair, Wm. Silcock, John Murray, E, Gas- kell Davies, Wm. Booth, and C. T. Whitley. After the notice convening the meeting had been read by Mr. John Dun, the CHAIRMAN said that it was very gratifying to the directors in meeting once again in their old headquarters to be able to present a report which was so very satisfactory. They had heard how ready dis- count and interest—the two chief sources which supplied the profit to banks—were so unprecedentedly low, that it had been a great difficulty to find employment for the money. Under those circumstances, they had been able to provide the usual dividend at the usual interest, and to carry forward the sum of £34,600 to the next account. This was a fact upon which they might congratulate themselves. (Hear, hear.) It showed that their business had been increasing, and their reserve fund strengthened, and the present position of the bank was in every way satisfactory. In these somewhat gloomy times, they had to report more profits, more share- holders, and many more customers than ever they had on any previous return, which augured well when the good times came back—as come they would he was cer- tain. They would like to see good harvests secured,and a satisfactory arrangement of foreign tariffs. If that took place, they would soon see a general return to con- fidence and awakening of commerce and enterprise which had been paralysed since the great failings of the Barings and other large companies. In the purchase of the bank of Sir Samuel Scott, Bent and Co.. Cavendish Square, London, they had secured an excellent and high class business in the west end of London, and in that of Messrs. Shrubsole and Co., Kingston-on-Thames, they had a profitable opening in what was looked upon as one of the I leading suburbs of the metropolis. By those trans- actions, they were increasing the stability of the bank. In the acquisition of those banks, and in other amalga- mations they had every reason to congratulate them- selves. There was one thing, however, that they must drop. He was not fond of retrograde movements, but it was at the suggestion of some of their customers that they thought of curtailing their name. (Hear,hear, and laughter.) " Parr's Banking Company and Alliance Bank Limited" was a mouthful to pronounce, and a labour to write,and they hoped at no distant date to ask the consent of the shareholders to curtail that long title. (Applause.) The name of Parr was now nearly as familiar, well-known, and respected in the metropolis as it had long been in Warrington. (Applause). He was sure that that announcement would be satisfactory to everyone present in that room. (Applause.) Before sitting down he must allude to the death of the oldest member of the Board—Sir Gilbert Greenall.His was a name which Warrington had loved to honour, a name which had been associated with that of Parr for many years, a gentleman any bank might be proud to have on its directorate. His almost patriarchial age prevented latterly his attending their meetings, but they would never forget his genial presence and his courtly manner. While sympathising with his family in their bereave- ment, he wished to express the director's extreme regret at their own loss. He concluded by proposing that the report (a eopy of which appeared in our last issue) now furnished,be adopted,aed that a dividend of 19 per cent. per annum,! tee from income tax be now declared for the quarters ending June and September. Colonel GAMBLE C.B. seconded the adoption of the report. He regretted the absence of Mr. Cecil Parr, but he hoped that he was enjoying the holiday he had so well earned. He had great pleasure in reading the re- port, and he hoped that they would be able to retain the same dividend next year.. _ _

The resolution was carried unanimously. Mr. A. J. FRASER moved that the election of Sir Horace B. T.Farquhar,Bart.,as a director be confirmed. He did not think, after the remarks by the Chairman,he need say anything about the business of Sir Samuel Scott, because it was a business which they had every ' reason to believe would continue to be successful. Sir Horace was the leading spirit in the bank, and it would be a great advantage to retain his interest, if not his active services. He would be of great advantage as a general adviser to the Board. Mr. J. R. BIICSTON seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. Mr. J. CHARLTON PARR moved a vote of thanks to the directors who had served them during the past half- year. He had great pleasure in doing so, as they in- , curred great responsibilities, and those responsibilities must increase every year. There were many millions lying idle which under other circumstances might be employed advantageously and profitably. He hopcd the directors would continue to be able to recommend them to declare their usual handsome dividend, and at the same time, in the words of the report, to be able to say that the "position and prospects of the business con- tinue to be in every way satisfactory." Dr. WHITE in seconding the motion expressed his plea- sure at seeing Mr. Parr present that day. , The motion was carried unanimously. The CHAIRMAN replying on behalf of the directors said his work had been considerably lightened by the aid from his fellow-directors. Colonel MCCORQUODALE moved that a vote of thanks be given to the general manager,the managers,the secre- tary and other officers for their services during the past half year. He said that he had no hesitation in believing that they would thoroughly approve of the resolution. During the last year or two, they had had unsettled trade which of course affected banks very materially owing to so much money lying idle. If the officials' services were so valuable in good times, they were much more so now that the clouds were thickly about the horizon. In treublous times, the officials had even more care, and needed more discretion and judgment, and he believed that for the prosperity of the bank it was essen- ' tial to have good men in the various departments, in the head office in London, and in the various branches. He firmly believed that they had those good men with them. _ _ .

Mr.E. C. TURNER seconded the motion which was carried unanimously. Mr. Jourr Dux acknowledged the vote on his own behalf and on behalf of the other employees of the bank. During the last half- year. and especially during the last quarter, he said, there had been times in which it was difficult indeed to makemuch of the bank's money,and now they had to get a larger reserve fund. Mr. ARTHUR SiNcLeta moved a vote of thanks to the Chairman for presiding that day. He was glad to hear that the long name of the bank was to be cut down. He considered that the bank had a most able chairman in
Mr. Turner. Mr. H. DEAN seconded the motion which was unani- mously carried, and after Mr. Turner had replied, the meeting terminated.

div.head: HA.YDOCK COTTAGE HOSPITAL.
div.p: HA.YDOCK COTTAGE HOSPITAL.

The annual report and statement of accounts of the above hospital had just come to hand, and we extract the following from it :—" In submitting the eleventh annual report of the llaydock Cottage Hospital to the subscribers and friends of the Institution. the Committee have the pleasure of re'cording another year ot continued usefulness and progress. Sincere thanks are rendered to the friends who have so far generously assisted the ordinary and special funds. The recreation ground has been a great boon to the patients, adding to their comfort and pleasure, and hastening their recovery. It has been tastefully laid out, with a large central grass plot, and the borders planted with a good selection of trees and shrubs. In order to make it complete, some kind of rustic arbour is desired, but owing to shortness of funds the committee, do not, at present, see their way to supply this. They,therefore, venturO to appeal for special aid towards this object. Owing to the strike—when the ordinary income entirely ceased—the funds have fallen somewhat behind. Finan- cial help would be gladly welcomed. The Committee desire to recognise the disinterested and entirely volun- tary services, during another year, of its honorary officials, and the Committee desire to make g,i ate- ful acknowledgments to the donors of 9:if:s." The report of the hon. medical officer, Mr. T. E:nost Hayward, M.8.,F.R.C.5., shows that the finnalaer of patients under treatment during the year was 74 [pales, 9 females, total 83. Discharged recovered, 60; relieved, 12; died 4 ; remaining in hospital 7 ; total 83. The 78 new cases admitted during the year classified are as follows :—Cases of accidental injury to employees of Messrs. Richard Evans apd Co., Limited, at their col- lieries or works 46, cases of accidental injury to em- ployees of Messrs. S. W. Pilling and Co., on the Liver- pool, St. Helens, ard South Lancashire Railway-. 5, other cam s requiring surgical treatment 15, other cases reqiiiiing medical treatment, 12, total 78. Grateful acknowledgment is made of help received on several occasions from J. W. Watkins, Esq., 11,1. D., and Harold E. Watkins,Esq., L.R.C.P. (Lond.) and M.R.C.S. (Eng.). of Newton-le-Willows ; and also of the assistance rendered byJ. B. Naden, Esq., L.R C.P. (Loud.) and M.R.C.S. (Eng.) formerly of Haydock, and now of War- rington; and by S. E. Rossiter, Esq., L.R.C.P. and S. ), &c., of Haydock.

div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT ON THE CHESHIRE
LINES RAILWAY.

KNOCKED DOWN BY AN EXPRESS TRAIN. On Saturday night on the arrival at the Warring- ton Central Station of the null to Liverpgoi express, the officials were surprised to find a skirt and other portions of a woman's dress on the engine. The driver knew nothing about them, an there were no marks of blood, but it was otherwise clear that the clothing had been torn violently from the wearer. MQney and other articles were in Ur pocket. Inquiries were at once instituted, and later la- the evening it was ascertained that a woman had been knocked down between Cadishead and Partington, an that she was alive, and was being medically attended in her own house. On Sunday, the injured woman '915 conveyed to the Warrington Infirmary. Her name is Ann Taylor, aged forty-two, wife of a platelayer at Part- ington. She stated that she and her daughter were returning home along the railway from market, and that she knew nothing more of the occurrence than that he train knocked her down. She sustained severe injuries. receiving a fracture of her right leg and various lacerated wounds, from which she died on Thursday afternoon at five o'clock. The express, which was on an incline, was going at about fifty-five miles an hour at the time of the occurrence. The whole of Mrs. Taylor's dress and the underskirt were torn from her body. The deceased had a daughter named Mrs. Clark, residing in Knutsford- road, Warrington. An inquest will be held to-day (Saturday).

div.head: HALTON.
div.p: HALTON.

WESLEYAN BAND OF Hoek] OUTING.-011 Saturday afternoon the members of this society and their friends had their annual picnic to Overton Hills. Horses and lurries for the conveyance of the children were kindly lent by the following farmers :—Messrs. Jno. and James W. Baguley, J. Clarke, and J. Astbury ; while a four-m- -hand for the adults was supplied by Messrs. Booth and Sons of Runcorn. An excellent tea was provided at the Mersey View pleasure grounds; the number partaking of it being 110 children and 64 adults. The weather was rather threatening but beyond a heavy shower about five o'clock, which only lasted a few minutes, it did not interfere with the pleasure of the party, who enjoyed themselves immensely, and arrived home about nine Alock. Great credit is due to the society's officerS, who strove in such an energetic manner to make the trip a success.

DRAWING EXAMINATION.—The result of the drawing examination held in connection with the technical classes has just lnen received. Seven candidates sat, two of whom obtained positions in the second class, the others falling to satisfy the examiners, The results of the examinations generally have been far from satisfac- tory, and in consequence of this it is thought that the classes will be discontinued.

Houghton (chairman), S.-Davies, Effillin,g, G. Rat- cliffe, A. J. Jolley, A. Jolley, R. Heater], W. J.Shaw,. Clark, J. Hill, Smith, IV. Brilharry, Hi J`.. Longton, Mather, Dr. Patterson, J. C. SCHOOL COMMITTEE:• This committee recommended that Miss Miry Lee be appointed supernumary officer at the salary of £lB-per annum with rations, &a. ; also that Mr. lI.M. Mines, the superintendent be granted 14 days' holiday. They also acknowleged the receipt of a basket of currant bread from the Rev. Father Duggan of Warrington.—Mr. HEATON : Has the doctor allowed it ? (Laughter.)—Mr. Honaarox : Children like currant bread.—Mr. HEATON : It is very good if they do not have too much of it. (Laughter.)—The minutes were confirmed. COST OF LUNATICS.' A letter was read from the Chester Count' Asylum, stating that the cost of lunatics would be 7s. per head per week, which was a slight reduction on previous charges. EXAMINER'S REPORT.' The CLERK said that a satisfactory report had been received from Mr. Mozley, H.M. Inspector .of poor law schools. The report was dated April 1.3,',1894,,t and stated that religious knowledge was very fair, spelling good, reading good, penmanship good, arithmetic good, reading good, industrial skill very fair, state of school good, skill of teachers very fair. MISS WARD'S REMUNERATION: ' Toe CLERK reported that a certificate of probation first division, had been granted to Miss Ward, a remunera- tion was ordered to be given to her of £22 Bs:per annum. THE RECENT COUNTY COUNCIL INQUIRY:. A petition was sealed and sent to the Local Government Board with respect to the decision of the County Council to separate Grappenhall, Tnelwall, and extra municipal Latchford from the Warrington Union. Messrs. Shaw and Pilling will have charge of the petition. This was all the public business.
